- `parse_id` returns `Cow<str>`: borrowed when the id is unquoted (the common case), owned only
  when unescaping. It currently calls `raw.to_string()` unconditionally. NOTE this is worth
  nothing on its own — `GraphData` owns its strings, so the allocation is merely moved, not
  removed. It only pays off behind the streaming path, which is why no partial version of this
  change is worth shipping.
- `csv` gets the same treatment afterwards, and then `decstream.rs`'s `_ => None` arm is empty
  and every format streams both ways.

### A third normalization, and a third row ruled out

`decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` has the largest absolute numbers in the table (ts 2801ms, ffi
737ms) and the worst MB/ms of anything (0.028), which looks alarming until the right denominator
is used. That row carries 200,000 nodes AND 1,000,000 edges, so per ELEMENT it is 614ns against
the nodes-only row's 577ns. Edge ingest resolves two endpoints per edge; it is doing more work
per byte by construction. Not an anomaly — and bytes are the wrong unit whenever the element mix
changes, just as the engine ratio was the wrong unit in item 101.

## 103. pg-text now decodes straight into the store (2026-10-04)

Item 102's located target, built. pg-text was one of two formats (with csv) that had no
streaming decoder, so `deserialize` materialized a whole owned `GraphData` and rebuilt the store
from it — on a 9 MB / 200,000-node document the parse was 45.7ms, `from_graph_data` 65.4ms, the
whole decode 115.6ms.

| `decode pg-text` (ffi), min of three |                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------: |
| before                               |                                110.8ms |
| after                                |                     **77.2ms** — 1.44x |
| throughput                           | 0.083 → 0.119 MB/ms (pg-json is 0.176) |

Short of the ~2.3x the bridge's share suggested, and the reason is worth keeping: the
`StoreSink` still does the insertion work `from_graph_data` used to do. What the change removes
is the `GraphData` in the middle — the owned `Vec<Node>` with its per-node `String` id,
`Vec<String>` labels and `Vec<(String, Value)>` props — not the store building.

### One parser, two adapters

The tempting shape is a second borrowed parser beside the owned one. That would be two
implementations of one grammar that can drift apart, which is the divergence class the
byte-identity fuzzers exist to catch. Instead the grammar is parsed ONCE into `CowVal<'a>` —
strings as `Cow<'a, str>` — and the two forms are adapters over it:

- `CowVal::into_value()` → the owned `Value`, for `decode`;
- `CowVal::as_decval()` → the borrowed `DecVal`, for `decode_into`.

Borrowing is the common case and that is the point: **`unescape` is the IDENTITY on a body with
no backslash**, so `unescape_cow` borrows a quoted token that has no escape, and an unquoted one
always borrows. Only a genuine escape allocates.

`GraphSink::node` takes `props: &[(&str, DecVal<'_>)]` with a lifetime independent of the input,
which is what makes this legal: the borrowed views point either at `input` or at the
`Cow::Owned` strings held in two locals that are complete before any reference into them is
taken and that outlive the sink call. Nothing is cloned to make the call.

### Teeth — and the differential test is blind to half of it

| mutant                                                         | caught by                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `as_decval` swaps a temporal's `tag` and `iso`                 | `streaming_pg_text_decode_matches_the_graphdata_path`                        |
| `unescape_cow` never unescapes                                 | `lenke-codec`'s `quoted_control_chars_round_trip` — **NOT** the differential |
| the edge branch takes `&tokens[1..]` instead of `&tokens[2..]` | nothing, and correctly so — see below                                        |

The second is the instructive one. Sharing one parser removes drift, but it also means a GRAMMAR
bug makes BOTH adapters equally wrong, so a streaming-vs-bridge differential goes green through
it: 901 engine tests passed under that mutant. **The differential guards the ADAPTERS; the
round-trip tests in `lenke-codec` guard the GRAMMAR.** Both crates have to be in a mutation run
for this file, which is the [[mutation-must-include-core]] rule applying to `lenke-codec` too.

The third is an EQUIVALENT mutant, not an uncaught one: a `to` endpoint is by definition an id
token (no unquoted colon), and `parse_labels_props` skips any token without a `key:` separator,
so including or excluding it cannot change the result for a valid document. Recorded rather than
chased, and no test was contrived for it.

### Still open

`csv` is now the only format on the bridge, for both directions, so `decstream.rs`'s
`_ => None` arm has one occupant left. And on the TS side `decode pg-text` is 559-669ms against
native's 77.2 — the ratio went from 5.12x to 7.24x because native moved, making the TypeScript
pg-text decoder the widest codec gap in the table.

## 104. The TS pg-text decoder allocated eleven times a node (2026-10-04)

Item 103 left the TypeScript pg-text decoder as the widest codec gap in the table — 559.6ms
against native's 77.2 (6-7x) — and the profile named the spot immediately rather than after two
wrong guesses, which is what going to `bun --cpu-prof` first buys.

| self-time, TS `decode pg-text` |    before |
| ------------------------------ | --------: |
| `parseLabelsAndProps`          | **29.9%** |
| `tokenizeLine`                 |     13.1% |
| `#commitProperties`            |      6.1% |
| `labels`                       |      5.8% |
| `parseScalar`                  |      5.6% |
| `parseId`                      |      3.0% |

About half the decode is the parser and about a quarter is graph building.

### The Map existed only for a case that is rare

`parseLabelsAndProps` collected into a `Map<string, PropertyValue[]>` and then unwrapped it in a
second loop. That is a Map per LINE plus a one-element array per PROPERTY plus the result object
— about eleven allocations a node on a three-property document — and all of it to handle
REPEATED keys, which is the exception.

It now writes straight into the result object, and a `Set` of promoted keys is allocated lazily,
only once a key actually repeats. `promoted` mirrors the Rust decoder's own list rather than
testing `Array.isArray`: a value that is already an array must not be appended to unless this
parser is what made it one. `parseScalar` cannot return an array today, so `Array.isArray` would
be sound — but only by that incidental fact, and the lazy `Set` costs nothing in the common case.

Key ORDER is unchanged. The old code's `Map` preserved insertion order, but it was unwrapped
into a `Record` at the end, and a JS object orders integer-like keys first regardless — so the
final object was already subject to that, and writing directly into it changes nothing.

### And the unescape regex ran on every quoted token

`body.replace(/\\(.)/g, …)` scans the whole string even when it cannot match, and an escape is
the exception: every quoted id, key and value in a document paid for the scan. `unescapeBody`
guards it with `body.includes('\\')` — the same identity the Rust decoder relies on. `parseScalar`
halved, 5.6% → 2.7%.

| `decode pg-text` (ts), min of three |                     |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------------: |
| before                              |             559.6ms |
| after                               | **479.0ms** — 1.17x |
| ratio to native                     |       7.24x → 6.21x |

### Teeth

| mutant                                                                    | caught by                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| promotion never recorded, so a third repeat re-wraps instead of appending | `repeated keys decode to a list…`, the 300-seed round-trip, and both streaming tests                               |
| a repeated key overwrites instead of listing                              | the same four                                                                                                      |
| `unescapeBody` never unescapes                                            | **a hardening test** — `a label or key containing a newline cannot forge a new element on decode`, plus two others |

The third is the one worth noting: dropping the unescape is not merely a wrong value, it is an
element-forgery vector, because an unescaped newline inside a label or key would split the line.
That test existed already and is exactly the right net for this change.

### What is left in that decoder

`parseLabelsAndProps` is still 25.1% of a now-smaller total: the remaining cost is two
`token.slice` allocations per property, which `parseId`/`parseScalar` need as substrings —
removing them means passing offsets instead, a more invasive change. `tokenizeLine` is 15.0%
and untouched.

## 105. The biggest cost in TS edge ingest is not the double lookup (2026-10-04)

`decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` is the largest absolute number in the cross-engine table — ts
2801ms — and NDJSON is the primary snapshot/reload format, so it is where TypeScript users
actually spend time. The profile found a textbook target immediately:

| self-time, TS NDJSON decode of 200,000 nodes + 1,000,000 edges |           |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| **`indexEdgeLabel`**                                           | **22.7%** |
| `JSON.parse`                                                   |     17.3% |
| `getVertexById`                                                |     11.3% |
| `labels`                                                       |      8.1% |
| `#commitProperties`                                            |      7.6% |
| `validateLabel`                                                |      6.5% |

`indexEdgeLabel` costing more than `JSON.parse` is a striking enough result to chase, and what
it does looks indefensible: it probes FIVE maps with `has` and then `get` — about ten hash
lookups an edge where five would do, several on a vertex-id STRING key. Over a million edges
that is ~5,000,000 redundant lookups. `indexVertexLabel` has the same shape.

### It is free money and it is not there

Collapsing every pair into one `get` with an undefined check, interleaved min of three with a
full rebuild each round:

| round | before |  after |
| ----- | -----: | -----: |
| 1     | 2845.9 | 2913.9 |
| 2     | 2893.0 | 2872.7 |
| 3     | 2766.1 | 2876.7 |

2766.1 against 2872.7 at the minimum — flat to marginally WORSE, inside a band that spans ~5%
for the same build. **REJECTED**, and recorded on `indexEdgeLabel` itself so the next reader
does not re-derive it.

The likely reason is that JSC caches the key's hash, so a `get` immediately after a `has` on the
same key is nearly free — the redundancy is real but it is not where the time goes. What that
function actually costs is the `Set`/`Map` INSERTIONS and the inner `Map`/`Set` allocated the
first time a vertex id is seen, neither of which the rewrite touched. A real win there means
changing the index SHAPE (one adjacency map per vertex instead of a nested map-of-label-to-set,
say), which is a data-structure change with its own correctness surface, not a lookup tweak.

This is the fourth rejected lever recorded in this pass, after the two `pull` layout levers and
the `Keyed`-wrapper bypass — and the second where the profile's hottest frame turned out not to
be actionable. A high self-time says where the program IS, not that the code there is wasteful.

### A flaky task, not a regression

`nx run-many -t test` failed once during this iteration and nx itself labelled
`@lenke/sync:test` a flaky task; the rerun passed. `packages/sync` was then run five times on
the changed tree and five times on a stashed baseline — 176 pass, 0 fail, ten for ten. Noted
rather than chased: nothing in `Graph.ts`'s indexers changes iteration order (the same `add`
calls in the same sequence), which is the only thing a sync test could notice.

## 106. `decode csv` was never measured, and it is the worst codec path (2026-10-04)

Item 103 left csv as the only format still on the engine's `GraphData` bridge in BOTH directions,
and item 101 measured its ENCODE side. Its decode side turned out to be absent from the
cross-engine bench entirely: `DECODABLE` listed `pg-json`, `graphson` and `pg-text` and stopped,
with no comment saying why. (`ndjson` is absent for a good reason — it has two dedicated decode
rows of its own.)

Adding it took one line, and the row works in both engines, so there was no hidden reason:

|              |      ts |     ffi | ts/ffi |
| ------------ | ------: | ------: | -----: |
| `decode csv` | 358.7ms | 135.8ms |  2.63x |

The ratio is unremarkable, which is exactly why it needed the other denominator. The csv document
for this fixture is 6.2 MB — the smallest of all five formats — so per byte:

| native decode            |     MB/ms |
| ------------------------ | --------: |
| graphson                 |     0.247 |
| pg-json                  |     0.176 |
| pg-text (after item 103) |     0.118 |
| **csv**                  | **0.046** |

**The worst codec throughput in the table in either direction**, and the one path still
materializing a whole `GraphData`. Item 102's stage split for pg-text put the bridge at 57% of
that decode; csv's own encode measurement in item 101 put it at ~64% there. So csv decode is the
last and largest instance of a cost whose shape is already understood and whose fix already has
three siblings in the tree.

Verified rather than assumed: the TS side decodes all 200,000 nodes back, and the ffi side loads
without the harness printing a failure line — which it would, since item 94 made a failing row
report its reason instead of a bare `n/a`.

### Why this is its own item

`csv::decode` parses the whole document into `Vec<Vec<Cell>>` before building anything, so a
streaming decoder is a restructure of `parse_csv` into a row iterator ON TOP of the borrowed-value
work pg-text needed. That is the same size of job as item 103, which took a full pass, and the
number above is what justifies spending one on it rather than guessing it was worth it.

## 107. The csv parser allocated a String per cell (2026-10-04)

Item 106's number justified spending a pass here: `decode csv` at 0.046 MB/ms was the worst
codec throughput in the table in either direction. Staging it first, over the 6.2 MB / 200,000-node
document, changed the plan:

| stage                                   |    ms |
| --------------------------------------- | ----: |
| `csv::decode` → `GraphData` (the parse) |  79.7 |
| `from_graph_data` (the bridge)          |  61.7 |
| whole                                   | 172.4 |

Unlike pg-text, where the bridge was 57%, here the PARSE is the bigger half at 46%. So the
streaming decoder was not the first move after all — the parse was.

### The obvious thing was not the cost. Again.

`parse_csv` opened with `let chars: Vec<char> = input.chars().collect()` — the whole document
materialized at four bytes a character, ~25 MB for 6.2 MB of input, before parsing began, then
walked one `char` at a time with index arithmetic. That looks like the answer.

It is not: scanning `input.as_bytes()` for the next structural byte and appending whole RUNS with
`push_str` measured **flat** — parse 79.7ms against 80.4ms. Kept anyway, because it is the simpler
shape and it is what makes the borrowing below expressible, but it won nothing. Third time in
this pass that a structural-looking cost was not where the time went.

### What it actually was

Every cell owned a `String` — `std::mem::take(&mut field)` — so the parse allocated **once per
cell**, about a million for that document. `Cell` now carries a `Cow<'a, str>` and borrows
whenever a field's content is one contiguous span of the input: an unquoted field, or a quoted
one with no `""` inside, which is nearly all of them.

|                                                    |  before |               after |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------: | ------------------: |
| parse                                              |  79.7ms |  **48.4ms** (1.65x) |
| whole decode, in process                           | 172.4ms |     119.4ms (1.44x) |
| bench `decode csv` (ffi), interleaved min of three | 133.6ms | **106.6ms** (1.25x) |
| throughput                                         |   0.046 |         0.058 MB/ms |

A field assembled from SEVERAL runs promotes to an owned `String` at the moment it stops being
one span, so the rare shape costs exactly what it used to.

### A measurement trap worth recording

The first bench reading of this change said 135.8 → 132.7ms, i.e. nothing — taken with
`BENCH_ENGINES=ts,ffi`, where the TypeScript engine runs first in the same process. Isolating the
engine (`BENCH_ENGINES=ffi`) and interleaving gives 133.6 → 106.6. **Running two engines in one
process perturbs the later one**, so a per-engine A/B has to measure that engine alone. That is
how a real 1.25x nearly got recorded as flat.

### Teeth, and the one that needed a weird document

| mutant                                               | caught by                                                              |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| the `""` escape dropped instead of written           | `a_quote_in_an_id_or_label_round_trips`, `quoting_labels_and_formulas` |
| a second run REPLACES the first instead of promoting | **nothing** at first — 31 tests green                                  |
| a bare CR outside quotes kept in the field           | the same new test                                                      |

The promotion path is the genuinely new logic and nothing produced a multi-run field. Two inputs
do, and both are shapes this decoder has always accepted from a foreign file: a quote that OPENS
mid-field (`ab"cd"` is one field reading `abcd`, because the quote switches on quoting for the
rest of it rather than starting a new field), and a bare CR outside quotes, which is dropped
wherever it appears (`ef\rgh` is `efgh`, assembled from the run before and the run after).
`a_field_made_of_several_runs_still_reads_whole` pins both.

### Ninth and tenth screen false positives

`bench_all` flagged `dedup out.out` at 1.16x SLOWER and `pred AND exists` at 1.16x SLOWER — both
query rows a csv parser cannot reach. Interleaved min of three: dedup 9565.4 against 9748.9
(1.02x) and pred 546.8 against 549.5 (1.005x). `dedup out.out` flagged 1.29x FASTER in item 103's
sweep from a different baseline and spans 9565-11068 for the same binary.

### Still open

The bridge is untouched: `from_graph_data` is still ~60ms of the 119ms decode, and csv remains
the only format on it in either direction.

## 108. Every textual format now streams on DECODE (2026-10-04)

> **Corrected in item 109.** This item was first written, and its commit titled, "streams both
> ways". That is wrong: it is true of DECODE only. csv ENCODE still goes through
> `lenke_codec::serialize(&to_graph_data(store), format)` — the engine's `serialize` has
> streaming arms for pg-json, graphson and pg-text and a `_` arm for csv. The body below was
> already narrower ("all decode straight into the host's sink"); the heading was not.

The last piece of the bridge story. csv was the only format left on `from_graph_data`, in either
direction — ~60ms of what item 107 had reduced to a 119ms decode, a second traversal over a
`Vec<Node>` the parse had just built and nothing else needed.

| `decode csv` (ffi), interleaved min of three, engine ISOLATED |                         |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------: |
| before                                                        |                 103.3ms |
| after                                                         |      **75.4ms** — 1.37x |
| with item 107                                                 | 133.6 → 75.4, **1.77x** |
| throughput                                                    |     0.046 → 0.082 MB/ms |

`decstream.rs`'s `_ => None` arm is now unreachable for every textual format: pg-json, graphson,
pg-text and csv all decode straight into the host's sink.

### One row walker, not two

`csv::decode` is expressed THROUGH `csv::decode_into` via a new `GraphDataSink`, so the row shape
— which cell is the id, which are fixed, where the `=== EDGES ===` split falls — is implemented
once. The alternative, a second walker beside the owned one, is two implementations of one layout
free to drift apart.

Three reusable pieces landed in `decstream.rs` to make that cheap, and they are what any future
codec needs:

- `value_to_decval(&Value) -> DecVal<'_>` — an owned value viewed as a borrowed one;
- `decval_to_value(&DecVal) -> Value` — the reverse;
- `GraphDataSink` — a sink that collects into `GraphData`.

The values handed to the sink are still built OWNED, per row, and then viewed. That is the
deliberate limit of this change: the per-cell allocation item 107 measured is untouched, and what
goes away is the whole-document materialization plus the bridge's second pass. Pushing borrowing
all the way down would mean rewriting `decode_cell`'s sentinel/override/list/temporal branches to
produce borrowed values — a much larger job for the remaining slice.

### Teeth, and the shared-adapter blindness again

| mutant                                               | caught by                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `value_to_decval` swaps a temporal's `tag` and `iso` | `csv::tests::temporal_columns_round_trip` — **NOT** the engine differential |
| `decode_into` never emits the edge section           | 5 tests, including the differential                                         |
| `GraphDataSink` drops a node's labels                | the differential, and two csv round-trips                                   |

The first is the pg-text lesson (item 103) confirmed a second time, and now with a named cause:
once `decode` is expressed through `decode_into`, a bug in the SHARED adapter makes both sides
equally wrong, so a streaming-vs-bridge differential cannot see it. **The differential guards the
wiring; the codec crate's round-trips guard the values.** A mutation run for these files has to
cover both crates.

### Screen, and the count so far

`bench_all`: 70 comparable rows, two flagged — `one pred` 1.33x and `two preds` 1.32x, both
FASTER, and both query rows a csv decoder cannot reach. Noise in the harmless direction, so not
chased. For the record this pass has now seen ten screen flags that min-of-three showed to be
noise and two more in the favourable direction; the screen remains useful only as a prompt to
measure.

## 109. Correcting item 108, and the last bridge is csv ENCODE (2026-10-04)

### The correction

Item 108 was titled, in both the audit and the commit, "every textual format now streams both
ways". **That is wrong.** It is true of DECODE only. The engine's `serialize` is:

```rust
match format {
    "pg-json" => Ok(serialize_pg_json(store)),
    "graphson" => Ok(serialize_graphson(store)),
    "pg-text" => serialize_pg_text(store),
    _ => lenke_codec::serialize(&to_graph_data(store), format),   // csv
}
```

csv encode still materializes a whole `GraphData`. Item 108's BODY was already narrower — "all
decode straight into the host's sink" — so the error was the heading generalizing past what the
work did. Item 108's heading now reads "on DECODE" and carries a pointer here; the commit title
cannot be changed and is wrong in the history.

Worth naming the failure mode: four decode arms were closed, and the heading was written about
the arm I had been staring at rather than about the pair. The `_` arm in `serialize` was ten lines
away in a file I had edited that same iteration.

### Re-pricing after the codec work

|                  |      ts |    ffi | ts/ffi |
| ---------------- | ------: | -----: | -----: |
| `decode csv`     | 332.6ms | 75.0ms |  4.44x |
| `decode pg-text` | 505.5ms | 80.5ms |  6.28x |

Both ratios widened because NATIVE moved (decode csv was 135.8ms before items 107 and 108, and
pg-text 110.8 before item 103), not because TypeScript regressed.

Normalizing by document size — the denominator items 101 and 102 established as the only one that
can say whether a codec is slow in absolute terms:

| native encode |     MB/ms |     | native decode  | MB/ms |
| ------------- | --------: | --- | -------------- | ----: |
| ndjson        |     0.591 |     | graphson       | 0.245 |
| graphson      |     0.563 |     | ndjson (nodes) | 0.182 |
| pg-json       |     0.414 |     | pg-json        | 0.177 |
| pg-text       |     0.223 |     | pg-text        | 0.114 |
| **csv**       | **0.055** |     | csv            | 0.083 |

`encode csv` is 4x worse than the next-worst encode and 10x worse than ndjson's. Item 101 staged
it: ~72ms of its ~113ms is `to_graph_data`. So it is both the worst-priced codec path and the only
remaining user of the bridge — the same shape of fix, with the decode side's result (1.37x from
removing the materialization alone, item 108) as the expectation.

### Why it is not done in this item

The decode side needed one row WALKER shared by two entry points. The encode side needs the
column discovery shared too: csv emits a header derived from a first-seen pass over every
element's keys and types, so a streaming encoder is a TWO-pass shape over a re-iterable source,
and `encode(&GraphData)` has to be expressed through the same implementation or the two will
drift. That is a ~100-line cross-crate API, and csv encode output is compared byte-for-byte
against the TypeScript engine by the `codec` fuzzer. Starting it in the tail of an iteration is
how a byte divergence gets shipped into a codec; it gets its own pass.

## 110. csv encodes from the store, and the bridge is gone (2026-10-04)

Item 109's named target, and the end of `to_graph_data` as a serialization path. csv encode was
the worst-priced codec in the table at 0.055 MB/ms, with ~72ms of its ~113ms being the bridge.

| `encode csv` (ffi), interleaved min of three, engine ISOLATED |                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------: |
| before                                                        |             113.4ms |
| after                                                         |  **97.0ms** — 1.17x |
| throughput                                                    | 0.055 → 0.064 MB/ms |

### Less than the decode side won, and the reason is in the design

The decode side got 1.37x from removing its materialization. This gets 1.17x because csv's two
passes need the SAME values: the column set comes from every element's keys and types, then the
rows are written from those values. So the driver still materializes the props per element
(`Vec<Vec<(String, CValue)>>`) and what goes away is the `CNode` wrapper around them — the
per-node id `String`, the `Vec<String>` labels, and the second traversal.

The refinement, not taken here: pass 1 does not actually need VALUES. First-seen key order can be
had from presence bitsets alone, and a typed column's `ColType` is implied by its `Column`
variant — except for a `Gen` column, where list-versus-scalar does need a value. That would make
pass 1 allocation-free, and it reaches into store internals for a byte-identity-critical output,
so it wants its own pass.

### A closure-based source was abandoned mid-iteration

The first design passed the codec a re-iterable source as `&mut dyn FnMut(&mut NodeEmit)`. It
does not compile in any spelling I could find: `&[(&str, &Value)]` inside a `dyn FnMut` argument
elides to independent higher-ranked lifetimes, and the bound on a generic wrapper would not unify
with the bound on the function it called — "implementation of `FnMut` is not general enough",
through explicit `for<'x>` binders and single-lifetime aliases alike.

Replaced with a two-phase builder — `CsvColumns::observe` then `CsvColumns::writer` then
`CsvWriter::node_row` / `edge_row` — where the CALLER owns the iteration. No higher-ranked
lifetimes, and the layout that must not be duplicated (fixed cells, label joining, field
guarding, header spelling) still lives in `lenke-codec`. The two drivers each repeat a for-loop
twice; that is the right thing to duplicate.

### The suite caught a behavioural divergence

`serialize_csv` first returned `String`, and `flat_codec_rejects_a_record_property` failed: csv
is a FLAT format and must reject a map/record property with `E_UNSUPPORTED`. The `GraphData` path
did it with one up-front `has_map_property` scan over the whole graph — a moment a streaming
encoder does not have. It now returns `Result` and raises when it meets the value.

That message existed twice already (`lib.rs`'s up-front check and `PgTextSink`), and this would
have been a third copy, so it is now `flat_map_property_error()` with all three calling it.

### The eleventh screen false positive, and a row to stop chasing

`bench_all` flagged `pred AND exists` at 1.16x SLOWER. Interleaved min of three: 545.9 against
548.8, i.e. 1.005x. **That row has now flagged ~1.16x in FOUR separate sweeps in this pass and
measured flat in all four isolated A/Bs** (549.1/547.3, 548.2/547.2, 546.8/549.5, 545.9/548.8) —
including for a csv codec change that cannot reach the GQL query path at all. In `bench_all` it
reads ~640ms; isolated it reads ~549ms for the same binary. Treat a `pred AND exists` flag from
the sweep as noise unless an isolated A/B says otherwise.

## 111. The traversal row stopped measuring traversal, and what it was hiding (2026-10-04)

Re-pricing after the codec work turned up a row reading **0.0ms on both engines**: `query: 1-hop
traversal`, which is `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*)`. Items 95 and 97 gave the
TypeScript engine the 1-hop count shortcut and native already had one, so both now answer it from
the edge bucket's size without walking anything.

So the bench had no traversal measurement at all, and the row's NAME no longer matched what it
measured — the same failure as item 94, except this time my own optimizations caused it. A
shortcut landing is exactly when a row named for the slow path stops being one.

Renamed to `count 1-hop [shortcut]` and kept as the GUARD for that shortcut: if it returns to
hundreds of ms, the shortcut has stopped firing. Two rows added that actually walk:

|                           |       ts |       ffi |      ts/ffi |
| ------------------------- | -------: | --------: | ----------: |
| `traverse 1-hop + filter` |  790.0ms | **1.4ms** | **551.94x** |
| `traverse 1-hop project`  | 1049.8ms |    88.6ms |      11.85x |

The filter row puts a predicate on the far endpoint, which defeats the bucket-size shortcut, and
returns ONE row — so it measures traversal rather than row materialization. `age > 500` matches
nothing, which does not reduce the work.

### 552x is real, and I checked before believing it

1.4ms to visit 1,000,000 edges is 1.4ns an edge, which is the shape of a predicate being proved
unsatisfiable from column statistics rather than evaluated. It is not. Three selectivities on the
same 200,000-node fixture, native:

| predicate                 |    ffi |  answer |
| ------------------------- | -----: | ------: |
| `x.age > 500` (none)      | 0.95ms |       0 |
| `x.age > 44` (about half) | 1.03ms |  499950 |
| `x.age >= 0` (all)        | 1.13ms | 1000000 |

Every answer is right and the time barely moves with selectivity, which is what a COLUMNAR masked
count looks like: take the `KNOWS` bucket, read the `to` endpoint column, gather `age`, compare,
popcount — all over dense arrays. TypeScript walks `Edge` objects to `Vertex` objects and reads a
property per edge. The TS answers match too (0 / 49950 / 100000 on the 20,000-node equivalent), so
both engines are doing the same work, 552x apart.

This is now the widest ts/ffi gap anywhere in the table, and nothing measured it until this item.

### What to do about it, and what not to pretend

Closing 552x would mean a columnar representation in the TypeScript engine — an architecture
change, not an optimization. What IS available on the precedent of items 95, 97 and 99 is a
FILTERED-count shortcut: `MATCH (a:L)-[:T]->(x) WHERE <pred on x> RETURN count(*)` can walk the
edge bucket, evaluate the predicate on the far endpoint and tally, skipping the binding and row
pipeline that item 98 measured at ~487ns a row before any work. That should be worth a few times,
not three orders of magnitude, and saying so up front is the point.

## 112. The filtered-count shortcut in TypeScript, and the elision that made it a win (2026-10-04)

Item 111 priced `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE x.age > 500 RETURN count(*)` at 552x
ts/ffi — the widest gap in the table — and said what was available short of a columnar
rewrite: walk the edge bucket, evaluate the predicate against the endpoints, tally. Built.

`detectCountShortcut` now admits a one-hop `count(*)` that carries a `WHERE`, provided every
free variable in the predicate resolves to the start node, the far node or the relationship.
The tally loop keeps ONE `Map` as the binding and overwrites at most three keys an edge, so the
row pipeline that item 98 measured at ~487ns a row is skipped entirely.

| `traverse 1-hop + filter` (ts, isolated, interleaved, min of three) |    ms |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----: |
| before                                                              | 760.7 |
| first attempt                                                       | 845.5 |
| after                                                               | 615.9 |

**1.24x. The first attempt was 1.11x SLOWER than the general path**, which is the useful part of
this item. The tally confirmed `a:Person` on every edge endpoint with `labels.has()` (88ns an
edge, item 97). The general path never pays that, because it SEEDS from the label bucket — the
label is free there by construction. So the shortcut was spending, per edge, what the path it
replaced spent zero on. Reusing `vacuousLabel` (item 97: a label every vertex carries is
provably no-op, `verticesByLabel.get(n).size === vertexCount`) to drop both endpoint checks
turned −11% into +24%. A shortcut is not faster for skipping a pipeline; it is faster only if it
also skips what the pipeline got free.

### The differential, and why its first version proved nothing

Eight cases compare the shortcut against the general path (`ORDER BY c` as the oracle, since the
projection guard declines that spelling and routes it to the general path). The fixture
originally built vertices with `properties: {}`, so `b.n > 3` was NULL on every edge and both
sides agreed on 0 — the differential passed without the predicate ever being true. Fixtures now
carry `{ n: i }` on nodes and `{ w: a }` on edges. Same family of fixture blindness as items 96,
100 and 105; it is the recurring failure in this log.

### Mutants

Four, all caught. Mutant B is the one worth recording: rewriting
`if (asTruth(pred.fn(env)) === true)` as `if (pred.fn(env))` looks like a pure simplification and
is a byte-identity break — `asTruth` THROWS on a non-boolean, so the plain form silently accepts
`WHERE $p` with `$p = 5`, which native rejects. Pinned:

```ts
test('a non-boolean WHERE raises on the tally path too', () => { … });
```

Declines are tested too (`a WHERE on a shape the tally cannot compute is declined`): a predicate
over a variable the tally cannot bind falls through to the general path rather than guessing.

No Rust changed, so no `bench_all` sweep. Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware`
0, `oxfmt --check` clean, `nx run-many -t test` 21 projects green, all seven fuzzers green.

## 113. Eleven generator layers, and the two that were pure packaging (2026-10-04)

Item 111 left `traverse 1-hop project` — `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) RETURN x.age AS n`,
1,000,000 rows — at 11.89x ts/ffi and ~1.0s absolute. Unlike items 95/99/112 it cannot be
answered by a shortcut: a projecting traversal has to produce every row.

### Where the second actually goes

Stage-isolated TS shapes over the 200,000-node / 1,000,000-edge fixture:

| shape                                     |        ms |
| ----------------------------------------- | --------: |
| `RETURN count(*)` (shortcut, item 112)    |       0.1 |
| `WHERE r.w > 500 RETURN count(*)`         |     318.2 |
| `WHERE x.age > 500 RETURN count(*)`       |     417.0 |
| **`RETURN 1 AS n`** — a constant per edge | **911.7** |
| `RETURN a.age AS n`                       |     992.0 |
| `RETURN x.age AS n`                       |    1025.9 |

Producing a CONSTANT for each of a million rows is 911ns a row — 89% of the row cost, with the
property read worth only ~110ns of it. Same conclusion as item 98 (which measured 487ns a row on
a node scan), twice as expensive because the expansion adds layers.

`bun --cpu-prof`, windowed past the fixture build (the load is 4s of a 5.8s profile and swamped
the first reading — `indexEdgeLabel` and `addEdge` were the top two frames until the window was
applied):

|           |                                  |
| --------: | -------------------------------- |
| **35.9%** | `generatorResume`                |
| **25.5%** | `(anonymous)` — the layer bodies |
|      6.5% | `projectBinding`                 |
|      6.1% | `Map`                            |
|      4.3% | `expand`                         |

61% is generator plumbing. The hottest leaf stack is **11 nested generator layers**, each resumed
once per row: four executor generators, `flatMap`, another executor generator, `flatMap`, then
three `map` layers, under `Array.from`.

### The obvious lever priced at 1.2% and was dropped

`expand → outSteps → edgesMatching → yield* set` is three generator layers plus a delegation to
produce one `{ edge, node }`. Collapsing it for the common directed single-label case looked like
the fix. Priced against a 1,000,000-element `Set` first:

| shape                               |     ms | per edge |
| ----------------------------------- | -----: | -------: |
| 3 layers (what `expand` does today) | 20.6ms |     21ns |
| 1 layer                             |  8.3ms |      8ns |
| no generator at all                 |  1.8ms |      2ns |

12ns an edge, so 12ms of 1025 — **1.2%**. NOT SHIPPED. A generator layer is cheap; eleven of them
are not expensive because they are generators.

### What was shipped: the projection tail stops packaging rows it never sorts

`applyProjection` wraps every row in `{ b, keys: orderBy.map(…) }` so the ORDER BY / DISTINCT /
paging stages downstream have something to sort, then unwraps it with `map(r => r.b)`. With no
`ORDER BY`, no `DISTINCT`, no `SKIP`/`LIMIT` and no aggregation, every one of those stages is a
pass-through — and the wrapper is still built: an object AND an empty `keys` array per row, with
two generator layers to put them on and take them off. The guard returns
`map(b => projectBinding(…), bindings)` directly.

Min of three, interleaved (stash → build → probe → pop → build → probe), three rounds:

| TS shape                 | before |     after | ratio |
| ------------------------ | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| `RETURN x.age` (far)     |  979.6 | **877.7** | 1.12x |
| `RETURN 1` (constant)    |  883.5 | **784.5** | 1.13x |
| `RETURN a.age, x.age`    | 1042.4 | **953.4** | 1.09x |
| node scan `RETURN n.age` |  150.6 | **137.4** | 1.10x |

9-13%, same direction in all twelve comparisons. The bench row reads 1024.6 → 917.6. The win is
on every non-sorting projection, not just the hop — which is why it beats item 98's retracted
version: that removed one layer of eleven, this removes two AND both per-row allocations.

**The first reading was not trustworthy and said so.** Un-interleaved single runs gave +6.2%,
+7.6% and −0.9% on the three shapes — disagreeing on the SIGN, all under the ~10% floor CLAUDE.md
says needs an isolated harness. Interleaving is what made it a result rather than a hunch.
`query: project 3 columns` in the cross-engine table reads 122.6 → 129.1, within that row's own
historical spread (120.5-126.8) and a single un-interleaved run; the probe's node-scan equivalent
is the number to believe.

### Teeth

Each of the five guard conjuncts dropped in turn (replaced by `true`), restored from a pristine
copy under `target/` between mutants, each run under `timeout 600`. All five caught by
`@lenke/gql:test`. Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check`
clean, 21 projects green, seven fuzzers green plus `differential` on seeds 11 / 404 / 9001. No
Rust changed, so no `bench_all` sweep.

## 114. A start-only predicate is a vertex question, and one wrong answer on the way (2026-10-04)

The filtered 1-hop tally from item 112 walks the edge bucket and evaluates the predicate per
edge. For a predicate that reads only the START node that is the wrong cardinality: the answer is
decided per VERTEX, and each vertex contributes its degree. 1,000,000 predicate evaluations where
200,000 would do.

### First, the lever that was wrong, priced and dropped

`edge.from` / `edge.to` are GETTERS — each is a `getVertexById` keyed by the endpoint's id string,
so the tally materialized BOTH endpoint vertices per edge even for `WHERE r.w > 500`, which reads
neither. Making them lazy (fetch an endpoint only for a surviving label check or a bound variable)
looked free. Interleaved min of three, three rounds:

| TS shape, 1,000,000 edges | before | after |             |
| ------------------------- | -----: | ----: | ----------- |
| `WHERE x.age > 50` (far)  |  402.7 | 468.8 | 1.16x WORSE |
| `WHERE a.age >= 0`        |  483.4 | 485.2 | flat        |
| `WHERE r.w > 500` (rel)   |  326.3 | 318.8 | flat        |

Worse in all three rounds on the dominant shape and nothing on the shape it was built for. NOT
SHIPPED. The profile had already said so and I did not read it closely enough first:
`getVertexById` was 4% of that query, so ~5% was the whole ceiling, and the two hoisted branches
cost more than the lookups saved. Price the ceiling before writing the change.

### The real finding was in the profile's margin

`bun --cpu-prof` on `WHERE r.w > 500`, windowed past the fixture build:

|           |                                             |
| --------: | ------------------------------------------- |
| **35.5%** | the tally loop body                         |
| **34.5%** | the compiled-expression closure chain       |
| **16.1%** | `properties` — the bag getter, via `propOf` |
|      4.1% | `generatorResume`                           |

`properties` is `elementProperties.get(id) ?? {}`: a string-keyed Map lookup per property read,
paid by every property read in the TS engine. Structural, not a cheap win — recorded, not chased.

### The first attempt at the per-vertex path measured nothing, and that was the bug

Added the per-vertex branch, and the shape did not move at all. Traced rather than assumed (a
temporary marker on each branch): **the branch was never reached.** `HopPred`'s `startVar` /
`farVar` / `relVar` were filled from the PATTERN, not from the predicate — so
`MATCH (a:Person)-[r:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE a.age > 50` claimed all three slots, and no caller could
tell a start-only predicate from one that needs an edge. The tally was also binding `x` and `r`
a million times for a predicate that never looks at them.

They now come from `freePredicateVars(where)`. That **changes the direction of trust**: the
existing caller uses that set to REJECT a predicate naming an unknown variable, which is safe if
it over-reports; eliding a binding is safe only if it does not UNDER-report. Its `walk` switch was
exhaustive but unchecked, so a future `Expr` kind would have silently broken the second use. It
now carries a `const unhandled: never = e` default, making completeness a compile error.

### The numbers

Interleaved min of three, three rounds, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges:

| TS shape                       | before |     after | ratio |
| ------------------------------ | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| `WHERE a.age > 50`             |  473.0 | **122.6** | 3.86x |
| same, `<-` direction           |  571.5 | **123.3** | 4.63x |
| `WHERE a.age >= 0` (all match) |  490.7 | **120.2** | 4.08x |
| `WHERE a.age > 500` (none)     |  525.6 | **118.8** | 4.42x |
| `WHERE x.age > 50` (far-only)  |  529.0 | **478.2** | 1.11x |
| `WHERE r.w > 500` (rel-only)   |  426.3 | **244.5** | 1.74x |

~4-5x, and it is a cardinality change rather than a constant factor: the ratio IS the edge:node
ratio, so it grows with degree. The far-only and rel-only shapes gain from the binding elision
alone. The cross-engine table's new `traverse 1-hop + start filter` row reads 103.8ms on TS.

**The table had no row of this shape**, which is why a 4-5x miss sat unnoticed next to a row that
looks like a near-duplicate of it. Added, with a comment saying why both stay.

### A shipped wrong answer, found by the new differential

The start-only differential failed on its multi-type case, and the cause was not the new path:

```text
MATCH (a:Person)-[]->(b) WHERE <any predicate> RETURN count(*)   ->  0, always
MATCH (a:Person)-[]->(b) RETURN count(*)                         ->  correct
```

Item 112's tally opened with `const types2 = types; if (!types2) return rowOf(0);` — a guard
written to satisfy the narrowing. But `types === undefined` means an UNTYPED relationship, i.e.
EVERY type, which is exactly what `edgesOfTypes` already takes `undefined` to mean. So every
filtered count over `-[]->` answered 0 whatever the graph held, for two commits. Fixed by passing
`undefined` through, with its own regression test rather than leaving it caught incidentally.

That is the third shipped wrong answer this pass whose only witness was a differential against the
general path (see items 101, 112). A `return 0` inserted for a type-checker is worth the same
suspicion as a `unwrap()`.

### A 1.15x regression, a falsifiable guess, and the fix

With both walks inline, `far-only` — a shape the new branch never executes — read **1.17x slower**
in all three rounds. The guess was closure size: the returned closure had grown past an inlining
threshold, the JS analogue of [[pull-alignment-is-load-bearing]]. Testable, so it was tested:
both walks moved to module scope, leaving the closure dispatch-only. The regression went away AND
the untouched shapes got faster (`far-only` 1.17x slower → 1.11x faster; `rel-only` 1.16x →
1.74x). Prediction confirmed, so the two functions stay at module scope and the comment says it is
measured, not stylistic.

### Teeth

Nine mutants, pristine copy under `target/`, restored between each, every run under `timeout 600`.
**Two survived the first pass and both were real gaps:**

- dropping the `pb === undefined` guard (the per-vertex path adds a whole degree without looking
  at a far endpoint) — no case paired a far-endpoint LABEL with a start-only predicate.
- removing the `deg === 0` check — the no-edge fixture leaves the adjacency index EMPTY, so the
  loop body never ran. The case that reaches it is a vertex with edges of a DIFFERENT type.

Both now covered; all nine caught except one, which survives by design: undoing the free-variable
elision is a ROUTING change, so answers stay correct and only the speed moves. Mutant G (zeroing
the untyped degree sum) being caught is what proves the suite reaches the per-vertex path at all.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, seven fuzzers green plus `differential` on seeds 3 / 77 / 1234 / 55555. No Rust changed, so
no `bench_all` sweep.

## 115. The fuzzer could not see the TS engine, and two divergences it then found (2026-10-04)

No optimization this item. Three shipped wrong answers this pass (101, 112, 114) were each caught
by a differential against the general path and by nothing else, and the last one — a filtered
count over an untyped `-[]->` answering 0 — survived the differential FUZZER and the whole suite
for two commits. That is the thing worth fixing.

### Why the fuzzer could not have caught it

Reproducing the bug as a mutant and running the fuzzer reported **SURVIVED**. It is not survivable;
the fuzzer never saw the mutant. `@lenke/gql`, `@lenke/core` and `@lenke/serialization` all resolve
through `exports` to `dist/esm/index.mjs`, so an edit to their `src` reaches a fuzzer only after an
nx build — and `fuzz.ts` declared no such artifact:

| fuzzer         | imports built TS packages | declared `needs` (before) |
| -------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `differential` | gql, core, serialization  | `['rust']`                |
| `write`        | gql, core, serialization  | `['rust']`                |
| `algo`         | core, serialization       | `['rust']`                |
| `gremlin`      | gremlin, core             | `['rust', 'gremlin']`     |

`gremlin` is the same situation and WAS declared. So every TS-side fuzz run compared the Rust
engine against whatever `@lenke/gql` dist happened to be on disk — **the exact trap `fuzz.ts`'s own
header is about, on the other side of the comparison.** This loop's earlier ticks were valid only
by luck: each had just run `nx build @lenke/gql` for an A/B measurement.

FIXED: a `ts` artifact (`nx run-many -t build -p @lenke/gql @lenke/serialization`; nx pulls
`@lenke/core` in as a dependency) declared by `differential`, `write` and `algo`. With it, the
reproduced bug is caught on every seed tried.

It bit once more while writing this up — a mutant sweep passed `--no-build`, left the mutant in the
dist, and the next clean-tree run reported a value divergence that was the stale mutant. `--no-build`
is only safe when the last build was of the tree being measured.

### What the generator could not reach

Every relationship this fuzzer's count family drew was TYPED, no `count(*)` ever carried a `WHERE`,
and the direction was always `->`. So the whole FILTERED half of the shortcut ladder — the per-edge
tally and the per-vertex start-only path, items 112 and 114 — was generated zero times, and an
untyped relationship never at all. The family now draws the relationship spelling (`[:T]`, `[e:T]`,
`[]`, `[e]`), the direction, both endpoint labels and which slots the predicate reads
independently, so the cross-product is reached.

Four shapes are TARGETED rather than left to the cross-product, each because it was a mutant that
survived once the family existed: a non-vacuous far label with a start-only predicate; a start
vertex of degree > 1; a non-vacuous START label, both directions. Randomly they appeared ~4 times
in 20,000 and were caught on 1 seed in 5 — and the CI gate is random-seeded, so that is not a gate.

| mutant                                    | 5 seeds |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------: |
| the real shipped bug (untyped answers 0)  |  caught |
| far-endpoint label ignored                |  caught |
| multi-type dedupe dropped                 |  caught |
| degree not summed (`n += deg` → `n += 1`) |  caught |
| start label dropped                       |  caught |

25/25 after the targeting; 9/25 before it.

### Coverage floors, including for the band that paid

`hopFilter` 508-572 generated / 361-430 non-zero and `hopUntyped` 98-124 / 91-110, both floored.
The untyped spelling has its own shapes rather than riding a 1-in-4 relationship draw: measured
that way it was 40/19, and **any** shape later added to the arm diluted it under its floor — which
is how the floor announced itself, correctly, the first time I added four more shapes.

The family's extra width came from the adjacent trailing-SKIP/LIMIT band (0.03 → 0.015). The first
attempt instead shifted every later threshold by +0.015 to preserve each later band's width, which
looked tidier and was wrong: each query draws from its own PRNG seeded per case, so moving a
boundary changes only the queries whose `p` crosses it — and shifting eight boundaries moved a lot
of them. Seed 9 went red on an unrelated pre-existing divergence it had simply never drawn before.
Taking the width from one neighbour leaves every boundary at and beyond 0.72 untouched, and all
nine seeds tried are green with every pre-existing family back at its original coverage. The band
that paid now has a counter of its own (`page` 263-311/109-128), because a band with no counter can
be halved again by the next person with nothing noticing.

### Two pre-existing divergences found, neither fixed here

Both are on a clean tree at `788ac52b`, both reduced to a minimal repro, and **neither is
generated**, so this suite stays green on a question that is about engine semantics rather than
about any change.

**1. A non-boolean `WHERE` when an edge TYPE is absent.**

```text
MATCH (a:T)-[:ABSENT]->(b) WHERE a.n RETURN count(*)   ts [{"x":0}]   native E_INVALID_VALUE
MATCH (a:T)-[:ABSENT]->(b) WHERE a.n RETURN a.n        ts []          native E_INVALID_VALUE
MATCH (a:NOSUCH)          WHERE a.n RETURN count(*)   ts [{"x":0}]   native [{"x":0}]      agree
MATCH (a:T)-[:E]->(b)     WHERE a.n RETURN count(*)   both E_INVALID_VALUE                 agree
MATCH (a:T)-[:ABSENT]->(b) WHERE 5   RETURN count(*)   both E_INVALID_VALUE                 agree
```

Native evaluates a dynamically-typed truth operand when the match is empty because an EDGE TYPE is
absent, but not when a NODE LABEL is absent — inconsistent with itself across the two ways a match
can be empty. The projecting form (`[]` vs the error) is already absorbed by the declared
`boolean-context-dynamic-operand-under-seek` entry; the `count(*)` form escapes it only because a
count over no rows is `[{"x":0}]` rather than `[]`.

**2. `FALSE AND <data exception>` — native skips the exception, TS raises it.**

```text
MATCH (n:T) WHERE n.k = 3 AND starts_with('a', n.num) IS NULL RETURN n.k
    ts: E_INVALID_VALUE        native: [{"x":3}]
```

Fixture: `k` is 1 on vertex 1 and 3 on vertex 2; `num` is a number on vertex 1 only, so the right
operand is a type error there and NULL on vertex 2. **Swapping the operand order changes neither
side**, so it is not left-to-right short-circuiting: native seeds candidates from `n.k = 3` out of
the AND-chain and never visits vertex 1, while TS evaluates the conjunction per row. Each engine's
null-argument handling is identical in isolation (`starts_with`, `ends_with`, `contains`, `upper`,
`size`, `substring`, `||` all return NULL on both; a non-null wrong TYPE raises on both), so the
divergence is entirely the seeding.

This is the mechanism the declared entry's `reason` already describes — but that entry's `matches`
accepts it only when the permissive side returns EMPTY, and here the seek narrows to a NON-empty
set, which the registry refuses by design because that is how it detects the `CALL`-body laziness
bug. So it is a genuine byte-identity violation of a declared-conformant family (the entry cites
ISO US008/UA004 as making both outcomes conformant), and widening the entry would blind the
detector. Fixing it means either TS replicating native's seeding exactly or native abandoning the
seed, which the entry already notes is not perf-neutral. **A decision, not a defect to patch in a
perf tick** — left for the user.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects green,
all seven fuzzers green, `differential` green on seeds 1-5, 7, 9, 11, 13. No engine code changed.

## 116. One object per row instead of three, and column order was unguarded (2026-10-04)

Re-profiled `traverse 1-hop project` after item 113. Still the widest out-of-band TS row; the hot
stack is now **10** nested generator layers (was 11), and at ~40ns a resume removing one more is
~4% — under the floor. So the layers were not the target this time. The allocations were.

|           | after item 113    |
| --------: | ----------------- |
| **37.2%** | `generatorResume` |
| **26.5%** | the layer bodies  |
|      7.0% | `projectBinding`  |
|      6.5% | `Map`             |
|      3.8% | `mapToRow`        |
|      3.3% | `withBinding`     |

`RETURN x.age AS n` emits `{n: 42}` — one object. The pipeline allocated three: a binding `Map`,
then `projectBinding`'s projected `Map`, then `mapToRow` copying that `Map` into the object. The
middle one exists only for the ORDER BY overlay and DISTINCT's row keys, and item 113 already
established the shape where neither is present. `projectRow` writes the row object directly, so
`projectedRows` replaces `toArray(map(mapToRow, applyProjection(…)))` for that shape.

Min of three, interleaved, three rounds:

| TS shape               | before |     after | ratio |
| ---------------------- | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| hop project 1 column   |  902.2 | **830.5** | 1.086 |
| hop project 3 columns  | 1005.3 | **880.3** | 1.142 |
| hop project `RETURN *` |  805.4 | **753.4** | 1.069 |
| node scan, 1 column    |  136.1 | **126.3** | 1.078 |
| node scan, 3 columns   |  144.0 | **127.3** | 1.131 |

The gain tracks COLUMN COUNT (3 columns gains more than 1), which is the signature of removing a
per-column copy rather than a per-row constant. `query: project 3 columns` reads 108.0 → 86.5 and
`traverse 1-hop project` 939.7 → 855.3 (ratio 10.49x → 9.76x).

### A "regression" in a control that was not a control

The first run showed DISTINCT consistently 2-6% SLOWER in all three rounds — a path this change
does not touch. The guess was last item's closure-size effect, so the `case 'return'` arm was
collapsed back to a single call. It made no difference, **refuting that hypothesis here**, and the
movement persisted.

It was the probe. DISTINCT ran LAST in a process that had just built 3,000,000 rows, so it was
measuring a churned heap, not the change. Re-run with the four non-eligible shapes alone in their
own process at nine reps, four rounds:

| control   | before min | after min |
| --------- | ---------: | --------: |
| distinct  |      145.2 |     142.6 |
| order by  |      250.0 |     243.3 |
| limit     |        0.1 |       0.1 |
| aggregate |       18.7 |      18.3 |

Flat, with the rounds interleaving. Same lesson as the `BENCH_ENGINES=ts,ffi` perturbation in item
94: **a control measured downstream of heavy allocation is not a control.** Note the absolute
DISTINCT numbers differ between the two probes (211ms vs 145ms) for exactly that reason.

### The real find: nothing checked column order, anywhere

Mutating `projectRow` to walk `proj.items` in REVERSE — which reverses every output row's column
order — **passed the whole `@lenke/gql` suite AND the differential fuzzer on three seeds.**

The fuzzer cannot see it by construction: `canonResult` does `Object.keys(v).sort()` before
comparing. That is right for row order, which is unspecified ([[order-is-unspecified]]), and for a
nested element's `properties`, which is a storage question. It is wrong for COLUMN order, which the
RETURN clause fixes and which is part of the rendered bytes.

Verified the invariant actually holds before guarding it — both engines render declaration order
(not alphabetical, not storage order) across plain projections, `*`, GROUP BY, ORDER BY and
DISTINCT. So this was a held invariant with no test, not an undecided question.

Two gates added:

- `columnOrderOf` in the conformance harness, compared in the differential fuzzer before the value
  comparison so a column-order divergence reports as itself. The FIRST row suffices and is
  row-order independent: one projection yields one column list. Green on seeds 1-5, 7, 9; catches
  the reversal on all three seeds tried.
- `packages/gql/src/column-order.test.ts`, five tests: declaration order over alphabetical, every
  projection ROUTE agreeing (fast path vs ORDER BY / DISTINCT / LIMIT / SKIP / combined), aggregates,
  `RETURN *`, and a repeated column name keeping its first position with its last value — the
  behaviour a `Map` and a plain object happen to share, which is what makes the two routes
  interchangeable at all.

### Teeth

Nine mutants, pristine copy under `target/`, restored between each, each run under `timeout 600`.
Seven guard/behaviour mutants caught by the unit suite from the start; the two COLUMN ORDER mutants
(`proj.items` reversed, and the `*` branch's binding reversed) survived everything and are now
caught by both the new unit file and the fuzzer. That is the item: the optimization is worth 7-14%,
and looking for its teeth is what surfaced an unguarded invariant.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects green,
all seven fuzzers green. No Rust changed, so no `bench_all` sweep.

## 117. Two text parsers were concatenating a character at a time (2026-10-04)

Item 94 flagged `decode graphson` (1.28x ts/ffi) and `encode csv` (1.41x) as native-side
anomalies and left them unchased. **Both readings were wrong, because the denominator was
wrong.** The formats differ in density by 9x, so ms-per-element across formats compares nothing
(CLAUDE.md says MB/ms for exactly this). Same 200,000-node graph, per BYTE:

| format   |   MB | enc ts MB/ms | enc nat MB/ms | dec ts MB/ms | dec nat MB/ms |
| -------- | ---: | -----------: | ------------: | -----------: | ------------: |
| ndjson   | 23.4 |        0.319 |         0.666 |        0.102 |         0.195 |
| pg-json  | 20.6 |        0.377 |         0.648 |        0.104 |         0.199 |
| graphson | 82.0 |        0.436 |     **1.094** |        0.208 |     **0.247** |
| pg-text  | 12.2 |        0.117 |         0.295 |    **0.022** |         0.166 |
| csv      |  9.2 |    **0.071** |     **0.098** |    **0.023** |         0.114 |

GraphSON is the FASTEST format per byte on both engines. It only looked slow because it is 82MB
against pg-json's 20MB — there was never a native anomaly there, and item 94's note should be read
as a measurement artefact. **Item 94's "wasm is slower than TypeScript on `encode csv`" stands as
a separate observation; its graphson claim does not.**

The real outliers are the two worst TS cells, both ~0.022 MB/ms: **pg-text and CSV decode, 7.5x
and 5x behind native on the same bytes.**

### One cause, in two parsers

`tokenizeLine` (pg-text) and `parseCsv`/`splitList` (CSV) all built their output with
`current += line[i]` — one string concatenation AND one single-character string per character of
input. About 12,000,000 of each for the pg-text document and 9,000,000 for the CSV one.

Replaced with SPAN slicing: track where the token or field starts and slice once at the boundary,
only banking a partial when something genuinely interrupts the span. For CSV that is four things —
an opening quote, a closing quote, a doubled `""`, and a swallowed CR — so an ordinary field costs
one slice and no concatenation. `charCodeAt` replaces `line[i]`, removing the one-character
strings. This is the same fix applied to the Rust CSV parser in item 108.

Min of three, interleaved, three rounds:

| TS decode | before |     after | ratio |
| --------- | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| pg-text   |  528.2 | **332.2** | 1.59x |
| csv       |  380.9 | **263.5** | 1.45x |

Cross-engine table: `decode pg-text` 508.8 → 298.4 (6.50x → 3.83x ts/ffi) and `decode csv`
385.8 → 233.9 (5.01x → 3.07x). Both are now inside the 1.5-4x band the rest of the codecs sit in.

**Self-time UNDERSTATES this pattern, and that is worth knowing.** `tokenizeLine` was 16% of the
profile, which caps a fix at 1.19x — the measured win was 1.59x. The difference is garbage: 12
million short-lived strings cost collection time that the profiler attributes elsewhere or not at
all. So a 16% frame that is allocation-heavy is worth attacking; a 16% frame that is arithmetic is
not. `parseCsv` was also ~16%, which is why it was worth doing rather than deferring.

### Grepped for the pattern elsewhere

Four more sites: `packages/gql/src/lexer.ts` (×2), `packages/core/src/temporal.ts` (×2),
`packages/sync/src/client.ts` (×4). NOT changed — the lexer runs over a query string, not a
document (`query: count` is 0.0ms end to end, so lexing is not measurable), temporal parses short
numeric runs, and sync is outside the bench. Recorded so the next reader does not re-derive it.

### Teeth, and the one that mattered

Six mutants, pristine copies under `target/`, restored between each, each under `timeout 600`.
Five were caught immediately. The sixth is the item:

Dropping `quoted` from CSV's trailing-flush condition **survived**. The first reading was
"equivalent mutant — unreachable through the public API", because the disjunct only fires for a
final row that is ONLY a quoted-empty field. Checked instead of assumed, and it is reachable and
observable: `decodeNodes('id,:LABEL\n""')` raises `E_INVALID_VALUE` unmutated and returns `[]`
mutated — **a malformed document silently decoding to nothing.** Now pinned.

### The differential that makes the rewrites trustworthy

Both parsers' new cases were run against the ORIGINAL character-append versions and all pass
there too, so they pin each parser's contract rather than blessing the rewrite. That matters here
because the existing coverage was round-trips over documents the ENCODER produced, and the encoder
never emits a quote mid-field, a bare CR, or an unterminated quote — so the awkward cases had no
coverage at all. Added: a quote opening mid-field (`a"b c"d` is one field), `""` collapsing
without ending the field, a CR swallowed from mid-field, a CR kept inside quotes, empty-quoted vs
absent, an unterminated quote running to EOF, and `splitList`'s `\;` / `\\` escapes.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green, `codec` on seeds 1-3. No Rust changed, so no `bench_all` sweep.

## 118. CSV encode has no cheap win: two levers priced and rejected (2026-10-04)

No optimization shipped. Both candidates the profile pointed at measured nothing, and both are
now recorded next to the code they would have changed.

### First, a correction to item 117's own framing

Item 117 switched the codec comparison to MB/ms and concluded CSV encode was the worst cell
(0.071 ts / 0.098 nat). That denominator is right for DECODE, where the input is bytes and the
scanning work tracks them. It is misleading for ENCODE: the element count is what the encoder
walks, and a DENSER format does the same per-element work while emitting fewer bytes, so MB/ms
penalizes it. Per element, over the same 200,000 nodes:

| encode   | ts per element | nat per element |
| -------- | -------------: | --------------: |
| pg-json  |          273ns |           208ns |
| ndjson   |          366ns |           176ns |
| pg-text  |          519ns |           207ns |
| **csv**  |      **643ns** |       **467ns** |
| graphson |          941ns |           375ns |

CSV encode is mid-pack per element and GraphSON is the slowest — the opposite of the MB/ms
ranking. **Neither denominator identifies waste on its own; a profile does.** Both are recorded
here so the next reader picks the one that matches the direction of the work.

### Rejected: reading `this.#id` instead of the `id` getter

`get labels()` is `elementLabels.get(this.id)` — through the public getter — where
`get properties()` reads `this.#id` directly. `get labels` is 11.8% of a TS CSV encode by
`bun --cpu-prof`, so removing a hop on every labels read (and on the two adjacency getters, and
on `Edge`) looked free. Interleaved min of three, rebuilding both ways each round:

| TS shape        |                before |                 after |
| --------------- | --------------------: | --------------------: |
| encode csv      | 131.6 / 132.9 / 156.6 | 127.8 / 136.5 / 140.2 |
| encode pg-text  | 123.7 / 126.8 / 126.3 | 122.5 / 128.2 / 123.7 |
| encode ndjson   |    78.6 / 77.3 / 68.7 |    77.7 / 78.5 / 79.4 |
| IS LABELED scan |    97.1 / 85.8 / 85.1 |    92.4 / 84.9 / 91.8 |

Flat on every row, rounds disagreeing on the sign. JSC inlines a getter whose body is a
private-field read, so there was nothing to remove. What that getter costs is the string-keyed
`Map.get` and the `Set` the caller iterates — neither of which the change touched.

A fixture note: the probe's `hop + far label` row read 0.0ms on both sides because
`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x:Person) RETURN count(*)` is answered by the count shortcut. It
measured nothing, the same way item 94's `n/a` rows did. The row stays out.

### Rejected: a positional column pair instead of `types.get(key)` per cell

`buildRow` does `types.get(key)` for every CELL, and the types are fixed before the header is
written — so a 200,000-node/3-column encode re-answers a loop-invariant question 600,000 times.
**The Rust encoder was given exactly this treatment in item 108**, which is what made it look
like a sure thing.

The first read, three rounds at 7 reps, showed 1.11x — and the rounds disagreed on the sign, so
it got more samples. Five rounds, min of THIRTEEN reps each:

```text
before  113.2 / 115.2 / 122.7 / 126.7 / 111.9
after   118.0 / 122.7 / 115.1 / 118.1 / 117.4
```

Min 111.9 against 115.1: flat to marginally WORSE, rounds splitting 3-2 against it. A 3-entry
`Map` keyed by a repeated string is already about free (JSC caches the key's hash), while the
`{ key, type }` pair adds an object indirection and a destructure per cell. **The Rust win came
from avoiding a `HashMap` over owned `String`s, which is a different cost — a result from the
sibling implementation is a hypothesis here, not evidence.** That is the transferable lesson.

### What this leaves

CSV encode's profile is `buildRow` 12.5%, `get labels` 11.8%, `encodeNodes` 11.5%,
`get properties` 7.9%, `quoteField` 5.1%, `computeColumns` 3.5%. The two largest avoidable-looking
items are the two rejected above; the remainder is the per-cell encode-and-quote work the format
requires. There is no cheap win here, which is worth knowing explicitly rather than re-deriving.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green. No functional change — comments only.

## 119. A rejection that was priced with the wrong harness (2026-10-04)

Re-profiled `traverse 1-hop project` after items 113 and 116. `generatorResume` is now **42.3%**
and the layer bodies 24.0% — two thirds of the query, across 10 nested layers, so a layer is worth
roughly 5.5%. That number is what reopened a closed question.

### The same change was rejected in item 114, at 1.2%

`expand -> outSteps -> edgesMatching -> yield* set` is three generator layers plus a delegation to
produce one `{ edge, node }`. Item 114 priced collapsing it against an isolated micro-benchmark
over a 1,000,000-element `Set`:

| shape        |     ms | per edge |
| ------------ | -----: | -------: |
| 3 layers     | 20.6ms |     21ns |
| 1 layer      |  8.3ms |      8ns |
| no generator |  1.8ms |      2ns |

12ns an edge → 1.2% of the row → NOT SHIPPED. **That was the wrong harness.** Those generators are
monomorphic, two lines long, and the only thing in the loop, so the engine inlines them. In the
real pipeline a resume costs ~40ns — 10 nested layers deep with a megamorphic `next` — so the
micro understated the layer 5x.

This is the mirror of item 117's lesson. There, profiler self-time UNDERSTATED an
allocation-heavy frame (16% measured, 1.59x delivered). Here, an isolated micro UNDERSTATED a
generator layer in a deep polymorphic pipeline. **Both failure modes make a real cost look small,
and neither is visible from the number alone — only from asking whether the harness resembles the
caller.**

### Re-measured in situ

`expand` now reads the bucket directly for a DIRECTED hop with a single concrete edge type — one
layer instead of three. Everything else falls through unchanged. Min of five, interleaved, three
rounds:

| TS shape                       | before |     after | ratio |
| ------------------------------ | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| hop project, `->`              |  841.3 | **805.7** | 1.044 |
| hop project, `<-`              |  868.2 | **816.5** | 1.063 |
| 2-hop project                  |  130.5 | **120.4** | 1.084 |
| hop project, `-[]-` (CONTROL)  | 1592.2 |    1586.0 |  flat |
| hop project, untyped (CONTROL) |  857.9 |     849.2 |  flat |

**1.04-1.08x — above the micro's 1.2% estimate and below the 10% floor**, so it is reported as
what it is rather than rounded up. What makes it credible is not the magnitude but the shape of
the evidence: the same direction in 3/3 rounds on both directed spellings, two controls that do
NOT take the fast path sitting flat, and every row count identical (1000000 / 1999950 / 200000).
The cross-engine row reads 877.8 → 843.2.

One row in that probe is NOT evidence and is called out as such: `hop filter tally` moved
566.7 → 523.8, but it goes through `tallyHopCount`'s own `edgesOfTypes` walk and never calls
`expand`. It cannot have been affected, and its spread across runs (523-578) is wider than the
movement. Noise.

### Teeth

Four mutants, pristine copy under `target/`, restored between each, each under `timeout 600`, all
caught: the endpoint swapped (`edge.from` for `edge.to`), the index swapped (`edgesFromByLabel`
for `edgesToByLabel`), the `!== 'both'` guard dropped (an undirected hop would lose its in-edges
and its self-loop dedup), and the `label?.kind === 'label'` guard widened to `label !== undefined`
(a label expression treated as a plain name).

### Also looked at, and not pursued

The tick began on `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` — 2797ms, 3x the next TS number. Its profile is
`indexEdgeLabel` 21.3%, `JSON.parse` 18.1%, `addEdge` 12.7%, `labels` 7.3%, `getVertexById` 7.3%,
`#commitProperties` 7.0%. That is inherent (parse), already rejected with numbers
(`indexEdgeLabel`'s lookup pattern, recorded in `Graph.ts`), or the three-index maintenance the
adjacency shape requires. `validateLabel` at 3.5% looked anomalous at first — I divided 254ms by
one rep instead of two and got 212ns a call for two string comparisons. It is ~106ns, and
memoizing it (it is pure, and 1,200,000 calls collapse to one distinct label here) caps at 2.8%.
Not attempted.

## 120. Two pass-through generator layers removed, and both controls were wrong (2026-10-04)

Continuing item 119's layer count. The hot stack was 7 layers (down from 10). Two of them did
nothing but forward rows:

- **`flatMap(b => matchPattern(…), [binding])`** — a `flatMap` over a ONE-element array. Its own
  comment claimed it added "no generator frame per row"; `flatMap` is itself a `function*`, so
  every row's `next()` was threaded through a frame that existed to iterate a single item. Now a
  direct call.
- **`matchOrOptional`** — one generator whose `!matched && clause.optional` tail can only fire for
  OPTIONAL, so for every other MATCH it was `for (const m of …) yield m`. OPTIONAL keeps its own
  generator (it genuinely must know whether anything matched); a plain MATCH returns the stream.

Stack depth confirms both went: **26 → 20 frames.**

### The measurement, which does not support the model item 119 implied

| TS shape                         | before |     after | ratio |
| -------------------------------- | -----: | --------: | ----: |
| hop project                      |  782.2 | **761.8** | 1.027 |
| node scan project                |  122.1 |     122.1 |  flat |
| hop + WHERE                      |  763.8 |     769.2 |  flat |
| 2 patterns, small fixture (CTRL) | 1244.7 |    1214.8 |  flat |

~2-3% on the hop, flat elsewhere, rounds disagreeing on two rows. **Below the floor, and NOT
claimed as a win.** It ships as a simplification that provably does less work: two fewer frames
per row, and a comment that was factually wrong is gone.

**Correcting item 119's framing.** That item observed `generatorResume` at 42% over 10 layers and
reasoned "a layer is worth roughly 5.5%". Item 119 then removed TWO layers for 4-6%, and this item
removed two more for 2-3% — so the real figure is **1-3% per layer, and falling as layers are
removed**, not 5.5%. The share a profiler attributes to `generatorResume` is not divisible by
layer count: the cost is dominated by the innermost resume chain, so removing outer frames buys
less than the average suggests. Do not price the next layer at 5%.

### Both controls were invalid, which is the useful part

The first probe's two controls were each broken, in different ways, and one of them nearly
produced a false positive:

1. **`MATCH (a:Person), (b:Person) WHERE a.age = 1 AND b.age = 2`** — intended as the
   multi-pattern control. It is a 200,000 x 200,000 cartesian product and never finished; it took
   a 600s probe down. Anchoring both sides on an inline property (`{age: 1}`) did not help, which
   says the planner is not seeding the second pattern from it — **noted as a separate finding, not
   chased here.** The control now runs on its own 2,000-vertex fixture, where it is flat
   (1244.7 → 1214.8, answers identical at 4000000 and 81796).
2. **`MATCH (a:Person) OPTIONAL MATCH (a)-[:NOSUCH]->(x)`** — intended as the OPTIONAL control.
   It improved consistently, 367.0 → 341.7 across all three rounds, which looked like the change
   leaking into a path it must not touch. It is not a control at all: its FIRST clause is a plain
   MATCH, so it takes the removed pass-through like everything else. A control has to be checked
   for _not containing the thing being changed_, not just for having a distinguishing feature.

That is two bad fixtures in one probe, and it is the same failure as items 96, 100, 105 and 112 —
a fixture that cannot distinguish what it claims to. The one valid control is what makes the
numbers above readable.

### Teeth

Three mutants, pristine copy under `target/`, restored between each, each under `timeout 600`, all
caught: the `patterns.length === 1` guard widened to `>= 1` (a multi-pattern MATCH would run only
its first pattern), the OPTIONAL ternary inverted, and `optionalMatch`'s `if (!matched)` made
unconditional (an extra null row per binding even when the pattern matched).

An interrupted A/B also left the change sitting in `git stash` with the tree at HEAD — the same
hazard CLAUDE.md records for mutation loops, in a different wrapper. `git stash list` and
`git diff --stat` before continuing.
