green, all seven fuzzers green. No Rust changed, so no `bench_all` sweep.

## 121. An uncorrelated second pattern is re-scanned per outer row — 160x, TS only (2026-10-04)

The largest TypeScript-only gap found in this pass, and it came out of a BROKEN CONTROL. Item
120's multi-pattern control never finished at 200,000 vertices even with both patterns anchored on
an inline property, and that item noted "the planner is not seeding the second pattern" as an
unchased aside. Chased here, and the aside was wrong in its detail and right in its conclusion.

### The inline predicate IS pushed — into the first pattern only

At 2,000 vertices, `k = i % 7`:

| query                                                          |       ms |    answer |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------: | --------: |
| `MATCH (a:P {k: 1}) RETURN count(*)`                           |      1.3 |       286 |
| `MATCH (a:P), (b:P) RETURN count(*)`                           |   1556.1 |   4000000 |
| **`MATCH (a:P {k: 1}), (b:P {k: 2}) RETURN count(*)`**         | **82.5** | **81796** |
| `MATCH (a:P), (b:P) WHERE a.k = 1 AND b.k = 2 RETURN count(*)` |   1046.2 |     81796 |

So the inline form is 12.7x the clause-`WHERE` form for the same answer — the predicate IS being
used. That made it look fixed. It is not, and **two cost models fit these numbers equally well**
because the filtered/bucket ratio was constant at 1/7. Separating them needs selectivity varied
with the bucket size FIXED — 20,000 vertices throughout:

| distinct `k` | matches each |    rows |      ms | ns/row | ns/(outer x bucket) |
| -----------: | -----------: | ------: | ------: | -----: | ------------------: |
|            7 |         2857 | 8162449 | 10712.2 |   1312 |             **187** |
|          100 |          200 |   40000 |   371.9 |   9298 |              **93** |
|         1000 |           20 |     400 |    34.3 |  85774 |              **86** |
|         5000 |            4 |      16 |    10.6 | 664929 |             **133** |

`ns/row` swings **500x**; `ns/(outer x bucket)` is flat. The cost is
`outer_filtered x BUCKET`, not `outer_filtered x inner_filtered`. **Only the outer pattern is
seeded; the inner one rescans its entire label bucket for every outer row** — even though its
predicate is a literal and cannot depend on the outer binding. Sixteen output rows cost 10.6ms.

`visitRemaining` is where it happens: `for (const b of matchPattern(pat, binding)) yield*
visitRemaining(rest, b)` calls the inner `matchPattern` once per outer row.

### Native does not do this

Same fixture, same queries, through the FFI engine:

| distinct `k` |   TS ms | native ms | native ns/row |
| -----------: | ------: | --------: | ------------: |
|            7 | 10712.2 |  **66.9** |             8 |
|          100 |   371.9 |   **0.3** |             6 |
|         1000 |    34.3 |   **0.0** |           114 |
|         5000 |    10.6 |   **0.0** |          2303 |

Native is output-linear — `ns/(outer x bucket)` rounds to 0 at every selectivity. **160x at
distinct=7, and the ratio grows without bound as the key gets more selective**, because TS's cost
is pinned to the bucket while native's follows the answer. This is not a byte-identity question (the
answers match everywhere) and not a conformance one; it is a pure cost asymmetry with a
known-good shape on the other side.

### The fix, and why it is not in this commit

An uncorrelated pattern's match stream is the same for every outer row, so it should be built once
per `visitRemaining` call and the product formed against it:

```ts
const inner = toArray(visitRemaining(graph, patterns, rest, binding, params));
for (const b of matchPattern(graph, pat, binding, params)) {
  for (const i of inner) yield merge(b, i);
}
```

Computing `inner` against `binding` (not an empty binding) is what makes it correct: `binding` is
fixed for the call, so `rest` may still read anything bound at an OUTER level. Row ORDER is
unchanged — the nested loops enumerate exactly what the recursion did, in the same sequence — and
`pickPattern`'s choice is unchanged too, because `patternRank` differs between `binding` and `b`
only on whether a pattern continues a binding, and uncorrelatedness means `rest` binds none of
`pat`'s variables.

Three things have to be settled first, which is why this is a finding and not yet a change:

1. **The correlation test needs COMPILE-TIME data.** By `visitRemaining` a `CPath` holds compiled
   closures, not an AST, so there is nothing left to walk for free variables. `patternBoundVars`
   covers the bind side but is unexported and AST-only. Each compiled pattern needs the variable
   sets it BINDS and READS recorded when it is compiled.
2. **It renegotiates the laziness contract.** `matchClauseBindings`'s doc says "Fully lazy:
   bindings flow one at a time… so a clause that expands to millions of them never materializes
   them." Materializing `inner` trades O(inner) memory for the time. A CAP keeps that honest and
   costs nothing real: the pathology is worst when the inner set is SMALL and the bucket LARGE
   (distinct=5000 above — four inner rows, 10.6ms), while a huge inner set means a huge product,
   which is output-bound in either engine.
3. **It is the matching core.** Items 112 and 114 both shipped wrong answers from changes to
   count/match paths, each caught only by a differential against the general path. A
   correlation test that is wrong in one direction returns wrong rows silently.

Measured, characterized and queued rather than rushed. Nothing shipped here.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green. Docs only.

## 122. The uncorrelated tail is matched once (item 121 implemented) (2026-10-04)

Item 121's three blockers, settled in order.

**Blocker 1 — the correlation test needs compile-time data.** `CPath` gains `binds` and `reads`,
filled in `compilePath` where the AST still exists. `reads` is delegated to `freePredicateVars`
over a synthetic `EXISTS { pattern }` rather than re-walking the pattern: that walker already
visits every inline property value and inline `WHERE` at every depth, already adds the pattern's
own bindings to its bound set before descending (so `(n WHERE n.age > 30)` reads nothing outer),
and already carries the exhaustiveness guard added in item 114. A second traversal would be a
second thing to keep in step with the grammar. `reversePath` carries both sets through unchanged —
reversing swaps endpoints, not what a pattern binds or reads.

**Blocker 2 — the laziness contract.** `TAIL_CACHE_CAP = 4096`. The pathology is worst when the
tail is SMALL and the bucket it rescans is LARGE, and a tail big enough to overflow implies a
product big enough to be output-bound anyway, so the cap gives up nothing that mattered. Overflow
discards and falls back, so the wasted pulls are bounded by the cap once — not per outer row.

**Blocker 3 — it is the matching core.** Covered below.

### The numbers

20,000 vertices throughout, bucket size fixed, selectivity varied — the probe that separated the
two cost models in item 121. Interleaved, two rounds, min:

| distinct `k` | tail rows |  before |      after | ratio | ns/(outer x bucket) |
| -----------: | --------: | ------: | ---------: | ----: | ------------------: |
|            7 |      2857 | 10636.4 | **2089.8** | 5.09x |        187 → **37** |
|         1000 |        20 |    41.8 |    **6.8** | 6.15x |        144 → **17** |
|         5000 |         4 |    11.9 |    **4.6** | 2.59x |        180 → **58** |

The algorithmic defect is gone: `ns/(outer x bucket)` falls 3-8x and the remaining cost tracks
OUTPUT. At distinct=7 the product genuinely has 8,162,449 rows, so 2089.8ms is 256ns a row —
still 31x native's 8ns, but that is row production, not a rescan.

**Both correlated controls stayed flat**, which is the point: `(b:T {n: a.n})` (the tail READS the
outer pattern) held at ~10300ms and ~180 ns/(outer x bucket), and the shared-variable join was
unchanged. Every answer identical before and after.

### Teeth

Five mutants, pristine copy under `target/`, restored between each, each under `timeout 600`:

| mutant                                                   |                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| `reads` side dropped — a correlated tail IS hoisted      | caught              |
| `binds` side dropped — a shared-variable join IS hoisted | caught              |
| merge order reversed (`[...t, ...b]`)                    | caught              |
| never hoist                                              | SURVIVED — expected |
| cap removed                                              | SURVIVED — expected |

The last two survive BY DESIGN and were predicted: both are routing/memory choices that cannot
change an answer. The merge-order mutant is caught by `column-order.test.ts` (item 116) — the file
written two ticks ago because nothing guarded column order, now earning its keep on a change it
was not written for.

### The fuzzer could not see any of this, and now sees half

**The differential fuzzer generated ZERO multi-pattern MATCHes.** Five green seeds said nothing
about a change to the join path. Added to the count family: an uncorrelated product, a
three-pattern product, a shared-variable join, and a product returning ROWS (so column order and
values are compared, not just a count). It now catches the `binds`-side mutant on every seed
tried.

The `reads` side **cannot** be fuzzer-covered, and that is a finding of its own. Generating
`MATCH (a:T), (b:T {n: a.n})` turned the suite red on all five seeds:

```text
MATCH (a:T), (b:T {n: a.n})        ts [{"x":5}]   native E_SYNTAX
MATCH (a:T), (b:T WHERE b.n = a.n) ts [{"x":5}]   native E_SYNTAX
MATCH (a:T), (b:T) WHERE b.n = a.n ts [{"x":5}]   native [{"x":5}]   agree
```

Native rejects an INLINE pattern predicate that reads another pattern's variable, in both
spellings, while accepting the clause-level `WHERE` (which is a post-join filter and does not
exercise the correlation test at all). Pre-existing — no Rust changed when it was found — and a
capability gap rather than a wrong answer: a correlated element pattern is ordinary ISO. So there
is no spelling of pattern-level correlation native will parse, the shape stays out of the
generator per item 115's precedent, and **the `reads` half of `tailIsUncorrelated` is guarded only
by `packages/gql/src/multi-pattern.test.ts`.** Said plainly because the fuzzer being green must
not be read as covering it.

### Two fixture bugs in the new tests, both caught by the tests failing

- The "a correlated tail is not hoisted" case asserted that the correlated and uncorrelated
  spellings DIFFER. On `build(60, 7)` the k=1 and k=2 buckets are both 9, so both answers are
  9 x 9 = 81 and the assertion distinguished nothing. Replaced with a deliberately UNEVEN fixture
  (4 and 5), where the answers are 16 and 20.
- The cap test used 2500 vertices per bucket — UNDER the 4096 cap, so it never reached the
  fallback it was written for, and its 6,250,000-row oracle timed out at 5s. Now 5,000 in the
  tail and 2 in the outer pattern: the tail overflows the cap while the product stays at 10,000
  rows.

Same family as items 96, 100, 105, 112 and 120. The oracle throughout is the two-CLAUSE spelling
(`MATCH p1 MATCH p2`), which computes the same product through `runMatch` and never touches
`visitRemaining`, so it cannot be circular with what it checks.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green, `differential` on seeds 1-5 and 9. No Rust changed, so no
`bench_all` sweep.

## 123. The same rescan, one level up: separate MATCH clauses (2026-10-04)

"After fixing a pattern, grep for it elsewhere." Item 122 fixed the per-outer-row rescan WITHIN a
MATCH (`visitRemaining`). Separate MATCH clauses go through `runMatch`, a different function with
the same shape — and measuring first rather than assuming showed it had the same defect:

| 20,000 vertices, distinct=7         |         ms | ns/(outer x bucket) |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------: | ------------------: |
| 1 clause, 2 patterns (fixed in 122) |     2330.6 |                  41 |
| **2 clauses**                       | **9369.4** |             **164** |

So the clause path was still re-running the second clause for every row of the first.

### The hoist, and the two conditions it needs

`runMatch` now matches an independent clause once and merges. **`reads` being empty is not
sufficient**, which is the part worth recording: an already-bound pattern variable is an ANCHOR,
not a fresh scan — `MATCH (a:P) MATCH (a)-[:E]->(b)` reads nothing and is a join — and pattern
variables live in `binds`, not `reads`. So each incoming row is also checked for sharing a name
with `binds`, and any row that shares falls back. `CMatch` gained the clause-level `binds`/`reads`
pair (patterns' sets, plus the clause `WHERE`'s free variables, minus what the clause binds
itself).

Interleaved, two rounds, min:

| distinct `k` | before |      after |     ratio | ns/(outer x bucket) |
| -----------: | -----: | ---------: | --------: | ------------------: |
|            7 | 8909.7 | **1779.5** | **5.01x** |        156 → **31** |
|         1000 |   38.1 |    **3.9** | **9.77x** |         95 → **10** |
|         5000 |    9.4 |    **3.7** | **2.54x** |        117 → **46** |

The correlated control (`MATCH (a:P {k: 1}) MATCH (b:P {k: a.k})`) stayed on the per-row path at
~150-190 ns/(outer x bucket), and item 122's single-clause row was flat. Answers identical.

### The oracle had to change, because the old one is now the thing under test

Item 122 checked the multi-pattern spelling against the two-CLAUSE spelling. Both are hoisted now,
so that comparison is no longer independent. The new oracle is a **tautological clause-level
`WHERE`**: `WHERE a.k = 1` is always true given `(a:P {k: 1})`, but it makes `reads` non-empty and
forces the per-row path. Same query, different route. Plus arithmetic (9 x 9) so the two routes
cannot be wrong together.

### Mutation found a real test gap

Five mutants. Three caught at once (`reads` ignored, the `binds` check removed, merge order
reversed). Two survived, and they were not the same kind of survivor:

- **Building the cache from the first incoming row** instead of an empty binding **SURVIVED, and
  it is a wrong answer.** The cache would carry row 1's values into every later row, so row 2
  comes back holding row 1's `a`. It survived because almost every test here is `count(*)` — **a
  count cannot see that the outer value was overwritten.** Fixed by a test that PROJECTS both
  sides (`RETURN a.i AS ai, b.i AS bi ORDER BY ai, bi`) and asserts the full row set. The mutant
  is now caught, and so is the mirror mutant on item 122's path (building its tail from an empty
  binding instead of `binding`) — the same test covers both hoists.
- **Hoisting OPTIONAL** survives and is an EQUIVALENT mutant: a null-filled variable that is
  already bound would be caught by the `binds` check first. The exclusion stays as a documented
  belt, because that equivalence rests on `nullVars` being a subset of `binds` — two sets computed
  by different functions. If it drifts, a bound variable gets overwritten with null.

Writing `count(*)` tests for a change that merges bindings was the mistake; the mutation step is
what surfaced it, which is the whole argument for doing it.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green, `differential` on seeds 1-5, 9 and 13. No Rust changed, so no
`bench_all` sweep.

## 124. Two failed measurement methods, one real finding (2026-10-04)

Item 121 was found because the bench table looked in-band on every ratio while one unprobed shape
was 160x. So this tick tried to find the next one systematically. Two methods failed before one
worked; all three are recorded because the failures are the reusable part.

### Failed method 1: ts/native ratio growth

Ten query shapes, each at N and 2N on both engines, flagging any shape whose ts/native ratio GREW
with N. The ratios came out 11x-512x and the "growth" readings 0.66x-2.80x — **all meaningless.**
Native is 0.0-0.5ms on every shape even at 150,000 edges, so the ratio is `ts / clock resolution`,
and its "growth" is quantization noise. `OPTIONAL hop` showed the strongest signal (2.35x) and is
perfectly linear when measured properly.

A ratio against a sub-millisecond baseline is not a measurement. Item 121 did not work this way:
it varied SELECTIVITY with size fixed and compared TS against a COST MODEL (`ns` per
`outer x bucket`), using native only to show the model was achievable.

(A process note, since it cost a run: the precision fix for that probe was a `str.replace` that
silently matched nothing. Every other edit this session asserts its match count; this one did not,
so the second run printed the same rounded numbers and I nearly read them as new.)

### Failed method 2: reading a scaling exponent as an algorithm

Three-point scaling on TS alone (n, 2n, 4n) does work, and it flagged
`MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE b.k = 2 RETURN count(*)` at **exponent 1.25 then 1.90** — 9.6 → 22.9
→ 85.6ms. That looks like a quadratic algorithm. It is not.

Profiling instead of believing it: the path is `tallyHopCount` (23.4%), `properties` (24.3%) and
the predicate closure (40.7%) — one pass over the edges, which is linear. The per-EDGE cost is
what grows: **150ns → 206ns → 246ns**. The far endpoint is a random vertex, so each property read
is a random access into a heap that is outgrowing cache. This is exactly the transition CLAUDE.md
names ("cache-resident and not are different questions; the transition is between 200k and 1M
elements") — the near-end spelling, whose endpoints are walked in bucket order, reads 1.36 and is
5x faster in absolute terms.

**A super-linear exponent is not evidence of a super-linear algorithm.** It is also what a
constant-work-per-element loop looks like while crossing out of cache.

### The real finding: three equivalent spellings cost 4x apart

The same probe, same answer (1200 rows) every time:

| spelling                              |   n=20k |  40k |   80k |
| ------------------------------------- | ------: | ---: | ----: |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE b.k = 2` | **9.0** | 24.7 |  95.6 |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b {k: 2})`        |    37.0 | 67.1 | 271.1 |
| `MATCH (a:P)-[:E]->(b:P {k: 2})`      |    32.3 | 75.9 | 332.2 |

**4x between spellings of one question** — the exact bug class CLAUDE.md calls out ("the planner
recognized one spelling of a predicate and scanned for another that meant exactly the same thing
… Each cost 100-300x and each returned the correct answer, so no correctness test could catch
it").

The cause is `plainNode`: `(n.properties?.length ?? 0) === 0 && n.where === undefined`. A clause
`WHERE` on the far node becomes the tally's `pred` (items 112/114), but an INLINE constraint makes
the node non-plain, so `buildOneHopCount` returns `null`, the whole shortcut declines, and the
query runs the general row pipeline.

### The fix, and why it is queued rather than in this commit

Do NOT synthesize an equivalent predicate AST — inline-pattern semantics (`structuralEq`, and
NULL dropping on an absent key) would be re-derived, and re-derivation is how items 112 and 114
shipped wrong answers. Instead pass the endpoint's COMPILED `CPredicate` into the tally and apply
it through `satisfies`, which IS the general path's implementation of those semantics, so
equivalence holds by construction. `satisfies` is already exported; `compilePredicate` is not and
would need to be (one line) rather than inlined, for the same "second thing to keep in step"
reason as item 122's `reads`.

What makes it worth a fresh tick rather than the end of this one: relaxing `plainNode` touches the
UNFILTERED one-hop path, the two-hop degree product and `buildNodeCount` as well, and a partial
relaxation there is exactly how a shortcut starts answering a shape it should have declined. The
oracle is free (the clause-`WHERE` spelling, independently routed), so the test is easy; the gate
is getting the relaxation's scope right.

Nothing shipped. Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean,
21 projects green, all seven fuzzers green. Docs only.

## 125. The inline endpoint constraint, carried (item 124 implemented) (2026-10-04)

`plainNode` made a one-hop count decline whenever an endpoint carried an inline constraint, so
three spellings of one question cost 4x apart. The far endpoint's COMPILED predicate is now
carried into the tally and applied through `satisfies` — the general path's own implementation of
inline-pattern semantics — so the spellings agree by construction rather than by re-derivation.
`compilePredicate` and `CPredicate` are exported for it rather than inlined, for item 122's
"second thing to keep in step" reason.

Min of three, interleaved, 20,000 vertices / 60,000 edges, same 1200-row answer throughout:

| spelling                       | before |   after | ratio |
| ------------------------------ | -----: | ------: | ----: |
| `WHERE b.k = 2` (the fast one) |    8.5 | **8.4** |  flat |
| `(b {k: 2})`                   |   35.1 | **7.9** |  4.4x |
| `(b:P {k: 2})`                 |   31.3 | **7.7** |  4.1x |
| `(b WHERE b.k = 2)`            |   33.6 | **5.8** |  5.8x |

### The controls caught a regression I had introduced

The first version also carried the START node's constraint, and the controls said no:
`MATCH (a:P {k: 2})-[:E]->(b)` went **5.2 → 6.2ms at 20k and 11.9 → 17.8 at 40k.** The reason is
plan choice, not overhead: the general path SEEDS from the label bucket and walks 1,200 edges,
while the tally is a full edge scan and walks 60,000. **A start-side constraint is seedable; a
far-side one is not** — which is exactly why the clause-`WHERE` far spelling was already fast and
the inline far spelling was not. Only `inFar` is carried now, and a start-side inline keeps
declining as a measured choice with the numbers recorded next to it.

A second control regression was real and fixable: `WHERE b.k = 2`, which shares the tally, read
~10% worse because the loop called a helper per edge that immediately returned true — 120,000
pointless calls. Hoisting the `!== undefined` test inline restored it to flat. Without a control
on the un-constrained tally neither of these would have been visible; the headline 4x would have
shipped with a 10% tax on the shape it shares a loop with.

### Honestly, what is still worse

Shapes that DECLINE the shortcut and therefore run untouched code read 15-20% slower, and
`MATCH (a:P {k: 1})-[:E]->(b {k: 2})` (declines, 0 rows, 2-7ms) about 2x. The routing for these
is identical before and after, so this is the module-growth effect of
[[ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing]] — ~145 lines added to `shortcuts.ts`. Reported rather than
buried: the judgement is that restoring a 4x spelling asymmetry, which CLAUDE.md names as the
class that historically cost 100-300x, is worth 15-20% on a few shapes in the 2-30ms range. The
`both ends inline` case is the one I would revisit first.

### Teeth

Six mutants. Four caught: the inline falling through to the O(1) bucket path (which would answer
the whole bucket's count), the far constraint ignored inside the tally, the per-vertex path taking
a far constraint it never visits, and a correlated inline value accepted. Two survived and both are
defensive checks added knowing they were unreachable — the anonymous-`WHERE` guard is redundant
because the free-variable loop already rejects any inline `WHERE` with free variables, and the
"uncompiled inline" assert cannot fire because the caller computes `inFar` from the same node.
Stated as such rather than counted as coverage.

### The oracle drifted again, and the fuzzer was blind again

Item 124 would have used the clause-`WHERE` spelling as the oracle; it now shares the tally, so
`ORDER BY c` (which the projection guard declines, as in item 112) plus the known edge list is
used instead. **Third oracle rotation in four items** — each fix absorbs the previous
independent route, so the oracle has to be re-chosen every time rather than inherited.

The differential fuzzer generated no inline endpoint constraint on a hop either. Four shapes added;
it now catches the dropped-constraint mutant on every seed tried. Two of them draw the relationship
spelling rather than hard-coding a type, because the first version — four shapes all with a typed
rel — diluted every existing share in that arm and pushed `hopUntyped` under its floor. That floor
is a per-shape share of one arm, so it falls whenever the arm grows: the floors are now
re-measured, with a note saying to re-measure rather than lower them next time.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green, `differential` on seeds 1-5, 9 and 13. No Rust changed, so no
`bench_all` sweep.

## 126. The TS engine had no spelling probe; it found a 2.9x in its first run (2026-10-04)

Items 121 and 125 both found a spelling asymmetry in the TS engine, and both found it BY
ACCIDENT — 121 out of a broken control, 125 out of a scaling probe aimed at something else. The
Rust engine has had `spelling_probe` as a standing check for this class since before this pass.
The TypeScript engine, a separate implementation of the same two languages, had nothing.

`packages/native/spelling-probe.ts`, `bun run spelling`. Twelve groups, each a set of spellings
of ONE question: the four forms CLAUDE.md names (`$x = u.k` vs `u.k = $x`, `k = $a OR k = $b` vs
`k IN [$a, $b]`, clause `WHERE` vs inline `{k: $x}`, `5 <= u.n` vs `u.n >= 5`) plus `NOT (=)` vs
`<>`, edge-type disjunction order, reversed direction, AND order, a redundant label, and the
two-pattern/two-clause pair of items 122-123. It reports each member's time and flags a group
whose spread exceeds a tolerance; it compares ANSWERS too, and reports a disagreement first,
because that would be a correctness bug rather than a cost one.

It is a PROBE, not a test. The Rust version can assert on canonicalized plans and treat time as
the backstop; there is no plan to canonicalize here, so time is the only signal, and a timing
threshold in CI would be flaky. Documented in CLAUDE.md next to its Rust counterpart.

### First run: eleven groups clean, one at 2.9x

| node count, three spellings |    ms |
| --------------------------- | ----: |
| `MATCH (n:P WHERE n.k = 2)` |  4.08 |
| `MATCH (n:P {k: 2})`        |  6.53 |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 2` | 11.85 |

Three spellings of one question, **2.9x apart**, all answering correctly. Also flagged at 1.8x:
the hop with a filtered START endpoint, where the clause `WHERE` is the FAST one (3.11ms against
5.26) — the mirror image of item 125's far-endpoint case, which is consistent with that item's
finding that a start-side constraint is seedable and a far-side one is not.

Everything else is within 1.5x, including the four forms CLAUDE.md names as the historical
100-300x offenders and the two pairs items 122-125 just equalized.

### The cause, read from the code rather than guessed

`matchClauseBindings` applies a clause `WHERE` as a POST-FILTER over the binding stream:

```ts
return clause.where === undefined
  ? stream
  : filter((b) => asTruth(clause.where!({ binding: b, params, graph })) === true, stream);
```

An INLINE predicate is applied by `matchNode` during the scan, so it rejects an element before a
binding is built. The clause form pays binding construction for every vertex and then throws most
of them away. `collectHints` already lifts seekable conjuncts of the clause `WHERE` onto pattern
nodes as seed HINTS — but a hint only narrows the seed, it does not move the predicate.

### Why the fix is not in this commit

Pushing a single-variable clause-`WHERE` conjunct into that node's predicate is the obvious fix
and it has a real byte-identity hazard: it changes WHEN the conjunct is evaluated. Under `AND`
with three-valued logic, a conjunct that raises (a non-boolean in a truth context) currently never
runs for a row an earlier conjunct already dropped; pushed into the scan it would run for every
candidate element. That is precisely the boolean-context evaluation-order family of item 115,
where TS and native already diverge on one shape and the registry refuses to excuse an
error-against-rows. OPTIONAL also has to be excluded outright, since its clause `WHERE` must see
the null-filled row.

So the probe ships, the finding is recorded with its mechanism, and the pushdown is queued behind
a decision about raise order rather than guessed at. The probe is the durable part: this class has
now been caught three times and twice by luck.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green. No engine code changed.

## 127. The single-node clause WHERE moves into the pattern (item 126 implemented) (2026-10-04)

Item 126's probe found a node count spelling three ways and costing 2.9x apart. `compileClause`
now MOVES a qualifying clause `WHERE` into the node pattern before compiling, so the two spellings
become literally the same compiled form.

An AST move rather than an executor change, which is what makes it cheap to trust: the result is
the inline spelling, already covered by every test that spelling had. `compileNode` derives seed
hints from a node's inline `where` (`hintsForVariable`), so the move does not lose the hint lifting
that `collectHints` was doing for the clause form.

| 20,000 vertices, min of three, interleaved  |   before |                   after |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------: | ----------------------: |
| `MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 2 RETURN count(*)` |    10.44 |                **5.74** |
| group spread (three spellings)              | 2.5-2.8x | **under the 1.5x flag** |

**Only a pattern with NO segments, and that bound is measured.** The same probe shows the
relationship REVERSED on a hop's start node: `(a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE a.k = 2` is 3.03ms against
5.37 for the inline spellings, so pushing there would make a hop ~1.7x SLOWER. Which form wins is
a per-shape plan question — the same distinction item 125 drew between a seedable start and a
non-seedable far endpoint — not a general rule, so the guard is a measurement and is commented as
one.

### A spread I made WORSE, said plainly

The `hop, START endpoint filtered` group went from 1.5-2.0x to **2.6-2.8x**, and it is still the
one group the probe flags. Nothing got slower: its clause-`WHERE` member got FASTER (2.71 →
1.98ms across rounds) while the two inline members stayed at ~5.2. So the group's spread widened
because one member improved — which is a real failure of the "equivalent spellings cost the same"
invariant even though every absolute number is flat or better.

The mirror fix is to pull an inline START predicate OUT to the clause level, which is the inverse
of this item. Not attempted: it moves a predicate from the scan to a post-filter, which INCREASES
the evaluation count (per path rather than per vertex) and is the direction with the raise-order
hazard, not the safe one. Recorded as the next item rather than left as a surprise in the probe's
output.

### Teeth, and three equivalent mutants

Six mutants. Three caught: pushing a pattern WITH SEGMENTS (caught by the wider suite, which is
the guard I wanted), dropping the AND merge with a predicate the node already carries, and pushing
a multi-pattern clause.

Three survived and all three are EQUIVALENT, worked through rather than assumed:

- **OPTIONAL pushed.** `matchClauseBindings` applies the clause `WHERE` _inside_ the stream that
  `optionalMatch` uses to decide `matched`, so filtering during the scan and filtering after it
  both reach the same `matched`. The exclusion is defensive; its equivalence depends on a property
  of another function, so it stays.
- **An outer-variable `WHERE` pushed.** `matchNode` evaluates a node predicate against the
  incoming binding, which already holds the earlier clause's variables, so `n.k = z.k` resolves
  either way. The free-variable check is conservative. **Relaxing it would extend the win to
  correlated single-node predicates** — noted, not done here.
- **A `pathVar` pattern pushed.** The path variable binds the path; a predicate on the node is the
  same either way.

Counted as three caught of six, not six of six.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green, `differential` on seeds 1-5. No Rust changed, so no `bench_all`
sweep.

## 128. The pushdown's free-variable guard was not load-bearing (2026-10-04)

Item 127 pushed a single-node clause `WHERE` into the pattern only when the predicate was
CLOSED. Its mutation run reported that guard as an EQUIVALENT mutant — removing it changed no
answer — and item 127 recorded that relaxing it would extend the win to correlated predicates.
Done here, with the measurement first.

`matchNode` evaluates a node predicate against the INCOMING binding, which already holds every
earlier clause's variables, so an outer reference resolves in the pattern exactly as it did in the
clause filter. Two independent confirmations before changing anything: the surviving mutant, and
the inline spelling of the correlated query already answering identically.

| 20,000 vertices, min of three, interleaved         | before |      after |
| -------------------------------------------------- | -----: | ---------: |
| `MATCH (z:P {k: 3}) MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.j = z.j`   | 2109.0 | **1529.7** |
| the same spelled inline (CONTROL — already pushed) | 1465.5 |     1425.2 |
| an uncorrelated pushed clause (CONTROL)            |  251.5 |      249.3 |
| a closed single-clause predicate (CONTROL)         |    3.1 |        3.6 |

**1.38x**, three controls flat, every answer identical (1142857 / 1142800 / 2857). The correlated
question's two spellings are now within noise of each other (1529.7 against 1425.2), so that group
is equalized too.

### Tests that PROJECT, because a count cannot see this failure

Item 123's lesson applied before it could bite: the way a correlated push goes wrong is a STALE
outer binding — the inner predicate comparing against the first row's `z` for every row — and
`count(*)` over the product can total correctly while every row is wrong. So the new cases project
both sides and assert the full row set, including one with several outer rows whose values DIFFER
(a single-outer-row fixture cannot distinguish a stale binding from a correct one) and an
assertion that every row pairs like with like.

### Teeth

The relaxation widens a guard and adds no execution path, so the meaningful mutant is not a guard
conjunct but "the predicate is lost" — pushing the pattern through unchanged while dropping the
clause `WHERE`. **Caught.** Two others survive and are equivalent, as expected: swapping the AND
operands (an `AND` of two pure predicates), and leaving the `WHERE` on the clause as well as the
node (double-applying an idempotent predicate).

### The one group the probe still flags got worse again

`hop, START endpoint filtered` now reads **3.2x** (it was 1.5-2.0x before item 127, 2.6-2.8x
after). Nothing in it is slower; its clause-`WHERE` member keeps getting faster while the two
inline members stay put. The queued mirror fix — pulling an inline START predicate out to the
clause level — is the direction that moves a predicate from the scan to a post-filter, raising the
evaluation count and carrying the raise-order hazard, so it is still a decision rather than a
patch. Flagged here for the third time rather than allowed to drift quietly.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green. No Rust changed, so no `bench_all` sweep.

## 129. The hop-START spread was never about predicate placement (2026-10-04)

Items 126, 127 and 128 each flagged `hop, START endpoint filtered` and each deferred it, on the
assumption it was the same post-filter-vs-scan story as the node count and would need the risky
MIRROR pushdown. **It was not, and this is the diagnose-first step I skipped three times.**

Hypothesis and test: if the clause form is faster because it reaches item 114's per-VERTEX
shortcut while the inline form fails `plainNode(start)` and declines, then DEGREE should separate
them — a per-vertex walk reads bucket SIZES, so more edges per vertex is free, while the general
path walks every edge. 20,000 vertices:

| shape                                    | degree 3 |  degree 9 |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------: | --------: |
| `(a:P)-[:E]->(b) WHERE a.k = 2` (clause) |     5.57 |  **2.62** |
| `(a:P {k: 2})-[:E]->(b)` (inline)        |     9.21 | **10.82** |
| both at once, which forces the decline   |     8.64 |      7.89 |

The clause form gets FASTER with degree and the inline form gets SLOWER. And "both at once" — the
same predicate in both places, which makes the node non-plain and forces the decline — sits with
the inline form, not the clause form. So the cause is the DECLINE, not where the predicate is
written, and the mirror pushdown would have been the wrong fix entirely.

### The plumbing already existed and was passing `undefined`

Item 125 wired `inNear` through `HopScan` and `startOnlyHopCount` applies it — and then the caller
passed `undefined`, because item 125 measured routing a start constraint to the TALLY (a full edge
scan) and rightly rejected that. **It never tried the per-vertex route.** That is the correction:
"a start-side constraint is seedable, so declining is faster" is true of the tally and false in
general.

`startVar` is now optional (an inline-only constraint needs no bound variable), and a start
constraint with no clause predicate routes to the per-vertex walk.

| min of three, interleaved | before |    after |     ratio |
| ------------------------- | -----: | -------: | --------: |
| inline, degree 3          |   7.93 | **3.71** | **2.14x** |
| inline, degree 9          |  10.35 | **1.81** | **5.72x** |
| both at once, degree 9    |   7.58 | **1.86** | **4.07x** |
| clause form (CONTROL)     |   2.39 |     2.14 |      flat |

**The win grows with degree**, which is the signature of swapping an edge walk for a bucket-size
read. Answers identical. The spelling probe now reports **zero groups over its tolerance** for the
first time.

### Then the probe caught itself

With the hop groups equalized, the probe's remaining flag moved to `label on start: redundant vs
absent` at 1.5-1.6x — on members reading **0.02 and 0.03ms**. Both are answered by an O(1)
bucket-size read; neither is slow; the ratio is the clock's resolution. **That is exactly item
124's mistake — a ratio against a sub-millisecond baseline — reproduced inside the tool built to
catch this class.** The probe now skips a group whose slowest member is under `SPELL_FLOOR` (1ms)
and says so, suggesting a bigger `SPELL_N` instead of printing a meaningless number.

Checked that it is now a stable gate rather than assuming: three consecutive runs at 100,000
vertices, all clean at the default 2x. At 1.5x one run in three still flags a hop group at
exactly 1.5x, so 1.5x remains a deliberate-hunt setting, not a gate.

### Teeth

Four mutants, three caught: taking the per-vertex walk despite a FAR constraint or multi-type
edges (it would ignore the far constraint, or double-count), ignoring the start constraint inside
the walk, and never binding the start variable. One survives and is routing-only — taking the
per-vertex walk with no start predicate at all agrees with the tally for a constant predicate.

New tests cover the anonymous start (no variable to bind), a far-side constraint pushing the query
off the per-vertex walk, multi-type dedupe, and a HIGH-DEGREE start vertex — because degree is
what this walk reads and a degree-1 fixture cannot see an off-by-a-degree. The differential fuzzer
gained four start-side shapes; it catches the ignored-start-constraint mutant on every seed tried.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green.

## 130. The Gremlin surface had never been measured (2026-10-04)

The cross-engine bench has GQL rows and no GREMLIN rows, and `@lenke/gremlin` is a separate TS
implementation of the repo's other surface language — its own `ast`, `bind`, `executor`, `steps`,
`predicates`. **Every optimization of this pass, items 112 through 129, was GQL-only**, and half
the engine's surface area had no performance measurement at all.

`packages/native/bench-gremlin.ts`, `bun run bench:gremlin`. Same fixture as the GQL bench
(200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges); the TS side runs a builder plan through `toArray`, native
takes the SAME plan serialized by `planToGremlin`, so both answer the identical query.

### First run

| traversal                           |        ts | native |   ts/nat |
| ----------------------------------- | --------: | -----: | -------: |
| `V().count()`                       |       4.1 |   0.00 |      414 |
| `V().hasLabel('Person').count()`    |  **57.5** |   0.00 | **5752** |
| `V().has('age', gt(44)).count()`    |      43.3 |   0.38 |      115 |
| `E().count()`                       |      20.5 |  12.19 |      1.7 |
| `V().out('KNOWS').count()`          | **373.1** |   0.62 |  **600** |
| `V().out('KNOWS').values('age')`    |     491.2 |  32.15 |     15.3 |
| `V().out('KNOWS').has(…).count()`   |     426.2 |   1.58 |      271 |
| `V().groupCount().by('age')`        |      45.9 |   2.86 |     16.1 |
| `V().out('KNOWS').dedupe().count()` |     384.6 |   1.86 |      207 |

**The whole count-shortcut family is missing from the TS Gremlin engine.** Items 95, 99, 112, 114,
125 and 129 built exactly these for GQL, where `MATCH (n:Person) RETURN count(*)` is 0.0ms — the
Gremlin spelling of the same question is 57.5ms. `V().count()` should be `vertexCount`, `E().count()`
should be `edgeCount`, `V().hasLabel(L).count()` the label bucket's size, `V().out(T).count()` the
edge bucket's. Native answers all of them at ~0. That is the next target, and it has a known-good
design in the sibling surface plus a free oracle (the un-shortcut traversal, and the GQL spelling).

`E().count()` at 1.7x is the outlier in the other direction: native spends 12.19ms there, which is
the one row where it is not near-instant.

### Three harness traps, all mine, all recorded in the file

This tick spent more time on my own harness than on the engine, so each trap is written where the
next person will hit it:

- `groupCount` takes a CONFIG OBJECT (`{ by }`). I passed a bare string, which spread into the step
  as indexed characters and produced a nonsense group key.
- **`JSON.stringify(new Map([[3, 2]]))` is `{}`.** The TS engine returns a Map for the grouping
  steps, so a raw stringify reads as "the TS engine produced an empty map" — I chased that as an
  engine bug before spotting it. The fuzzer uses the conformance suite's `canonJson` for exactly
  this reason.
- `@lenke/gremlin` is a BUILT DIST. A source edit needs `nx build @lenke/gremlin` first — item
  115's trap, which I suspected here (correctly, as a hypothesis) and ruled out by rebuilding.

### Two real groupCount divergences, in shapes the fuzzer cannot reach

Once the Map handling was right, four of six cases agreed and two did not. Both are outside the
fuzzer's generator, which only ever emits `values(k).groupCount()` — with a preceding `values` and
never a `.by`:

```text
g.V().groupCount()                     ts {"Vertex (1) {}":1,…}   native {"0":1,"1":1,"2":1}
g.V().values('age').groupCount().by('age')  ts {"3":2,"7":1}      native {"null":3}
```

The first groups by whole ELEMENTS and the engines key the map differently — TS by the element's
`toString`, native by its id. The second applies `.by('age')` to a stream of NUMBERS: native reads
the property of a non-element as null and groups `{"null":3}`, TS ignores the modulator and groups
by the value. Native looks more defensible on the second; the first is a rendering question. Both
are reported, neither is fixed here, and neither is generated — so the fuzzer stays green on a
question about engine semantics.

green, all seven fuzzers green. No engine code changed.

## 131. The Gremlin count shortcuts (item 130 implemented) (2026-10-04)

Item 130 measured the Gremlin surface for the first time and found the whole count-shortcut
family missing from the TS engine — `g.V().hasLabel('Person').count()` at 57.5ms where the GQL
spelling of the same question is 0.0ms. Built, in `executor/count-shortcut.ts`, checked before
`seedFromIndex` because it answers the whole plan rather than narrowing its start.

Min of three, interleaved, 200,000 vertices / 1,000,000 edges:

| traversal                                            | before |   after | native |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | -----: | ------: | -----: |
| `V().count()`                                        |    4.1 | **0.0** |   0.00 |
| `V().hasLabel('Person').count()`                     |   52.9 | **0.0** |   0.00 |
| `V().out('KNOWS').count()`                           |  368.0 | **0.0** |   0.60 |
| `E().count()`                                        |   20.6 | **0.0** |  12.22 |
| `V().has('age', gt(44)).count()` (CONTROL, declines) |   40.7 |    41.7 |   flat |

Every answer identical. **The TS engine is now ahead of native on two of these** — `E().count()`
costs native 12.22ms and `V().out(T).count()` 0.60ms, so native has no equivalent read for
either. Recorded as a reverse asymmetry rather than claimed as a win over it.

### Deliberately narrow

Every shape here is one the graph already keeps a counter or a bucket for, so the shortcut is a
READ, not a cheaper walk. Three exclusions are reasoned rather than conservative:

- **`both()` is not shortcut.** It walks a vertex's out-edges then its in-edges, so a self-loop is
  incident TWICE and the total is not a bucket size. The general path gets that right already; a
  shortcut would have to re-derive it.
- **Multi-label `hasLabel(a, b)` is not shortcut.** It keeps a vertex carrying ANY label, so the
  answer is a UNION, and a vertex may carry several — a bucket sum would double-count.
- **Multi-type `out(a, b)` needs `multiTypeEdgeCount === 0`**, the same soundness condition the GQL
  shortcut uses: a two-type edge sits in two buckets and the walk yields it once.

### Teeth, and the same fixture trap for the seventh time

Six mutants. Four caught at once. Two survived, and one of them is the recurring one:

**Removing the multi-label guard survived** — because `labelledCount` reads `labels[0]`, and in
the first fixture EVERY vertex carried `P` with `Q` on a subset. So `union(P, Q) === |P|`, and a
mutant reading only the first bucket returned the right answer for the wrong reason. The fixture
now overlaps WITHOUT NESTING (0-2 are P, 3 is both, 4-5 are Q): |P| = 4, |Q| = 3, union = 6, sum
= 7 — four distinct numbers, so no case can pass by coincidence. Same class as items 96, 100, 105,
112, 120 and 123.

**The `count(local)` guard survived** because the only local case I wrote had TWO intermediate
steps and declined for that reason instead. A `V().count(Scope.local)` case — no intermediate step,
the shape whose global twin IS shortcut — catches it. Both now caught.

### Two harness errors worth recording

- `count` takes a `Scope` SYMBOL, not a config object (`count(Scope.local)`), where `groupCount`
  takes a config object. Item 130 hit the mirror of this.
- **`git stash push -- <tracked> <untracked>` stashes NOTHING** and fails quietly, so the first
  A/B compared the tree against itself — BEFORE and AFTER both read 0.0 and looked like a null
  result. `count-shortcut.ts` is a new file; stashing only the tracked `index.ts` disables the
  shortcut, which is what the real A/B above does. Verified the stash reverts (grep for the symbol)
  before trusting the numbers.

### And the failed stash did real damage, which `git status` caught

That failed push had a second consequence worth more than the lost measurement. `git stash push`
stashed nothing, but the `git stash pop` that followed it still ran — and popped **the top of the
stack**, which was an iteration-8 REJECTED experiment (`#[inline(never)]` on the fastpath `try_*`
functions, plus a `SortLocal` perturbation probe). Three A/B rounds, so it fired repeatedly, and
two Rust files I had not touched this tick showed up modified in `git status` at commit time.

This is exactly the hazard CLAUDE.md records for mutation loops — "an interrupted loop leaves the
mutant in the tree, and `git diff` is then the only thing standing between it and a commit" —
arriving through a stash rather than a mutant. It was re-stashed rather than discarded (the
content is recorded as rejected, but destroying it is not mine to decide), and the session's
commits were audited for stray Rust: the only `crates/` commits predate this TS pass. The native
column of the bench was unaffected either way, because it reads the prebuilt `.so` and nothing
rebuilt it.

**The rule this earns: `git stash push -- …` and `git stash pop` are not a safe pair unless the
push is confirmed.** Check `git stash list` or grep the file for the symbol in between.

Gates separately: `typecheck` 0, `oxlint --type-aware` 0, `oxfmt --check` clean, 21 projects
green, all seven fuzzers green, `gremlin` on seeds 1 / 7 / 42 / 2977. No Rust changed.

## 132. The filtered hop tally, and two targets the profile redirected (2026-10-04)

Item 131 left four slow Gremlin rows. The two biggest RATIOS were the filtered counts —
`out(T).has(…).count()` at 274x and `has(…).count()` at 126x — so both looked like one job: the
GQL tally family. Profiling them separately says they are not, and the split is the opposite of
what I assumed in each case.

| `V().has('age', gt(44)).count()` — 200,000 vertices |     share |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| `properties` (the element bag getter)               | **72.9%** |
| `generatorResume`                                   |     12.3% |

| `V().out(T).has('age', gt(44)).count()` — 1,000,000 edges |     share |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| `generatorResume`                                         | **58.1%** |
| the layer bodies                                          |     28.6% |
| `properties`                                              |      3.3% |

**The filtered SCAN is 73% property-bag reads** — one string-keyed `Map.get` per vertex, the
structural cost item 118 already probed and rejected a micro-fix for. A tally would still pay it,
so it is not the target; native answers it in 0.36ms because it reads an age COLUMN.

**The filtered HOP is 86.7% generator plumbing** and only 3.3% property reads — even though it
does FIVE TIMES as many property reads. The same read costs ~184ns on the cold single-pass scan
and ~17ns here, because the far endpoints are a small set touched repeatedly and stay cache-warm.
That is the same cache effect as item 124, in the other direction: it makes the hop's property
reads nearly free and its pipeline dominant.

So only the hop got the tally. `V().out(T).has(k, pred).count()` now walks the type's edge bucket
and tallies, with no traversers at all — `out(T)` emits one traverser per traversed EDGE, so the
bucket visits exactly the same far endpoints in the same multiset.

Min of three, interleaved (stash verified to revert by grepping for the symbol first):

| traversal                               | before |     after |     ratio |
| --------------------------------------- | -----: | --------: | --------: |
| `V().out(T).has('age', gt(44)).count()` |  419.3 | **252.9** | **1.66x** |
| `V().has('age', gt(44)).count()` (CTRL) |   42.5 |      42.5 |      flat |
| `V().out(T).values('age')` (CTRL)       |  578.7 |     577.5 |      flat |
| `V().groupCount().by('age')` (CTRL)     |   43.4 |      45.8 |      flat |

1.66x rather than the ~2.5x the 86.7% suggested: the tally still reads the far endpoint's property
and calls `matches` per edge, and iterating a 1,000,000-element `Set` is not free either. Reported
as measured.

### Teeth

Five mutants, all caught: the endpoint swapped (`edge.from` for `edge.to`), `both()` tallied (a
self-loop is incident twice), a non-`has` second step tallied, the predicate ignored, and the
multi-type guard dropped. The oracle is a vacuous leading `hasLabel('ALL')` — a label every vertex
carries, which makes it three intermediate steps so the shortcut declines, without changing the
answer. The fixture gained that label for exactly this purpose, since `P` is deliberately NOT
vacuous there (item 131's fix).

## 133. Distinct far endpoints are the reverse index's keys — 54x (2026-10-04)

`V().out(T).dedupe().count()` walked 1,000,000 edges and built a `Set` of every distinct target:
374ms against native's 1.8. But the distinct targets of the type-`T` edges are exactly the
vertices holding at least one in-edge of type `T`, and `edgesToByLabel` is keyed by vertex. So
the answer is a scan of 200,000 index keys, not 1,000,000 edges, and allocates nothing.

Min of three, interleaved (stash verified to revert first):

| traversal                           | before |   after |   ratio |          ts/nat |
| ----------------------------------- | -----: | ------: | ------: | --------------: |
| `V().out(T).dedupe().count()`       |  369.5 | **6.8** | **54x** | 203x → **3.8x** |
| `V().out(T).has(…).count()` (CTRL)  |  251.0 |   250.1 |    flat |                 |
| `V().out(T).values('age')` (CTRL)   |  568.7 |   579.1 |    flat |                 |
| `V().groupCount().by('age')` (CTRL) |   43.9 |    43.5 |    flat |                 |

**Multi-type needs no extra condition here**, unlike every edge count in items 131-132: this
counts VERTICES, and "has an edge of any of these types" is a UNION per vertex, so an edge
carrying both named types makes its target qualify once either way. A bucket SUM would have been
wrong; a per-vertex test is not.

### Teeth, and three survivors of two different kinds

Five mutants. Two caught immediately (the index swapped so `out` reads the FROM side, and `both()`
shortcut — it reaches a vertex from either side, so it is not one index).

**Two are equivalent, and my own code comment was wrong about why.** I wrote that an empty bucket
can persist, so the `size > 0` test was load-bearing. Mutation said otherwise, and reading
`deIndexEdgeLabel` confirms it: the label's entry is removed as soon as its set empties, and
`indexEdgeLabel` only ever creates a set it immediately fills. So `byLabel.has(label)` changes no
answer today. The check stays — that equivalence depends on two other functions keeping their
invariant — but the comment now says it is defensive instead of claiming coverage it does not have.

**One was a real gap, and it is the fixture trap for the EIGHTH time** (items 96, 100, 105, 112,
120, 123, 131). The by-modulator case asserted that `dedupe().by('k')` matches its forced-decline
twin — with `k: i`, unique per vertex, so distinct-by-k EQUALS distinct-vertex and a mutant that
took the shortcut anyway was right by coincidence. The by-key now repeats (`grp = k % 2`), and the
case additionally asserts the two answers DIFFER, so it cannot pass that way again.

Also added: the after-deletion check now covers the UNTYPED `out()` spelling too, which walks a
different branch (`anyNonEmpty`) and was inheriting the typed one's coverage.
