predicate, bypassing the binding round trip and the shared dispatch — with the warning attached
that the micro will understate the win, not overstate it.

Deliberately NOT concluded: that closures are expensive (+0.27ms says they are nearly free) or
that `getVertexById` is the problem (+3.93ms, real but a quarter of the accessor).

### The `@lenke/native:test` flake, finally characterized

Items 159-161 recorded this flake three times without capturing it. This time the full suite
exited 1, and chasing it produced the explanation: **nx prints its "Nx detected a flaky task"
banner from its own stored history, on PASSING runs too.** The run that exited 1 showed 38/39
tasks served from cache and that banner, with no failing test anywhere in the output.

Isolated and uncached, `@lenke/native:test` is 792 pass / 0 fail; five further uncached
FULL-SUITE runs all exit 0. So the banner is not a failure signal and should not be read as one —
which is most of why this looked like an intermittent failure across three items. The underlying
intermittent exit remains real but rare and still uncaptured; what is new is that the banner that
made it _look_ frequent is unrelated to whether the current run passed.

Gates separately: full TS suite exit 0 (after the above — one run exited 1, then five uncached
runs clean and the package isolated at 792 pass), `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check`
exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds. No engine code changed — this item
moves two bench thresholds and annotates a comment — so the bench screen IS the deliverable and
the two corrected rows are reported above.

## 164. Drive the hop-count walks from the vertex side — 1.4-1.8x dense, 7-9x selective, 20.6x empty

Item 163 priced this row and named the target: a direct evaluator for the common far predicate,
to bypass what the profile showed as 38% of the query in the compiled property accessor. **That
diagnosis was wrong, and the first thing this item did was disprove it.**

### Retracting the megamorphism hypothesis

Item 163 explained a 14x micro-vs-real gap as a MEGAMORPHIC call site: the accessor is shared by
every compiled expression shape, so a monomorphic micro could not see it. Two things undercut
that before any code was written. The probe that measured 89ms had compiled exactly ONE
expression shape, so its call sites were not polymorphic; and `propOf` turned out to be a
one-line `?.properties?.[key] ?? null`, not a dispatcher.

The real variable is ACCESS ORDER. `farOnlyHopCount` iterates `graph.edgesToByLabel`, keyed by
vertex id, so it touches 200,000 vertices and their property bags in hash order, chasing a
`getVertexById` plus two pointers into cold memory for each. Item 163's micro iterated an ARRAY
in creation order:

| iteration order, same work                     | ns/vertex |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| creation order (item 163's micro)              |        39 |
| **the edge index's own order (the real walk)** |   **177** |
| a plain shuffle                                |       129 |
| bare, creation order (no binding round trip)   |        29 |
| bare, edge index order                         |       135 |

177ns against the 171ns the profile attributed to the accessor — it matches because the cost was
never the accessor. **135 of those 177ns are pointer chasing in random order; only 42ns is the
expression layer.** So a direct evaluator would have bought at most a quarter of what item 163
expected it to, and the recorded target was replaced rather than built.

### The change

Both walks (`farOnlyHopCount` and its `startOnlyHopCount` twin, which were already structurally
identical) now iterate VERTICES via a new `candidateVertexSource`, which buys two separate
things:

- **Order** — creation order, so the vertex and bag accesses are sequential.
- **Short-circuit** — the degree is summed only for vertices the predicate KEEPS, where the old
  walk summed it for all 200,000 before testing anything. This is why the old walk was flat in
  selectivity and the new one is not.

`candidateVertexSource` is a plain function beside the existing `candidateVertices` GENERATOR,
not a replacement: a `yield*` frame per vertex is invisible in a micro and is not invisible
across 200,000 of them (the generator note in item 136). The twins stay as two separate
module-scope functions, as this file's own comment requires — parameterizing one hot walk cost an
unrelated shape 1.17x in item 119.

### The raise-parity problem, and why the fix is free

Testing the predicate before the degree is known means a vertex the old walk NEVER REACHED (its
`deg === 0` continue came first) could now surface a fault. That is the class of items 139, 142,
144 and 145, and it is reachable: `1 / (x.n - 30)` raises `E_INVALID_VALUE` on one vertex.

So the predicate runs inside a `try`, and the `catch` looks the degree up and **re-throws only
when the general path would have evaluated that vertex**. A fault on a degree-0 vertex is
swallowed, because the old walk never evaluated it; a fault anywhere else still raises. The
happy path pays nothing measurable — guarded 52.26ms against 51.81ms unguarded, and 14.86
against 14.68 — so this is correct by construction rather than by trade-off.

The prototype also measured the cheaper, safe-but-timid option (vertex order, degree still looked
up first, visitation set untouched): **1.33x only**. The short-circuit is where the win lives, so
the guard is what makes the item worth having.

### Measured, isolated, min-of-three, interleaved

| row                          | before (min, range) | after (min, range) |             ratio |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------: | -----------------: | ----------------: |
| far `age > 45` (49% pass)    |   92.63 (92.6-93.5) |  52.67 (52.7-55.5) |         **1.76x** |
| far `age > 85` (4.4% pass)   |   78.46 (78.5-82.1) |     8.65 (8.7-9.5) |          **9.1x** |
| far `age > 500` (0% pass)    |   80.14 (80.1-81.5) |     3.89 (3.9-4.6) |         **20.6x** |
| start `age > 45` (49% pass)  |   62.67 (62.7-63.1) |  44.29 (44.3-44.9) |         **1.41x** |
| start `age > 85` (4.4% pass) |   62.08 (62.1-62.2) |     8.80 (8.8-8.9) |          **7.1x** |
| CONTROL node count           |                0.07 |               0.05 |              flat |
| CONTROL plain hop count      |                0.07 |               0.07 |              flat |
| CONTROL node property filter |   12.50 (12.5-12.8) |  11.45 (11.5-12.0) | flat, overlapping |

Every claimed row has non-overlapping ranges and all three controls are flat. **The structural
change is in the columns, not the ratios:** before reads 93.5 / 82.1 / 81.5 across selectivities
(flat — it always did the whole scan) and after reads 55.5 / 8.7 / 3.9. That is the shape native
has.

The cross-engine screen agrees, with the `ffi` column flat: `traverse 1-hop + filter` 102.1 →
50.3 (68.7x → 33.9x against native) and `+ start filter` 75.7 → 43.0 (30.6x → 17.2x). Both rows
are the ones item 163 had just corrected, so these ratios are honest ones.

### Teeth: 19 tests, 7 mutants, and a survivor that was fixture blindness

| mutant                                             | result              |
| -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |
| swallow EVERY fault, not just degree-0 ones        | caught — 4 failures |
| invert the raise guard (re-throw only at degree 0) | caught — 5          |
| count the vertex instead of its degree             | caught — 11         |
| the untyped branch sums only the first bucket      | caught — 1          |
| a missing index row reads as degree 1              | caught — 10         |
| a multi-type hop takes only the first type         | caught — 1          |
| **drop `matchesLabel` entirely**                   | **SURVIVED all 17** |

The survivor is the valuable one. `candidateVertexSource` already narrows to the seed label's
bucket, so `matchesLabel` only matters where the label expression is NARROWER than the seed — and
the fixture had no such vertex carrying in-edges. Pure fixture blindness, the same failure as item
156's ring. Two tests fix it: a conjunction (`:Dst&Tag`, where the seed bucket includes an
untagged vertex that HAS an in-edge) and a disjunction (`:Dst|Src`, where `seedLabel` gives up
and `matchesLabel` is the only filter, with a non-matching vertex that has an in-edge). Both kill
it.

Degrees in the fixture are deliberately uneven — `x1` has two in-edges, `x2` one, `x3` none —
because a 1:1 fixture cannot tell a degree sum from a vertex count, which is this walk's entire
job. The degree-0 vertex is new coverage: the old walk never visited one, and it must contribute 0.

**Three of my own expectations were wrong and the tests said so.** Two were arithmetic: I read
`1 / (x.n - 30) < 99` as excluding a reached vertex when it is true for both of them, so the
swallow case counts 3 and not 2. The third used `-->`, which led somewhere else entirely.

### Found, not fixed: two edge-pattern spelling divergences

`MATCH (a)-->(x)` returned `[]` from the TS engine — ZERO rows for a `count(*)`, where an empty
match must still yield one row with 0 (the `age > 99` test in this very file returns 0 correctly).
Checked against the authoritative ISO BNF rather than memory:

```
<abbreviated edge pattern> ::=
    <left arrow> | <tilde> | <right arrow> | <left arrow tilde>
  | <tilde right arrow> | <left minus right> | <minus sign>
```

So `->` IS ISO and `-->` / `--` are Cypherisms. Both engines were asked:

| spelling                | TS                        | native                  |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `(a)->(x)` — **ISO**    | answers correctly (`c=1`) | **rejects, `E_SYNTAX`** |
| `(a)-->(x)` — Cypherism | returns `[]`              | rejects, `E_SYNTAX`     |
| `(a)--(x)` — Cypherism  | returns `[]`              | rejects, `E_SYNTAX`     |

> **CORRECTION (item 165).** The second and third rows above are MIS-DIAGNOSED. I wrote that TS
> "silently accepts two Cypherisms and answers them malformed". It does not. **`--` is the ISO
> simple comment introducer** (`<simple comment introducer> ::= --`), so `(a)-->(x)` lexes as
> `(a)` followed by a comment running to end of line, and the query TS actually ran was
> `MATCH (a)`. Both engines handle `--` comments correctly.
>
> The real defect those two rows were pointing at is broader and has nothing to do with edge
> spellings: **TS accepts a query with NO RESULT CLAUSE** (`MATCH (x)` alone, or
> `MATCH (x) WHERE x.n = 1`) and returns `[]`, where native raises `E_SYNTAX`. Fixed in item 165.
>
> The FIRST row stands, and item 165 found it is wider than one spelling: native is missing all
> seven abbreviated forms AND three of the seven full forms.

Gates separately: 19 new tests (875 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0 (it caught an unnecessary type assertion), `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 165. A query with no RETURN answered `[]` instead of refusing — and item 164's diagnosis of it was wrong

Item 164 wrote `MATCH (a)-->(x) RETURN count(*) AS c` in a test, got `[]`, and concluded TS was
silently accepting a Cypherism. **That was wrong.** `--` is the ISO SIMPLE COMMENT INTRODUCER
(`<simple comment introducer> ::= --`), so the query lexed as `MATCH (a)` followed by a comment
running to end of line. Both engines handle `--` comments correctly; the AST made it obvious —
the `RETURN` clause was simply absent.

Which exposed the real defect: **`MATCH (a)` parsed at all.**

### The rule, from the BNF

```
<ambient linear query statement> ::=
    [ <simple linear query statement> ] <primitive result statement>
<ambient linear data-modifying statement body> ::=
    <simple linear data-accessing statement> [ <primitive result statement> ]
<primitive result statement> ::= <return statement> [ <order by and page statement> ] | FINISH
```

Mandatory for a query, optional for a data-modifying statement. `parseLinearQuery`'s own comment
already said so — "optionally ending in RETURN or FINISH (a write-only query needs neither)" —
and nothing checked it. Ten shapes slipped through, each answering `[]` where native raised
`E_SYNTAX`:

|                            | TS before | TS after   | native     |
| -------------------------- | --------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| `MATCH (x)`                | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x) WHERE x.n = 1`  | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x)-[:E]->(y)`      | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `LET k = 1`                | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x) LET k = x.n`    | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x) ORDER BY x.n`   | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x) LIMIT 1`        | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x) FILTER x.n = 1` | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `FOR i IN [1, 2]`          | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |
| `MATCH (x) WITH x`         | `[]`      | `E_SYNTAX` | `E_SYNTAX` |

**A read with nothing to return read as an EMPTY ANSWER rather than a bad query** — the worst
shape a divergence can take, because `[]` is a plausible result. Ten divergences closed.

`isWrite` lists the writing kinds EXPLICITLY (`insert`, `merge`, `set`, `remove`, `delete`)
rather than negating the read-only ones, so a new clause kind defaults to needing a RETURN
instead of silently inheriting permission to drop it.

### The fix broke the predicate wrapper, and nine tests said so immediately

`parsePredicate` (which every declarative validator goes through) wrapped its input as
`MATCH (_v) WHERE <src>` — itself a result-clause-less query, now a syntax error. Nine validator
tests failed on the first run. The wrapper now ends in `RETURN 1 AS _r`, and its clause-count
guard moves from 1 to 2; a predicate smuggling its own `RETURN` still fails, because the
wrapper's trailing `RETURN` then becomes trailing input. Both are pinned by tests, since the
wrapper is internal and was only covered indirectly.

### Teeth: 24 tests, 7 mutants, 7 caught

| mutant                                    | result               |
| ----------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| drop the check entirely                   | caught — 12 failures |
| only RETURN counts, so FINISH is rejected | caught — 1           |
| every clause looks like a write           | caught — 12          |
| no clause looks like a write              | caught — 23          |
| SET is not a write                        | caught — 1           |
| the wrapper's clause count reverts to 1   | caught — 10          |
| the wrapper loses its RETURN              | caught — 12          |

The sixth **failed to apply** (`applied=0`, six leading spaces in my pattern against four in the
file) and the `applied=` assertion caught it rather than letting it read as a survivor. That is
the third time that guard has earned itself (items 155, 158, now this).

The `-- comment` pair is deliberately tested both ways: the two spellings that started this now
refuse, and `MATCH (x) RETURN count(*) AS c -- a trailing comment` still answers 2. Without the
second, this rule could have "fixed" the divergence by breaking comments.

`bun run lint` caught two real things: `isWrite` captured nothing so it belonged at module scope,
and moving it there put it between the file's `eslint-disable-next-line max-statements` comment
and `parse`, which silently transferred the disable onto `isWrite` — `parse` then failed the
statement cap at 117. The comment is re-attached.

### Native gaps found on the way (not fixed)

Pricing all seven variants of `<abbreviated edge pattern>` against their full-bracket
equivalents, on both engines, found native missing far more than one spelling:

| direction           | abbrev | full     | ts abbrev | ts full | native abbrev | native full  |
| ------------------- | ------ | -------- | --------- | ------- | ------------- | ------------ |
| pointing left       | `<-`   | `<-[]-`  | 1         | 1       | **E_SYNTAX**  | 1            |
| undirected          | `~`    | `~[]~`   | 2         | 2       | **E_SYNTAX**  | 2            |
| pointing right      | `->`   | `-[]->`  | 1         | 1       | **E_SYNTAX**  | 1            |
| left or undirected  | `<~`   | `<~[]~`  | 2         | 2       | **E_SYNTAX**  | **E_SYNTAX** |
| undirected or right | `~>`   | `~[]~>`  | 2         | 2       | **E_SYNTAX**  | **E_SYNTAX** |
| left or right       | `<->`  | `<-[]->` | 2         | 2       | **E_SYNTAX**  | **E_SYNTAX** |
| any direction       | `-`    | `-[]-`   | 2         | 2       | **E_SYNTAX**  | 2            |

**TS is fully conformant here and agrees with its own full spellings in all seven cases.** Native
is missing all seven abbreviated forms AND three of the seven full forms — the "or"-direction
combinations, which need matcher semantics it does not have. Plus a third gap: native implements
no `FINISH` at all (`MATCH (x) FINISH` and a bare `FINISH` both raise), though
`<primitive result statement>` names it. TS is the correct engine on all three, so none is
matched here.

### The intermittently-red gremlin fuzzer, diagnosed and fixed

The full fuzz sweep failed about one run in three — and the first instinct, that a green re-run
clears it, is wrong for a RANDOM-seeded gate. Eight runs of the differential fuzzer alone were
clean; the failure only appeared in the full sweep, so the sweep was looped with output captured
to a log, and the third caught it:

```
g.V().order(local).by(desc).bothE('CREATED', 'KNOWS').limit(2)      seed 100286502
    ts:     edges 7, 9
    native: edges 7, 8
```

**Pre-existing, not caused by this item**: the same seed fails identically on the pre-change
build, which is the first thing checked.

It is a positional slice over an unspecified order — exactly the class the fuzzer already skips
42 plans per run for. It slipped through because `slicedBeforeOrdering` tested
`indexOf('.order(')`, and `order(local)` LOOKS like it settles the sequence. It does not:
`Scope.local` sorts WITHIN each incoming element, so on a stream of scalars it is a no-op.
Confirmed against a real TinkerPop console rather than reasoned about:

```
V().id()                       -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
V().order(local).id()          -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
V().order(local).by(desc).id() -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

The skip rule now matches only a GLOBAL order (`/\.order\((?!\s*local\s*\))/`). The seed's skip
count goes 42 → 44 — two plans, not a blanket skip — and ten consecutive full sweeps are green
where roughly one in three was red.

Gates separately: 24 new tests (899 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across ten
consecutive sweeps on random seeds. No Rust changed, and no perf claim: this item is conformance,
so the bench is not the measurement.

## 166. Native was missing the whole `<abbreviated edge pattern>` production — 10 spellings

Item 165 priced this: all seven ISO abbreviated edge patterns raised `E_SYNTAX` in native, and so
did three of the seven FULL forms, while the TS engine answered every one and agreed with its own
full spellings. **The equivalent-spellings rule violated across engines rather than within one**,
which is why neither engine's own test suite could see it.

The last five items were TS and core; this one is native because a missing grammar production is
the largest remaining gap, and TS is already correct here.

| direction           | abbrev | full     | ts    | native BEFORE               | native AFTER |
| ------------------- | ------ | -------- | ----- | --------------------------- | ------------ |
| pointing left       | `<-`   | `<-[]-`  | 1 / 1 | **E_SYNTAX** / 1            | 1 / 1        |
| undirected          | `~`    | `~[]~`   | 2 / 2 | **E_SYNTAX** / 2            | 2 / 2        |
| pointing right      | `->`   | `-[]->`  | 1 / 1 | **E_SYNTAX** / 1            | 1 / 1        |
| left or undirected  | `<~`   | `<~[]~`  | 2 / 2 | **E_SYNTAX** / **E_SYNTAX** | 2 / 2        |
| undirected or right | `~>`   | `~[]~>`  | 2 / 2 | **E_SYNTAX** / **E_SYNTAX** | 2 / 2        |
| left or right       | `<->`  | `<-[]->` | 2 / 2 | **E_SYNTAX** / **E_SYNTAX** | 2 / 2        |
| any direction       | `-`    | `-[]-`   | 2 / 2 | **E_SYNTAX** / 2            | 2 / 2        |

All seven pairs now agree within each engine and across both.

### Three new tokens, and why the "or" directions were nearly free

`<->`, `<~` and `~>` were not tokens at all: `<->` lexed as `<-` plus a stray `>`, `<~` as `<`
plus `~`, `~>` as `~` plus `>`. The `<->` rule has to come BEFORE `<-` in the lexer or the longer
token never wins.

The three "or"-direction forms resolve to `Dir::Both`, and that follows from a convention the
engine already had rather than being a new decision: `~` carries NO direction here and already
means `Both`, so over a store where every edge is directed, left-or-undirected,
undirected-or-right and left-or-right are each `In ∪ Out`. The TS engine resolves all three to
`Both` too, which is what keeps the two byte-identical — so this cost a pairing table, not new
matcher semantics.

The `-`/`~` MIXES (`-[…]~`, `~[…]->`) are not ISO pairs but were already accepted here, so they
stay accepted: tightening them unilaterally would diverge from TS, which accepts them as well.
A separate question, recorded rather than bundled.

### One predicate instead of eight copies

`matches!(self.peek(), Some(Tok::Minus | Tok::LArrow | Tok::Tilde))` appeared at **seven** call
sites (the eighth was `rel` itself). Adding four delimiters would have meant getting all seven
right by hand — a shape where one miss leaves a production silently unreachable rather than
broken. They are now one `starts_rel` helper.

### Teeth: 9 native tests, 7 mutants, and a survivor that no count could ever catch

| mutant                                          | result               |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `->` resolves to `Both`                         | caught — 4 failures  |
| `starts_rel` drops `->`                         | caught — 4           |
| the abbreviated branch never fires              | caught — 4           |
| the lexer loses its `<->` longest-match         | caught — 2           |
| the lexer loses `~>`                            | caught — 3           |
| full `<-[…]->` resolves to `In`                 | caught — 2           |
| **`<-` resolves to `Out` (directions swapped)** | **SURVIVED all 960** |

The survivor is structural, not a thin fixture. **`count(*)` over `(x)->(y)` and over `(x)<-(y)`
both count EDGES**, so the two directions are indistinguishable by count at any size or shape —
no bigger or less symmetric fixture would have caught it. Only a BOUND ENDPOINT tells them apart,
so the new test reads `y.id` from a pinned start in both directions and both ways round:
`->` from `a` lands on `b` and finds nothing from `b`, `<-` the mirror. That kills it.

Nine tests (961 native, up from 952): every variant's direction, every abbreviated/full pair,
the three new full forms, the endpoint binding, chained and mixed-spelling hops, an untyped hop
finding an edge of an unrelated type, an abbreviated-only delimiter refusing a bracket, the
Cypher spellings still refused, and the comparison operators that share a prefix with `<-`/`<->`
(`<>`, `<=`, `<`) still lexing — that last because the `<` arm is the one this item edited.

### A conformance test, deliberately NOT fuzzer entries

The new forms needed a CROSS-engine check, since that is where the divergence lived. The obvious
move — adding the 7 pairs to the differential fuzzer's targeted list — was tried and **reverted**:
that band is `pick`ed from, so 18 added queries diluted every other shape's share and pushed
`hopUntypedNonZero` under its floor on some seeds. That is the dilution items 115, 125 and 152
each hit, and the file's own comment warns about it.

So the coverage is a deterministic `edge-pattern-conformance.test.ts` instead: 5 tests, 75
assertions, every pair checked within each engine AND across them, plus the directions by bound
endpoint, the isolated vertex a pair-counting bug would include, and the non-ISO spellings
refused identically. **Its teeth were verified**, not assumed: with the direction mutant applied
and the `.so` rebuilt, it fails on `MATCH (x:L {n: 2})<-(y:L)`; restored, it is green.

### The bench screen, and a flattering number with no mechanism

`bench_all`, two runs a side: `1hop_us` flat (119.3-119.6 against 119.3-119.8; 471-482 against
480-487; 1220-1245 against 1216-1242). But `filter_us` read **~7% FASTER** after, consistently
and with non-overlapping ranges at all three sizes (78.3-78.6 against 83.9-84.0, 312-321 against
339-346, 790-791 against 837-848).

**Not claimed.** `time_query` parses and optimizes OUTSIDE its timed region, so a parser change
cannot reach execution at all — the mechanism is absent, which makes this code layout, not a
win. Recorded because the usual failure here is the opposite (talking yourself out of a
regression); an unexplained improvement deserves the same scepticism as an unexplained
regression.

### Still open in native

`FINISH` remains unimplemented (`MATCH (x) FINISH` and a bare `FINISH` both raise `E_SYNTAX`),
though `<primitive result statement> ::= <return statement> [ … ] | FINISH` names it and TS
supports it. Left for its own item.

Gates separately: 9 new native tests (961 passing, plus 34 in `lenke-engine-core` which the
engine's own suite does not run), 5 new cross-engine tests, full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0, `fmt`/`fmt:check` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D
warnings` exit 0 on both crates (it caught two identical match arms, now merged), all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green across five sweeps on random seeds.

## 167. Drive the far side of a hop PROJECTION too — 2.2-2.6x, and a retracted target on the way

`traverse 1-hop project` was the biggest absolute TS query number left, 323.6ms against native's
77.4ms. The obvious target, and the one I started on, was **not** the answer.

### The target I retracted

The walk puts the far element into a binding `Map` and the compiled accessor takes it straight
back out, once per CELL. Specializing that away looked like the win. Prototyped against the real
graph, 1,000,000 rows:

|                                                        | ns/row |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -----: |
| today — binding `set` + a compiled accessor per cell   |    278 |
| direct bag read off `edge.to`, no binding, no accessor |    261 |
| the bag by id, never materializing the far `Vertex`    |    265 |
| **row floor — build and push `{n: 1}`**                | **84** |
| **walk floor — count the edges, build nothing**        | **59** |

**Removing the binding and the accessor buys 6%**, under the threshold this audit sets for
needing its own harness. The projection machinery was never the cost. Between the row floor (84)
and the real thing (261) sits ~180ns for ONE property read — which is item 164's finding again:
the far vertex is reached per EDGE, in edge order, so every read is a random lookup and a cold
pointer chase. Restructuring the projection cannot touch it, and neither prototype did.

### What the row order makes possible

The far vertex keys the OPPOSITE adjacency index, so the far endpoints can be walked in creation
order instead — and then the property is read once per far VERTEX rather than once per edge.
200,000 sequential reads instead of 1,000,000 random ones:

|                                                      |  ns/row |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------: |
| drive the far side, push one shared object           |      91 |
| drive the far side, spread-copy per edge             |     126 |
| **drive the far side, key loop over hoisted values** | **116** |

This is allowed only because **row order is unspecified** here, which is not my reading but the
cross-engine harness's own: _"Row order is unspecified and canonicalized out on purpose. Column
order is not."_ `resultsEqual` canonicalizes row order away, so reordering cannot break
byte-identity — and column order, which IS bytes, is preserved by rebuilding each row from the
keys of `projectRow`'s own output.

The rows are built FRESH per edge rather than pushing one shared object (91ns) because callers
may treat a row as their own; aliasing a million rows is a bug no measurement would show. The
key-loop form costs 25ns for that and is width-agnostic, which the spread is not.

Hoisting is sound because every item this path admits is a pure function of the far end: the
guard refuses a name that is neither endpoint, `!needsStart` means no item reads the start, and
the engine has no nondeterministic scalar (a bare `current_*` lowers to a param bound once per
query). So all of a far vertex's edges genuinely project the same cells.

### Measured, isolated, min-of-three, interleaved

| row                                    | before (min, range) | after (min, range) |     ratio |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------: | -----------------: | --------: |
| far-only, 1 column                     |     311.1 (311-330) |    138.8 (139-154) | **2.24x** |
| far-only, 2 columns                    |     337.8 (338-346) |    132.6 (133-155) | **2.55x** |
| far-only, 3 columns                    |     357.6 (358-365) |    136.5 (137-165) | **2.62x** |
| far-only, a far LABEL                  |     423.8 (424-429) |    171.7 (172-191) | **2.47x** |
| CONTROL start-driven (reads the start) |     312.4 (312-316) |    305.0 (305-319) |      flat |
| CONTROL node projection, no hop        |        83.9 (84-87) |       82.4 (82-85) |      flat |
| CONTROL count shortcut                 |                 0.1 |                0.1 |      flat |

The win GROWS with column count — 2.24x at one column, 2.62x at three — because a wider
projection adds cells to a template built once per far vertex rather than per edge. All three
controls are flat, the start-driven control confirming the untouched walk stayed untouched.

Cross-engine screen: `traverse 1-hop project` **323.6 → 117.2ms**, i.e. 4.18x behind native down
to **1.55x**. No other row moved.

### Teeth: 16 tests, 7 mutants, 6 caught — and one that CANNOT be

| mutant                                           | result                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| push one shared row object per edge (aliasing)   | caught — 1                             |
| one row per far VERTEX, losing the degree        | caught — 8                             |
| read the same index as the start-driven walk     | caught — 12                            |
| drop `matchesLabel`                              | **survived 42** → caught after 2 tests |
| take column order from a SORTED key list         | caught — 1                             |
| the dispatcher ignores a non-vacuous start label | caught — 6                             |
| **never take the far-driven walk at all**        | **survives, by construction**          |

`drop-far-label` survived for the same reason it did in item 166: `candidateVertexSource`
already narrows to the seed label's bucket, so the filter only earns its place where the label
expression is NARROWER than its seed. A conjunction (`:D&Tag`, the seed bucket holding an
untagged vertex that has in-edges) and a disjunction (`:D|S`, no seed at all) both kill it. Third
time this exact fixture blindness has appeared — it is now the first thing to check when a label
mutant survives.

**`never-far-driven` is uncatchable and should be**, which is worth stating rather than papering
over: disabling the walk yields the same rows in a different order, and row order is not a
contract. It is a PERFORMANCE mutant, and its guard is the measurement above, not a test. The
same reason item 94's note gives for why a passing probe is not evidence of correctness applies
in reverse here.

The fixture gives `h` three in-edges, `t` one and `iso` none, because a 1:1 fixture cannot
distinguish "one row per edge" from "one row per far vertex" — which is exactly what this walk
changes. Also covered: distinct row objects, column order against the projection, a far
expression, an absent property, both directions, a self-loop counted once (it sits in both
indexes and only one is read), a vacuous start label agreeing with the unlabelled spelling, and
fault parity in both directions.

### Two tests reworded, deliberately

`hop-projection.test.ts` had two tests asserting that the fused path matches the general path's
row ORDER, one of them named "in the same order as the general path". Both now compare multisets,
because their subject is agreement and order is not a contract; one of them also kept its point
exactly (that a self-loop row SURVIVES, independent of where it lands). A third test still pins
exact order and still passes — because its start label `P` is NOT vacuous in that fixture, so a
label has to be applied by iteration and the start-driven walk takes it. That reason is now
written down next to it, so nobody reads it as a general guarantee.

Gates separately: 16 new tests (899 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0 (one run exited 1
on the `@lenke/native:test` flake item 165 characterized; three further uncached full runs clean),
`bun run lint` exit 0 (it caught a missing blank line), `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green across four sweeps on random seeds — the gate that decides whether
reordering rows is actually free. No Rust changed.

## 168. The same flip in the Gremlin engine — 2.6x on the bench, and where it is NOT available

Item 167 made the vertex-side flip a pattern rather than a one-off, so this item did what the
method says and grepped for it elsewhere. The Gremlin bench had two large TS gaps, both
`V().out()`:

| traversal                 |    ts | native |     ratio |
| ------------------------- | ----: | -----: | --------: |
| `V().out().values(age)`   | 514.4 |   29.8 |     17.2x |
| `V().out().has().count()` | 130.1 |   1.53 | **84.8x** |

### Only one of them is available, and the reason matters

**`values(age)` cannot be flipped.** The Gremlin fuzzer compares results ORDERED unless a plan is
explicitly marked unordered (a multi-type hop or a reconverging branch), because TinkerPop
guarantees the output adjacency order of `V().out()`. So Gremlin's stream order is a contract
where GQL's row order is not — the opposite of what item 167 relied on. Checked before writing
any code, which is what stopped a change that would have failed the gate.

**`has(k, pred).count()` can be.** A count is order-free, so the far side can be driven: one
predicate test per far VERTEX, contributing that vertex's whole degree.

### What the existing shortcut was doing

`filteredHopCount` already existed — it walks the type's edge bucket and resolves `edge.to` per
EDGE, which is 1,000,000 random-order vertex lookups on the bench fixture. Its own comment says
that far-endpoint read costs "only ~17ns" because the far vertices "stay cache-warm", measured in
item 132. **That is true of the small unit fixture and not of 200,000 vertices** — the same
fixture-scale trap as item 163, and the reason an 84.8x row sat behind a shortcut that was
supposed to have fixed it. Prototyped over 1,000,000 edges:

| selectivity                     | edge-driven | vertex-driven |     ratio |
| ------------------------------- | ----------: | ------------: | --------: |
| `gt(44)`, ~50% pass (the bench) |     104.2ms |        34.1ms | **3.06x** |
| `gt(85)`, 4.4% pass             |     101.7ms |        29.8ms | **3.41x** |
| `gt(500)`, none pass            |     101.3ms |        25.3ms | **4.00x** |

Counts identical at all three. On the bench: **130.1 → 50.4ms, and 84.8x → 33.8x** against
native, with every other row flat and the bench's own cross-engine check still reading `same`.

**Raise parity comes free here**, unlike the GQL twin: the predicate is evaluated for exactly the
vertices carrying at least one edge of the queried type, which is exactly the set of far
endpoints the edge walk visits. No vertex gains or loses an evaluation. (And in the event — see
below — nothing throws anyway.)

The multi-type guard is kept: with several named types AND an edge carrying two of them, summing
per-vertex buckets would count that edge twice, so that case stays on the edge-driven walk, which
visits each edge once. A single type, or no two-type edge anywhere, takes the flip.

### Teeth: 25 tests, 7 mutants, 6 caught — and two lessons

| mutant                                          | result                           |
| ----------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| count the far vertex once, not its degree       | caught — 5                       |
| read the same index as the edge-driven walk     | caught — 7                       |
| the untyped branch sums only the first bucket   | **survived 23** → caught         |
| a multi-type hop takes only the first type      | **survived 23** → caught         |
| take the flip even with a two-type edge present | caught — 2                       |
| drop the predicate                              | caught — 10                      |
| **drop the degree-0 skip**                      | **survives — equivalent mutant** |

**My oracle was wrong first, and the file told me so.** I reached for `dedupe()` as the forced
decline, which this file's own header calls the identity "over a frontier that is already
distinct" — and the frontier after `out()` is NOT: vertex 2 is the target of two `E` edges, so
`dedupe()` folds 3 rows into 2 and reads as a wrong answer. Five tests failed that way. The
decline used instead is the SAME filter twice: `countShortcut` takes only `mid.length === 2`, so a
second `has` goes through the general walk, and an idempotent filter cannot change the count.

**The two survivors were fixture blindness with a specific shape.** Vertex 1 is the only far
endpoint whose in-edges span two types (`{E: 1, F: 2}`), and `k=1` FAILS `gt(1)` — so the one
vertex that could distinguish "sum the buckets" from "take the first" never reached the total.
`gt(0)` includes it and both mutants die. Fourth appearance of this class (items 156, 162, 166,
167), and it is always the same question: does the fixture contain an element that both differs
in the relevant way AND survives the filter?

**`drop-degree-zero-skip` is an EQUIVALENT mutant and should be left alone.** With the skip
removed, a non-endpoint vertex has `deg === 0`, so `n += deg` adds nothing — the count is
unchanged. It could only matter if the predicate threw, and empirically none does: a cross-type
`gt` is FILTERED, not raised, on both paths (I expected a throw, on the strength of the
predicate-comparator note in `predicates.ts`, and wrote two tests asserting one; both failed).
What is pinned instead is the behaviour the engine actually has, on both paths. The skip stays as
an optimization and as insurance, not as something a test can guard — saying so is more useful
than contriving a test that would pass either way.

### Found, not fixed: an intermittently red differential gate

A full fuzz sweep failed about 1 in 16, and the capture is a GQL divergence, not a Gremlin one:

```
FUZZ_SEED=2620441503
MATCH (n:T) CALL (n) { MATCH (n WHERE CASE WHEN (n.x > CASE WHEN ('' <> -2.5) THEN 1e-300
  WHEN (n.s > 0.5) THEN '…' ELSE n.m END) THEN (n.m IS NOT NULL) WHEN … END)-[:E]->(m)
  RETURN m.n AS mn } RETURN mn AS x ORDER BY x
    ts:     err E_INVALID_VALUE
    native: ok [{"x":5},{"x":11}]
    (evaluation-order: an evaluation-order difference, but no registry entry covers this shape)
```

**Pre-existing, not this item**: the same seed fails identically on the pre-change build, which
is the first thing checked. It is a nested `CASE` inside a `CALL` subquery's inline `WHERE`, where
TS evaluates something native does not — the shape of the `and-chain-seeding-divergence` already
on record. Recorded with its reproducing seed for its own item rather than left as unexplained
intermittent red.

Gates separately: 25 tests in the gremlin count-shortcut suite (730 in the package), full TS
suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, byte-identity fuzzers green
on 21 of 22 sweeps with the one failure captured, reproduced, and shown to pre-date this change.
No Rust changed.

## 169. The "`CALL`-body laziness bug" was never laziness — a missing truth-type check

Item 168 captured a reproducing seed for the divergence making the fuzz gate red about 1 run in 16. This item minimized it, and the minimization refuted two hypotheses before finding the cause.

### What it was not

The failing generated query was 300 characters of nested `CASE`, `cot`, `cos` and cross-type
comparisons. Minimizing it one ingredient at a time:

| shape                                    | ts                | native            |
| ---------------------------------------- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| `'' <> -2.5` standalone                  | `true`            | `true`            |
| `'a' > 0.5` standalone                   | `null`            | `null`            |
| `WHERE cos(0.0)` standalone              | `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `E_INVALID_VALUE` |
| `MATCH (n:T WHERE cos(0.0))` inline      | `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `E_INVALID_VALUE` |
| a CONTINUING `MATCH` re-binding `n`      | `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `E_INVALID_VALUE` |
| plain `WHERE`, non-boolean for SOME rows | `E_INVALID_VALUE` | `E_INVALID_VALUE` |
| **inside `CALL (n) { … }`**              | `E_INVALID_VALUE` | **rows**          |

So: **not** the cross-type comparison (both engines agree on all of them), **not** the
continuing-MATCH inline `WHERE` of items 157/158, and **not** the AND-chain seeding family that
item 115 recorded as "a decision, not a defect to patch in a perf tick". That family's signature
is a seek narrowing rows away, and the plain-`WHERE` row above shows seeding is not involved:
both engines raise there. `CALL` is the whole locus.

Minimal repro, which the audit did not previously have:

```
MATCH (n:T) CALL (n) { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(m)
  WHERE CASE WHEN n.x > 0 THEN true ELSE 1.0 END RETURN m.n AS mn } RETURN mn AS x
    ts: E_INVALID_VALUE     native: [{"x":11}]
```

### What it was

`pull_body`'s `Plan::Filter` arm derived its own keep-set:

```rust
let mask = eval(pred, store, &b)?;
let keep = match &mask {
    Col::Bool(bs) => …,
    other => (0..other.len()).filter(|&i| other.value_at(i).is_true()).collect(),
};
```

`is_true()` reads a NON-BOOLEAN as `false`. Every other filter in the engine routes through
`as_truth`, which rejects it. So a predicate that is a truth value for some rows and not others
silently dropped the offending rows inside a subquery body and raised everywhere else.

The divergence registry names this shape the "`CALL`-body laziness bug" and deliberately refuses
to absorb it — its matcher requires an EMPTY result on the permissive side precisely so this case
escapes and stays visible. **It was never laziness.** And `filter_keep`'s own comment is the rule
the arm broke:

> a second derivation of "which rows does this predicate keep" is exactly the kind of drift that
> makes two spellings of one query disagree

`pull_body` serves `CALL` bodies, `EXISTS` bodies, branch arms and the streaming driver, so all
of them had it.

### The obvious fix was a 20% regression, and the bench caught it

The right shape is to call `filter_keep` — one derivation, no drift. Measured on `bench_all`,
two runs a side:

| `filter_us` | without the fix | via `filter_keep` |
| ----------- | --------------: | ----------------: |
| 50,000      |       77.8-78.2 |              93.1 |
| 200,000     |     303.8-307.5 |       371.7-375.3 |
| 500,000     |     760.6-789.6 |       929.3-935.0 |

**~20%, non-overlapping and reproducible** — because `pull_body` is on the STREAMING path, not
only in subquery bodies, so this arm is hot. `filter_keep` tries a storage fast path first and
falls back to `eval_mask`; neither is free on this shape.

So the committed form is `as_truth(&eval(pred, store, &b)?)?` filtered to `Some(true)` — which is
exactly what `filter_keep`'s general path reduces to, so the SEMANTICS are its semantics (the
three-valued mask, UNKNOWN dropped) at the cost this arm already paid:

| `filter_us` | without the fix |           with `as_truth` |
| ----------- | --------------: | ------------------------: |
| 50,000      |       77.8-78.2 |                 74.3-80.5 |
| 200,000     |     303.8-307.5 | 305.2-321.8 (min of four) |
| 500,000     |     760.6-789.6 |               766.7-793.9 |

Overlapping at all three sizes — flat. `1hop_us` flat throughout as the control.

This is the second item running where this bench row moved for reasons unrelated to intent (item
166 saw it read 7% FASTER with no mechanism, attributed to code layout). The difference is that
this time the mechanism is real and the direction is a regression, which is exactly why a screen
with a control is worth running even when the change is a correctness fix.

### What the fix revealed about the registry

`DECLARED boolean-context-dynamic-operand-under-seek` fell from **23 occurrences per sweep to
0-3**. Most of what that entry was absorbing was THIS bug wearing the declared family's clothes —
error-against-empty, which its matcher accepts — not the irreducible seeding case its `reason`
describes. The entry is still used, so it is still earning its place, but it was covering an order
of magnitude more than it should have been.

### Coverage floors re-measured, with the reason recorded

Three floors then failed, and lowering a floor to make a suite pass is what the note above them
forbids. Two things had moved the band, and both are stated in the file rather than just the
numbers changed:

1. **Drift.** On the PRE-fix build, four runs read `hopFilter 386-445 / 269-302` and
   `hopUntyped 46-58 / 43-54` — already below the recorded `429-477 / 293-354` and `47-81 /
44-73`, from the arm gaining shapes over items 125-168, exactly as that note predicts.
2. **This fix.** The counters tally queries that PRODUCE ROWS, and queries that used to
   wrongly produce rows are now errors, so they leave the non-empty population. That is the fix
   working, not coverage being lost.

Twelve post-fix observations: `hopFilter 376-425 / 248-307`, `hopUntyped 35-59 / 26-53`.
`hopFilterNonZero > 250` had become unreachable at the low end (248). The new floors sit ~15-25%
under the observed minimum — the same margin the old ones had — and their job is unchanged: catch
a shape falling silently to ZERO. Eight consecutive full sweeps green afterwards.

### Teeth: 4 native tests, 3 mutants, 3 caught

| mutant                                      | result      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| revert to the `is_true()` derivation        | caught — 3  |
| keep every row (the filter stops filtering) | caught — 14 |
| treat UNKNOWN as TRUE                       | caught — 3  |

The third matters because the fix had to preserve three-valued semantics, not just add a type
check: a null operand must still DROP the row rather than raise or keep it. Four tests: the
per-row non-boolean in all three `CALL` positions (subquery clause `WHERE`, near-node inline
`WHERE`, far-node inline `WHERE`), an unconditionally non-boolean one (which was already rejected
and must stay so, since the fix must not have narrowed to the per-row case), an `EXISTS` body
(which shares `pull_body`), and a boolean predicate still filtering correctly at three
selectivities plus the UNKNOWN case.

Gates separately: 4 new native tests (965 passing, plus 34 in `lenke-engine-core`), full TS suite
exit 0, `bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt`/`fmt:check` exit 0, `cargo fmt --check` exit 0, `cargo clippy
--all-targets -D warnings` exit 0 on both crates, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across
eight consecutive sweeps, and the original seed `FUZZ_SEED=2620441503` now passes.

## 170. A fused walk for `V().out(T).values(k)` — 1.7x, and the probe over-promised by 1.5x

`V().out().values(age)` was the biggest remaining TS Gremlin number: 528ms against native's 32,
16.6x. Item 168 established that its ORDER is a contract (TinkerPop guarantees `V()`-then-adjacency
and the Gremlin fuzzer compares ordered), so item 167's vertex-side flip is unavailable here. What
is available is the pipeline itself.

### Priced against its own floors first

Over 1,000,000 edges, before writing anything:

|                                           | ns/row |
| ----------------------------------------- | -----: |
| `V().out(T).values(age)` — the pipeline   |    539 |
| a hand walk in the same order, eager      |    241 |
| the same as ONE generator (what can ship) |    251 |
| push a constant (array growth alone)      |     68 |
| count the edges (adjacency alone)         |     60 |

So ~288ns/row is pipeline machinery and ~180ns is the far vertex's property read — a random-order
lookup, irreducible AT THIS ORDER (item 164). Laziness costs only 10ns/row, which retires the
worry: `run` returns an iterable and the engines already differ on laziness under a zero-row
slice, so an eager array would change observable behaviour for a caller taking one value.

### TinkerPop settled two semantics before any code

`values(k)` **DROPS** an element lacking the key rather than emitting null — not a guess, a console
run: `V().count()` is 6 where `V().values('age').count()` is 4, and `V().out().count()` is 6
against `V().out().values('age').count()` 2. My first hand-walk floor used `?? null` and was
therefore measuring the wrong thing.

And a STORED null IS emitted (`[null]`), because in this engine null is a present value, not
absence. So the test is `value !== undefined`, not nullishness — the two cases differ and both are
pinned.

### The probe over-promised by 1.5x, and the reason is on the record

Wired up with the engine's own helpers, the row read **375.6ms**, not the 251 the probe promised.
The helpers are generators: `adjacentEdges` → `outEdgesOf` → `iterByLabel`, which `yield*`s into
`iterLabeled` — two delegation layers per edge that my probe had inlined away.
`harness-must-resemble-caller`, again, and this time the probe flattered the change rather than the
baseline.

The fix is not to re-derive the iteration. For a SINGLE named type on `out`/`in`, `iterLabeled` is
literally `yield* byLabel.get(labels[0]) ?? []` and `otherEndpoint` is `edge.to` / `edge.from`, so
iterating that one `Set` directly is provably the same order and the same edges. Multi-type,
untyped and `both` keep going through the helpers — which is what makes them correct for free,
including the dedupe of an edge carrying two of the named types and `both`'s two-sided walk over a
self-loop.

### Measured, controlled, three runs a side

|                         |                before |                 after |
| ----------------------- | --------------------: | --------------------: |
| `V().out().values(age)` | 464.1 / 541.7 / 533.9 | 276.5 / 273.0 / 281.8 |

Non-overlapping. **1.70x on the minimum** (464.1 → 273.0), and 14.6x behind native down to 8.8x.
Every other Gremlin row flat, and the GQL cross-engine screen untouched (this is a Gremlin-only
change). The bench's own cross-engine check still reads `same` on the row.

### Teeth: 16 tests, 8 valid mutants, 7 caught

| mutant                                     | result                 |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------- |
| emit null for a missing key (fast path)    | **survived** → caught  |
| emit null for a missing key (general path) | **survived** → caught  |
| drop a STORED null as well                 | caught                 |
| the wrong endpoint for `out`               | caught — 8             |
| the wrong adjacency index                  | caught                 |
| let `both` take the single-type fast path  | caught                 |
| accept any number of projected keys        | caught                 |
| fire when the plan tracks path             | survives — unreachable |

**The oracle is `unfold()`, not `dedupe()`.** Order is the contract, so the fused walk must match
the pipeline's SEQUENCE. `unfold()` over scalars is a no-op that makes the plan four steps, so the
shortcut declines and the same question goes through the pipeline. `dedupe()` would have been the
item-168 trap again: the frontier after `out()` has duplicates.

**Both missing-key mutants survived at first, for two different reasons, and both are worth
keeping:**

- The fast-path one survived because **bun's `toEqual` compares `[20, 30]` equal to
  `[20, 30, undefined]`** — so an INFLATED stream passed, and even the comparison against the
  piped oracle passed. Fixed with explicit `.length` assertions and `toStrictEqual`. Any test
  asserting "this element was dropped" needs a length check.
- The general-path one survived because the fast path and the general path have their own copy of
  the presence check, and only the fast path's was covered: no `both`/multi-type test had a
  reachable far vertex LACKING the key. Fifth appearance of this fixture blindness in this audit
  (items 156, 162, 166, 167, 168), always the same question — does the fixture contain an element
  that differs in the relevant way AND reaches the code under test?

`ignore-tracks-path` survives and should: `PATH_DEPENDENT_KINDS` contains none of `V`/`out`/
`values`, so `tracksPath` is always false for the only shape the shortcut accepts. The guard is
unreachable today and is kept as insurance against the shape guard being relaxed, not as something
a test can reach — the same honest treatment item 168's degree-0 skip got. A ninth mutant (return
an eager array) is NOT counted: an eager array is still re-iterable and still yields the same
values, so laziness is not unit-observable here. Its guard is the 10ns/row measurement.

### A method note: a `git stash pop` brought foreign work into the tree

Measuring the before state needed the change out of the way, and `git stash push` on a mix of
tracked and UNTRACKED paths does not stash the untracked one — so the pop left a dangling import
and the bench produced no output at all. Worse, the tree then held two modified Rust files that
were not mine: `#[inline(never)]` profiling annotations across `fastpath.rs` and an `order(local)`
guard in `exec.rs`. They are now in a stash labelled "NOT MINE - found in tree during item 170"
rather than discarded, and HEAD was restored for both files before continuing.

Two rules out of it: **an untracked file cannot be stashed by path**, so revert the tracked
reference instead (`git checkout HEAD -- <the file with the hook>`) and leave the new file
unreferenced; and **`git status` before every commit is not a formality** — `git diff --stat` on
directories the change should not touch is what caught this.

Gates separately: 16 new tests (743 in the gremlin package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0 (it caught three real things — a destructuring preference and two unnecessary type
assertions), `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across four
sweeps on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 171. Every write scheduled a notification nobody was waiting for — 1.76x per write, invisible to the bench

`decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` is the biggest absolute TS number, 2755ms against native's 760.
Subtracting the nodes-only row leaves ~2500ns per EDGE where native is ~535, so this went after
`addEdge`. What it found is not in `addEdge` at all.

### The measurement had to be fixed first

The obvious probe — every variant in one process — produced an IMPOSSIBLE ordering: `addEdge` with
no properties slower than with them, and with no id slower than both. Two separate faults:

- each timed body allocates a fresh 1.2-million-element graph, so the previous one is garbage and
  min-of-three does not fix cross-iteration GC at that size. One variant per PROCESS fixed it;
- "no id" is genuinely MORE work, not less — omitting it makes `addEdge` generate one with
  `rando()`. My assumption was backwards.

With that settled, per edge: `JSON.parse` 692ns, `addEdge` ~2690ns. So parse is 23% and the write
is the rest.

### What the profile said, and what is NOT the answer

|                                                         | % of the `addEdge` profile |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------: |
| `indexEdgeLabel`                                        |                       20.2 |
| `getEdgeById`                                           |                       13.9 |
| `#commitProperties`                                     |                        7.4 |
| `Set` constructor                                       |                        6.1 |
| `notify` + `scheduleNotify` + `setTimeout` + `tokensOf` |                        ~12 |

**`indexEdgeLabel` is retracted as a target.** It does 5 `Map.get`s and 3 `Set.add`s per edge and
allocates a Map and a Set per (vertex, direction) — 400,000 of each over this fixture. That is the
three-index design (`edgesByLabel`, `edgesFromByLabel`, `edgesToByLabel`), not a missing path, and
it confirms the recorded `ts-ingest-is-constant-factor` conclusion rather than overturning it.
`getEdgeById` is likewise one required `Map.get` for `addEdge`'s id-idempotence, at the
random-order cost items 161/162/164 already priced.

(Noted, not changed: the duplicate branch reads `if (this.getEdgeById(id)) return
this.getEdgeById(id)!` — two lookups where one would do. It is the cold path, so changing it would
be diff noise with no measurable effect.)

### The real find was deferred, which is why it hid

`markMutated` runs on every mutation and queues a microtask that bumps the reactive counters and
calls `scheduleNotify()` — a `clearTimeout` plus a `setTimeout` per write, whose `notify` then
iterates a listener set that in a bulk ingest is EMPTY.

It hid because a tight synchronous write loop never drains its own microtasks, so the cost lands
after the timer stops. Timing the loop and the drain separately over 1,000,000 edges:

|        |          loop |           drain |         total |
| ------ | ------------: | --------------: | ------------: |
| before | 2566.4-2709.8 | **258.5-262.2** | 2826.5-2972.0 |
| after  | 2539.6-2721.1 |   **31.5-32.3** | 2571.3-2753.4 |

The drain is **8.2x** with non-overlapping ranges; the loop is flat, which is correct — the
scheduling happens in the microtask, not the loop.

### The serving case is the real headline, and it has an ideal control

A per-write timer matters most to small writes, so that got its own harness: 200,000
`setProperty` calls on a warm graph, min-of-five, with the SUBSCRIBED case as the control — the
guard must change nothing when a subscriber actually exists.

|                          |     before (3 obs) |          after (3 obs) |                            |
| ------------------------ | -----------------: | ---------------------: | -------------------------- |
| no subscriber            | 92.2 / 92.6 / 92.3 | **52.3 / 60.2 / 55.3** | **1.76x**, non-overlapping |
| **subscribed (CONTROL)** | 90.7 / 96.2 / 94.0 |     91.3 / 94.7 / 93.1 | overlapping, flat          |

461ns per write down to 262ns with nobody listening, and 453 against 456ns when someone is. The
control is what makes this a removal of pointless work rather than a trade.

### The bench cannot see it, and that is the point

`decode ndjson (5 edges/node)` reads 2709.7 after against 2755.5 before — unchanged. The bench
times the synchronous `deserialize` call, and the work this removes was always deferred past it
(landing, if anywhere, inside the NEXT rep's window). **A cost that escapes the benchmark's timing
boundary can survive 170 audit items**, which is the generalizable lesson here: when a hot path
queues a microtask or a timer, measure the drain separately or the screen will call the change
free in both directions.

### Why it is safe

`subscribe` does not notify on subscribe, and `notify` reads the listener set as it is when the
timer fires. So the only behaviour that changes is this: a listener subscribing AFTER a write is no
longer told about that write. It is not owed that — it reads its first snapshot on subscribing and
already sees it. The reactive counters (`version`, `epoch`) still advance on every write, because
both are public and a caller may poll them without ever subscribing; skipping those would silently
freeze such a poller, and a mutant that did exactly that is one of the four below.

### Teeth: 6 tests, 4 mutants, 4 caught

| mutant                                                 | result     |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- |
| invert the guard (notify only when unlistened)         | caught — 9 |
| never schedule at all                                  | caught — 9 |
| skip the reactive BOOKKEEPING too, not just scheduling | caught — 5 |
| drop the debounce cancel (notify per write)            | caught — 2 |

The third and fourth are the ones worth having: the counters must keep moving for an unsubscribed
poller, and the subscribed path must still coalesce a burst into ONE notification (a 50-write
burst asserts exactly one call). Also pinned: a subscriber added after a write is silent for it and
notified by the next one — the behaviour change itself, asserted rather than left implicit.

Gates separately: 6 new tests (319 in the core package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit
0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps on
random seeds. No Rust changed, and the cross-engine screen is unchanged by construction — see
above.

## 172. The planner reversed away from its own seed pre-filter — 20x, and a filter that made a query 13x slower

`read: permission check` in `bench:usage` was the widest gap anywhere in the repo: **13 ops/sec in
TS against 39,000 in native** without indexes, 2800x. It is also 45x worse than `read: 2-hop
recommendation`, which is also a 2-hop query — so the shape mattered, not the hop count.

Two retractions came first, both priced:

- **An adjacency box** (the items 161/162 treatment for `edgesFromByLabel`). The row lookup is
  only 14ns isolated (46ns in context), a cached row reads 128ns against today's 174, and the
  dense-array ceiling is 97 — so 1.35x for a cross-cutting cache with invalidation on `addEdge`
  and `removeEdge`. Bad trade, dropped.
- **Coalescing the per-write microtask** left over from item 171. After that item's guard the
  drain is 31.5ms per 1,000,000 writes, so ~5% of a small write — under the threshold.

### The signature this repo is named after

The fixture is 20,000 users → 200 teams → 2,000 resources, so one user's permission check has a
10-row answer. Measured on the same pattern:

|                                    |        ms |    rows |
| ---------------------------------- | --------: | ------: |
| no filter                          |      6.77 | 200,000 |
| **start-only `WHERE u.name = $n`** | **87.87** |  **10** |
| the same with the tail UNLABELLED  |      2.26 |      10 |
| no filter, unlabelled tail         |      3.61 | 200,000 |

**Adding a filter made it 13x slower while returning 20,000x fewer rows** — and with an unlabelled
tail the identical filter made it faster, correctly. "A filter that makes a query slower is a
declined fast path, not the cost of filtering" is already written in `hop-projection.ts`; here it
pointed at the planner.

### The cause

`orient` reverses a pattern when the far end looks like the cheaper seed:
`estimateSeed(start)` = 20,000 Users against `estimateSeed(end)` = 2,000 Resources, so it flipped.
But `estimateSeed` only sees index seeks and label-bucket sizes — an **UNINDEXED** predicate
contributes nothing. So it could not see that `u.name = $n` selects 1 of 20,000, and reversing
demoted item 154's seed pre-filter (which can only gate the side it names) to a post-filter.
Starting from 2,000 resources and expanding backwards materializes 200,000 rows to return 10;
the profile is `expand`, `walkSegments`, `withBinding` allocating a Map per row, and
`evalLabelExpr`.

The guard is three lines: **do not reverse when the start carries a pre-filter.** The asymmetry is
what justifies it without a selectivity estimate — if the predicate turns out to reject little,
staying put scans the seeds the unfiltered plan would have expanded anyway; reversing when the
predicate IS selective expands the whole far side instead of one seed.

### Measured, controlled, two runs a side

| row                                          |          before |             after |                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | --------------: | ----------------: | ---------------- |
| **TARGET start-only `WHERE`, labelled tail** |   60.35 / 65.81 |   **2.98 / 5.22** | **20.2x**        |
| RISK non-selective start `WHERE` (keeps all) | 116.35 / 121.09 |   113.65 / 117.50 | flat             |
| RISK half-selective start `WHERE`            |  96.73 / 109.26 | **55.10 / 55.42** | **1.76x faster** |
| CONTROL far-end `WHERE` (no prefilter)       |   75.24 / 82.00 |     81.79 / 92.30 | noise            |
| CONTROL unlabelled tail (never reversed)     |     2.38 / 2.42 |       1.98 / 2.02 | flat             |
| CONTROL one hop, start `WHERE`               |     2.03 / 2.04 |       1.66 / 1.70 | flat             |

**The risk cases are not risks**: not reversing is better or equal at every selectivity tried,
which is the asymmetry argument confirmed rather than assumed. The two CONTROL rows that moved
cannot be affected by construction — neither produces a `prefilter` (a far-end `WHERE` has a free
variable that is not the start; no filter has no `where` at all), so the guard cannot fire for
them; that movement is this probe's noise, which builds a 22,000-vertex graph per process.

On the bench row itself: `read: permission check` **13 → 573 ops/sec, 44x**.

### Teeth: 12 tests, 4 mutants, 4 caught — but only after testing the DECISION

| mutant                                                    | result                   |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| `reversePath` stops flipping the edge direction           | caught — 3               |
| `reversePath` pairs the wrong endpoint                    | caught — 3               |
| never reverse at all                                      | **survived 37** → caught |
| **reverse ONLY when a prefilter exists (the bug itself)** | **survived 37** → caught |

The last two are the point. **Orientation is answer-preserving by construction**, so no
result-based test can see it — including the mutant that restores the exact 20x defect this item
fixes. Items 167 and 168 hit the same wall and accepted it; here there was a way out, because
`orient` is exported: three tests call it directly with a hand-built `CPath` and assert which
endpoint it starts from, with and without a pre-filter, plus a third asserting the two differ so
the pair cannot pass for an unrelated reason. That turns a performance decision into something
deterministic.

The answer-based tests still earn their place — they caught the two reversal-machinery mutants —
and they cover the spellings (clause / inline anchor / inline `WHERE`) agreeing, the labelled and
unlabelled tails agreeing, a tail label that must still exclude, a `WHERE` reading both ends, and
a three-hop pattern so the guard cannot be segment-count specific.

### Found, not fixed: the inline spelling still reverses

`MATCH (u:User {name: $n})-[…]` is **17 ops/sec** where the clause form is now 573 — a **34x
spread between two spellings of one query**, which is the bug class this engine is named after.
The reason is mechanical: `pushWhereIntoNode` folds an inline anchor into the start node's
predicate, so it never becomes a `prefilter` and the guard cannot see it.

Extending the guard to "the start carries any predicate" would close it, but not safely as a
one-liner: an inline anchor on the start with a genuine INDEX SEEK available on the far end is a
case where reversing is right, and `estimateSeed` does not report whether its number came from an
index or from a label bucket. The refinement is to compare provenance, not just magnitude — refuse
to let a LABEL-BUCKET estimate beat a constrained start, while still letting an indexed one win.
Left for its own item rather than bundled in under-measured.

Gates separately: 12 new tests (911 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint` exit
0 (it caught two unnecessary type assertions), `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 173. A seed estimate's PROVENANCE, not its size — the inline spelling, 10.9x, and a 34x spread closed

Item 172 fixed the clause spelling and left its twin: `MATCH (u:User {name: $n})-[…]` ran at 17
ops/sec where the clause form reached 573 — **a 34x spread between two spellings of one query**,
which is the bug class this engine is named after. `pushWhereIntoNode` folds an inline anchor into
the start node's PREDICATE, so it never becomes a `prefilter` and item 172's guard could not see
it.

### Why the one-line extension was not safe

"Never reverse away from a constrained start" would close the gap and break a case where reversing
is right. Measured before touching anything, on the 20,000-user authz fixture:

|                                                   |       ms |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------: |
| inline start anchor, far end a plain label        |    42.67 |
| **inline start anchor AND an INDEXED far anchor** | **0.12** |
| unconstrained start, indexed far anchor           |     0.16 |

The last two are fast precisely BECAUSE the planner reverses onto a real index seek. So the rule
has to distinguish a number that means something from one that does not.

`estimateSeed` returned a bare count from two very different sources: `indexCandidates` (a real,
narrow seek) or `candidateCount(label)` (how many vertices carry a label, which says nothing about
that node's predicates — an unindexed one contributes nothing at all). It now reports
`{ count, indexed }`, and `orient` applies: **a LABEL-BUCKET estimate may not outvote a
constrained start; an INDEX SEEK still may.**

### Asking the cheap question first, and what it cost not to

Only `pred.props` and `seedHints` can produce a seek — those are the two things `indexCandidates`
reads — so "could the far end seek at all?" is answerable from the compiled pattern with NO graph
work. Checking that before estimating anything keeps the common case free.

Getting that order wrong was measurable, and both readings are recorded because they are the
evidence for the final shape: computing both estimates up front cost the clause shape item 172 had
just fixed **2.00 → 2.33ms** and the indexed-far-anchor shape **0.11 → 0.13ms**, each reproducible
— two seed estimates where item 172 had a short circuit.

### Measured, controlled, three observations a side

| row                                             |                before |                  after |                            |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------: | ---------------------: | -------------------------- |
| **TARGET inline anchor**                        | 38.44 / 38.68 / 42.67 | **3.53 / 3.57 / 4.23** | **10.9x**                  |
| **inline `WHERE` on the start node**            | 37.79 / 38.27 / 38.78 | **2.22 / 4.14 / 4.59** | **17.0x**                  |
| CONTROL non-selective inline start (`{age: 7}`) | 35.84 / 36.00 / 36.92 | **2.98 / 3.01 / 3.49** | 12.0x faster               |
| **RISK inline start + INDEXED far anchor**      |    0.11 / 0.12 / 0.12 |     0.12 / 0.13 / 0.15 | flat — the seek still wins |
| RISK unconstrained start + indexed far anchor   |                  0.16 |                   0.21 | flat                       |
| CONTROL no filter anywhere                      |                  3.63 |                   3.38 | flat                       |

On the bench row: `read: permission check (inline anchor)` **17 → 621 ops/sec, 37x**. The two
spellings now read 590 and 621 ops/sec — **a 1.05x spread where it was 34x**.

### A disclosed regression with no mechanism

`CONTROL clause WHERE` — item 172's own fix — reads **2.00-2.02 before against 2.13-2.37 after**,
six observations a side, non-overlapping. That is a real ~1.1x and it is reported rather than
buried, but the mechanism is absent: for that shape the new code is `constrained && !mightSeek(r)`
→ return, which performs ZERO seed estimates, exactly as item 172's `prefilter !== undefined` →
return did. Same plan, same rows, same graph work, differing by about five property reads on a
once-per-query call.

What it looks like instead is code layout: the module grew four small functions, and other rows in
it moved in BOTH directions (one-hop inline start 1.98 → 2.20 worse, no-filter 3.63 → 3.38
better). Items 166 and 169 recorded the same signature, one in each direction. Flagged, not
claimed as understood.

### Teeth: 19 tests, 6 mutants, 6 caught — the last only after a seedHints case

| mutant                                               | result                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| ignore provenance entirely (the old rule)            | caught                   |
| treat a LABEL BUCKET as indexed                      | caught                   |
| treat a real SEEK as unindexed                       | caught                   |
| an inline anchor stops counting as a constraint      | caught — 2               |
| the no-graph-work short circuit fires for everything | caught — 4               |
| **`mightSeek` ignores `seedHints`**                  | **survived 46** → caught |

The survivor is the same lesson as item 172, one level down. A clause `WHERE` on the FAR end is
lifted into that node's `seedHints`, not its `props` — so a `mightSeek` reading only props stopped
a legitimate reversal, and because orientation does not change answers, every result-based test
passed. `seedHints` is the second of the two things `indexCandidates` reads and needed its own
case: a hand-built `CPath` whose end node carries a hint, against a graph with an index on that
key, asserting the walk starts at the far end.

That is now the third time in two items that the only tests with teeth here are the ones calling
`orient` directly. The paired cases are what make them evidence rather than assertion: indexed far
anchor reverses / UNINDEXED far anchor does not, and constrained start stays / unconstrained start
reverses — each pair differing in exactly one input.

`bun run lint` exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across
