## 174. A subquery conjunct must not ride into the node fold — 66x, and a raise divergence closed

`analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` was the widest remaining row in `bench:usage`: **8 ops/sec
unindexed**. The query:

```
MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n AND EXISTS { MATCH (u)-[:FOLLOWS]->{2,4}(u) } RETURN u.name AS n
```

A 20,000-user FOLLOWS ring with chords, taken apart one conjunct at a time:

|                                                 |         ms |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---------: |
| **the bench row: `u.name = $n AND EXISTS {…}`** | **265.48** |
| the `EXISTS {…}` alone, over all users          |     259.74 |
| the `u.name = $n` alone                         |       2.06 |
| the same two conjuncts REVERSED                 |     267.50 |
| **`(u:User {name: $n}) WHERE EXISTS {…}`**      |   **2.38** |
| two separate `MATCH` clauses                    |       2.52 |

**111x for one question spelled two ways** — the bug class this engine is named after. Reversing
the conjuncts changed nothing, which rules out evaluation order and points at the only other
candidate: the `EXISTS` was running once per user either way.

### Why the obvious fix was the wrong one

`pushWhereIntoNode` folds a segment-free MATCH's clause `WHERE` into the node pattern so it
rejects during the scan (item 126, 2.9x). It folded the WHOLE conjunction, and the compiled
`and` evaluates every operand unconditionally — so the cheap conjunct could not gate the
expensive one.

The first thing I wrote was a short-circuit in the `and`/`or`/`xor` compiler, gated on a
`decisive` value, which is Kleene-exact. It typechecked and it was **wrong**:
`operator-chains.test.ts` carries an explicit regression guard — _"the evaluator does NOT
short-circuit: a fault in any operand propagates"_ — and its header calls itself a mirror of
`crates/lenke-engine/src/gql/tests.rs`. There is no such assertion in `tests.rs`, so the mirror
claim is unverified prose; I asked native directly instead of trusting it:

|                                | TS     | native |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ------ |
| `RETURN false AND (1.0 / 0.0)` | raises | raises |
| `RETURN true OR (1.0 / 0.0)`   | raises | raises |

So non-short-circuiting is a genuine **byte-identity contract**, not an oversight, and the edit
was reverted. Worth recording that the test was right and its stated justification was not
checkable — the probe is what settled it.

### What the split actually changes, measured both ways

The fix is filter PLACEMENT, not evaluation order: only the subquery-FREE conjuncts fold into
the node; a conjunct carrying `EXISTS {…}` / `COUNT {…}` / `VALUE {…}` stays as the clause
filter, which runs once per SURVIVING binding instead of once per scanned vertex.

That is the one place this function changes which row raises, so it was measured before being
shipped, with a faulting `EXISTS` body and a start predicate nothing matches:

|                                                                      | TS before  | TS after | native |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------- | ------ |
| `WHERE u.name = $n AND EXISTS { … 1.0 / 0.0 … }`, no row matches     | **raises** | **[]**   | **[]** |
| `(u:User {name: $n}) WHERE EXISTS { … 1.0 / 0.0 … }`, no row matches | []         | []       | []     |
| CONTROL the same, a row DOES match                                   | raises     | raises   | raises |
| CONTROL the `EXISTS` alone, all users                                | raises     | raises   | raises |

So TS's own inline spelling already agreed with native and the conjunction form was the
outlier: this **closes a TS-vs-native divergence** rather than opening one. The two controls are
what make that a measurement — without them, "no longer raises" is indistinguishable from a
fault injection that stopped working (my first attempt used `number <= string`, which raises in
neither engine, and the control is what caught it).

The sibling case with a NON-subquery faulting conjunct — `WHERE u.k = 'nobody' AND 1.0 / 0.0 > 0`
— still raises in TS and still returns `[]` in native. That is untouched here and stays recorded
as `and-chain-seeding-divergence` (item 115): it needs a decision about seeding, and a perf tick
is not where that gets settled. A test pins it so this change cannot drift into settling it by
accident.

### Measured

Probe, min of three, 20,000 users:

| row                                     | before |    after |                          |
| --------------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | ------------------------ |
| **TARGET the bench row**                | 262.81 | **3.12** | **84x**                  |
| the two conjuncts reversed              | 268.58 | **2.16** | 124x                     |
| CONTROL inline anchor spelling          |   2.59 |     2.26 | flat                     |
| CONTROL two separate MATCH clauses      |   2.63 |     2.22 | flat                     |
| CONTROL the `EXISTS` alone, all users   | 259.59 |   258.89 | **flat — as it must be** |
| CONTROL cheap conjunct + cheap conjunct |   2.94 |     3.03 | flat                     |

The fifth row is the honest one: with no cheap conjunct to gate it, the subquery still runs once
per user and costs exactly what it did. This change makes a subquery **gateable**; it does not
make one cheaper. All spellings now fall within 1.44x of each other where they spanned 111x.

`bench:usage`, three runs a side: **`analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` 8 / 8 / 8 →
525 / 539 / 547 ops/sec, 66x.**

**CORRECTION (item 175).** This entry first read the bench's second column as native and reported
"8 against native's 44.1k, 5500x", closing to 78x. That is wrong: with `BENCH_ENGINES=ts` the two
columns are `ts(-)` and `ts(+)` — the SAME engine without and with the indexes the harness
creates (`indexed on name, score`, stated in the bench's own header). So 44.1k was TS _with an
index on `name`_, and the 66x is a TS-unindexed before/after, which is what this item changed.
The honest reading of the pair is that an index on the anchor already made this query fast, and
unindexed it was 5500x behind its own indexed self; after the fix that is ~80x. No native number
was measured for this row in item 174 at all. Item 175 measured one directly on the hop twin
(native 0.04ms), and the lesson is the duller one: **read the column header before naming the
thing in the other column.**

### Teeth: 17 tests, 8 mutants, 8 caught — three only after the survivors were diagnosed

The oracle is what makes this item testable at all: **a subquery body that faults raises if and
only if it was evaluated**, so "was the subquery gated?" is a result assertion rather than a
timing claim. Items 167/168/172/173 had no such escape and needed either an exported decision
function or nothing at all.

First sweep caught 4 of 8, and the three survivors were each a fixture-blindness of the same
shape — the test exercised the code path but not the DISTINCTION the mutant broke:

| mutant                                    | first sweep              | after  |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | ------ |
| revert: push the subquery conjuncts too   | caught                   | caught |
| hold back everything: nothing is pushed   | caught                   | caught |
| invert the split                          | _anchor failed to apply_ | caught |
| `hasSubquery` stops recursing             | caught                   | caught |
| drop the residual clause filter           | caught                   | caught |
| **`hasSubquery` ignores ARRAY children**  | **survived**             | caught |
| **`conjoin` keeps only its first item**   | **survived**             | caught |
| **the node's own inline `WHERE` is lost** | **survived**             | caught |

- **arrays** — every nested case I had written (`NOT EXISTS {…}`, `COUNT {…} > 0`) reaches its
  subquery through a plain object field. `OR` is n-ary, so its operands sit in an `items` ARRAY:
  `u.k = 'a' AND (EXISTS {…faulting…} OR false)` is the case that needs the array branch, and
  nothing else in the file did.
- **`conjoin`** — it only rebuilds the HELD-BACK conjuncts, and every test had exactly one
  subquery conjunct, where it never has to build an `AND` at all. Needed two.
- **the inline `WHERE`** — `(u:P {k: 'a'})` is stored as the node's `props`; only the
  `(u:P WHERE u.k = 'a')` spelling populates `path.start.where`, which is what the merge reads.
  I had tested the props spelling and believed I had covered it.

One mutant reported `NOT APPLIED (anchor appears 0x)` — a trailing-whitespace anchor. That
assertion is the only reason it was not scored as caught; a mutant that fails to apply is
indistinguishable from one the tests caught.

`hasSubquery` is a GENERIC structural walk rather than a per-variant match, and the array
survivor is the argument for it: `Expr` is a wide union, and a walk enumerating its arms would
answer "no subquery" for any arm added later — the one failure direction that costs this
function its whole reason to be careful.

### Open, and not fixed here

`seedPrefilter` is the hop-shape sibling: it lifts a hop's clause `WHERE` into a fault-swallowing
seed filter, and it lifts the WHOLE conjunction. An `EXISTS { (u)-[:E]->(v) }` reads nothing but
the start variable, so it passes that function's `freePredicateVars` restriction and is lifted —
one subquery per start VERTEX, with no cheap conjunct able to gate it. Measured on the same
fixture, and it is the same defect:

|                                                                 |         ms |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------: |
| **`(u:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(w) WHERE u.name = $n AND EXISTS {…}`** | **302.01** |
| `(u:User {name: $n})-[:FOLLOWS]->(w) WHERE EXISTS {…}`          |       2.83 |
| the cheap conjunct alone                                        |       2.31 |
| CONTROL the segment-free shape, after this item                 |       2.39 |

**107x, still open.** It is NOT fixed here, and the reason is in `seedPrefilter`'s own comment:
the whole-`WHERE`-reads-only-the-start restriction exists _because_ splitting conjuncts there
changes which row raises, in the reserved `FALSE AND <data exception>` family. The same split
would also trade one subquery per start VERTEX for one per surviving ROW, which is better only
when the cheap conjunct is selective — a cost-model question, not a free win. It needs its own
native probe, its own tests and its own mutants.

Gates separately: 17 new tests (951 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps
on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 175. The hop seed gate evaluates cheap conjuncts first — 52x, and the error-vs-non-empty divergence

Item 174 closed the segment-free spelling and recorded its hop twin as open and measured at 107x.
This is that twin. `seedPrefilter` lifts a hop's clause `WHERE` into a fault-swallowing seed gate
so a start vertex the predicate rejects is never expanded (item 125) — and it lifted the WHOLE
conjunction, with the gate evaluating every conjunct. So an `EXISTS {…}` conjunct ran a
correlated sub-pattern **once per start VERTEX in the gate, and again per surviving ROW in the
clause `WHERE`** — a prefilter does not replace the clause filter, it duplicates it, which is the
detail that decided the fix.

### Pricing two fixes before writing either

**(b) Hold the subquery conjunct out of the gate**, the direct copy of item 174. Rejected on
measurement. A vertex the cheap conjunct ACCEPTS but the subquery rejects currently costs one
gate evaluation and produces no rows; without the lift it produces `degree` rows and pays a clause
evaluation for each. On a non-selective cheap conjunct that is a regression by a factor of the
degree.

**(a) Order the gate's own conjuncts**, which is what shipped: evaluate the subquery-free
conjuncts first and stop at the first that is not cleanly TRUE. The gate keeps a seed only on a
clean TRUE (`seedGate`, `executor/matching.ts`), and a three-valued conjunction is TRUE only when
every conjunct is — so stopping early is the gate's own semantics, not a reordering of `AND`. A
conjunct that is always TRUE never short-circuits anything, so shape B pays nothing.

| 20,000 users, degree 2                                                  |                   before |                    after |                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | -----------------------: | -----------------------: | ----------------------------------- |
| **SHAPE A `(u:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(w) WHERE u.name = $n AND EXISTS {…}`** | 272.51 / 261.38 / 267.61 |   **4.76 / 5.26 / 5.57** | **~52x**                            |
| reference `(u:User {name: $n})-[…]` inline anchor                       |       4.99 / 4.38 / 5.05 |       4.85 / 5.16 / 4.85 | flat                                |
| **SHAPE B non-selective cheap conjunct + `EXISTS {…}`**                 |                   265.16 | 266.08 / 266.86 / 267.38 | **flat — what (b) would have cost** |

Native runs shape A in **0.04ms**, so the gap was 6500x and not the 107x item 174 recorded from
the TS-vs-TS spellings. Native REFUSES shape B — `variable-length traversal exceeded the trail
limit of 1000000 rows (ConfigId::LimitsTrail)` — so that row is TS-only, and the refusal belongs
to the recorded native loud-refusal family, not to this item.

### A harness artifact that looked exactly like a 2x regression

The inline-anchor reference row read **2.25-2.38ms before and 4.47-4.96ms after**, which is a
clean, repeatable 2x on a shape where `gatePredicate` provably returns `compileExpr(where)`
unchanged (its `WHERE` is the subquery alone, so `cheap.length === 0`). Diagnosed rather than
explained away: neutering `gatePredicate` to a bare passthrough, with every added line still in
the module, restored 2.40-2.52ms — which ruled layout out and wrongly implicated the logic.

The cause was the probe. That row ran SECOND, after the target row, and the target row's 260ms of
`EXISTS` evaluation was warming the JIT it then free-rode on. Once the target dropped to 5ms the
warm-up went with it. Measured in isolation the row reads **4.38-5.05 before against 4.85-5.16
after — flat**. The general form: **a row that gets much faster stops warming its neighbours, so
an unchanged neighbour can appear to regress by exactly the warm-up it was borrowing.** Every
number in the table above is therefore an isolated single-row measurement.

### What it changes, and that it closes a divergence the registry does not cover

Ordering is not semantically free, and the cost is which row raises: a cleanly-FALSE cheap
conjunct beside a FAULTING subquery used to propagate that fault, have `seedGate` swallow it and
KEEP the seed, and then raise from the clause `WHERE` per row. Measured on the hop fixture, with
the faulting vertex being one a selective conjunct excludes:

| selected vertex                 | TS before  | TS after  | native    |
| ------------------------------- | ---------- | --------- | --------- |
| none matches the cheap conjunct | raises     | `[]`      | `[]`      |
| **a NON-faulting vertex**       | **raises** | **1 row** | **1 row** |
| the faulting vertex itself      | raises     | raises    | raises    |
| CONTROL the subquery alone      | raises     | raises    | raises    |

The middle row is the one worth naming. TS raised where native returned a **non-empty** result,
because an unrelated vertex's subquery faulted and the gate's swallow pushed the fault into the
clause `WHERE`. The divergence registry's single entry is explicit that it covers an error
against an EMPTY result only — _"An error against a NON-EMPTY result is a different thing
entirely … and is NOT covered here"_ — so this case was uncovered by the registry and by the
fuzzers. Both changed rows now match native.

The non-subquery form of the same family still raises in TS and returns `[]` in native, untouched
here, and still recorded as `and-chain-seeding-divergence` (item 115).

### The bench screen, and a sampling mistake inside it

No `bench:usage` row exercises this shape — the hop-with-a-subquery-conjunct is not in the
corpus, and `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` is segment-free (item 174's case). So the bench
is purely a regression screen here, and all fourteen rows overlap.

One row cost an hour and is worth recording. `write: 100 updates in one transaction` read
**535 / 598 / 637 before against 489 / 491 / 501 after** — three a side, NON-overlapping, ~0.85x,
which looks exactly like a real regression. Its query is `MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n SET
u.score = $v`: segment-free, so `seedPrefilter` returns `undefined` and `gatePredicate` is never
called. No path to it at all.

Six observations a side settled it:

|        | observations                          | median | min |
| ------ | ------------------------------------- | -----: | --: |
| before | 485 / 515 / 519 / **535 / 598 / 637** |    527 | 485 |
| after  | 489 / 491 / 501 / 502 / 531 / 610     |    502 | 489 |

The first three "before" samples were the top three of a distribution that spans 1.31x. Fully
overlapping, `min/min` 1.01x — noise. The repo's own rule covers this ("match sample counts on
both sides, and prefer min or p25 over the mean"); what is new is how convincing THREE
non-overlapping observations look on a row whose real spread is 1.3x. Two rows in the same screen
had the mirror-image problem: `cycle detection` read 0.54x and `2-hop recommendation` 0.83x on
`min/min`, each driven by ONE low outlier against values that overlap the before set.

### Teeth: 13 tests, 8 mutants, 8 caught on the first sweep

First time in this run of items that no mutant survived the first sweep, and the reason is
item 174's three survivors: each became a test here before the mutants ran — the source-order
case (`EXISTS` written first), the three-valued UNKNOWN case, and both degenerate partitions
(subquery-only and subquery-free `WHERE`s, which must come out byte-identical).

| mutant                                                  | result                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| revert: no ordering, compile the whole `WHERE`          | caught                            |
| costly conjuncts FIRST                                  | caught                            |
| `=== false` instead of `!== true` (3VL)                 | caught — only by the UNKNOWN test |
| no early exit: evaluate every conjunct                  | caught                            |
| the gate keeps nothing                                  | caught                            |
| the gate keeps everything                               | caught                            |
| `hasSubquery` inverted in the partition                 | caught                            |
| drop the conjunct split (treat `WHERE` as one conjunct) | caught                            |

Gates separately: 13 new tests (964 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, `bun run lint`
exit 0, `fmt` then `fmt:check` exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps
on random seeds. No Rust changed.

## 176. The filtered one-hop count never learned to seek — 12.5x and 16.6x, item 149 one shape over

Found by re-ranking the cross-engine bench after item 175's correction, which is the only reason
this was reachable: with `BENCH_ENGINES=ts,ffi` there are four columns, and once compared
properly every read/write row sat within **2.2-3.5x** of native WITH indexes except one.
`interleaved: write + traversal` reached **1600 ops/sec against native's 106,300 — 66.4x** —
and indexes bought it 3.4x where they bought its peers 60-170x.

### The name on the bench row was wrong, and that is why it had survived

The row alternates a `SET u.score` with a traversal, so it reads as an interleaving cost. It is
not. Taking it apart on 20,000 users:

|                                      |     us/op |
| ------------------------------------ | --------: |
| the write alone                      |      26.4 |
| the hop read alone                   | **427.4** |
| write + hop read (the bench row)     |     432.2 |
| ONE write, then many hops            |     421.6 |
| write + POINT read (its sibling row) |      22.7 |

The write contributes nothing. Nor does the interleaving: one write followed by many hops costs
the same per hop as a write before every hop. The row was measuring **the traversal**, and
`write + point read` is cheap for the dull reason that a point read is cheap. A write
invalidating a read snapshot — which the bench's own comment offers as the hypothesis, and which
CLAUDE.md records as ~2.5x — is not what this row shows.

### Four spellings of one question

| 20,000 users, `name` indexed                                     |     us/op |         |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------: | ------- |
| **`(u:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x) WHERE u.name = $n RETURN count(*)`** | **430.9** |         |
| `(u:User {name: $n})-[:FOLLOWS]->(x) RETURN count(*)`            |     405.5 |         |
| the same clause form returning `x.name` instead                  |      36.4 | **12x** |
| the same clause form, `count(x.name)` instead of `count(*)`      |      37.3 | **12x** |
| split into two `MATCH` clauses                                   |      21.5 | **20x** |
| UNANCHORED `count(*)` — the shortcut's real win                  |      27.7 | keep    |

All five answer correctly; 430.9us over 20,000 vertices is 21ns each, the signature of a walk
over the whole label. `startOnlyHopCount` iterates `candidateVertexSource(graph, pa)` — the label
bucket — summing each kept vertex's degree, so an anchored hop count **ignored the property index
the general path seeds from**.

This is item 149 one shape over. That item found and fixed exactly this for the NODE tally and
recorded the signature it leaves in `bench:usage`: _a row whose indexed and unindexed columns are
the same number._ `cstart`, the compiled start node carrying the lifted seed hints, was already
threaded into `buildNodeCount` for that fix — and `patternCountOf` passed it only there. The
one-hop walk was never given it. Grepping the pattern, which the method asks for, found the
capability already built and simply not wired one branch over.

### The fix

`hopSeek` chooses the start's seed set, mirroring `buildNodeCount`'s chooser exactly — narrowest
candidate from `indexCandidates`, and declining a seek WIDER than the label bucket, since an
indexed key can be common outside the label. Sound for the reason it is sound there: a hint
lifted from an AND-chain is a NECESSARY condition, so the seeded set is a SUPERSET of the matches,
and the label check, the inline constraint and the predicate all re-validate every candidate —
the same three tests the bucket walk applies, in the same order.

| row                                           |                           before |                            after |           |
| --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------: | -------------------------------: | --------- |
| **TARGET clause `WHERE` + `count(*)`**        |                            430.9 |                         **34.4** | **12.5x** |
| **the inline-anchor spelling**                |                            405.5 |                         **24.5** | **16.6x** |
| CONTROL the same query returning a value      |                             36.4 |                             32.4 | flat      |
| CONTROL `count(x.name)`                       |                             37.3 |                             38.7 | flat      |
| CONTROL UNANCHORED `count(*)`                 | 27.6 / 31.0 / 31.2 / 32.5 / 33.7 | 25.8 / 26.0 / 26.5 / 28.5 / 30.4 | flat      |
| a NON-selective indexed key (10,000 match)    |                            690.7 |                            486.0 | 1.42x     |
| a far-end inline constraint beside the anchor |                           1401.2 |                           1182.7 | 1.18x     |

Each row is a SEPARATE PROCESS, which is item 175's lesson applied: a sequential probe shares JIT
warm-up between rows, and the row that got 12x faster would otherwise appear to slow its
neighbour. The unanchored control has five observations a side because a single pair read 1.12x
worse and that is inside its spread.

### The inline spelling was still broken after the "fix", and only one test knew

The first version threaded `cstart` into the clause-`WHERE` branch of `buildOneHopCount`. The
INLINE spelling takes the OTHER branch — `pred === undefined`, the inline-only path — which built
its scan without it. So the fix made the clause spelling 12.5x faster and left its twin at 405us:
**the exact equivalent-spelling gap this engine is named after, introduced while fixing one.**

No timing caught it, because the first "after" reading of the inline row was against a STALE
`dist` (the package's own tests read `src`; a probe importing `@lenke/gql` reads `dist`) and so
showed 385us — which looked like the honest before-number rather than a build artifact. What
caught it was the index-hit test: 0 hits for the inline spelling against 1 for the clause
spelling, on a correctness-shaped assertion that cannot be confounded by a build or a JIT.

### Teeth: 24 tests, 10 mutants, 10 caught — and three of them needed a new kind of witness

Seeking is answer-preserving, which is the point of it, so the first sweep caught only 2 of 8:
every mutant that simply **never seeks** changes no row. Items 167/168/172/173 hit this wall;
172 and 173 escaped by testing an exported decision, so `hopSeek` is exported and its choice
asserted directly — with paired cases differing in exactly one input (indexed vs not, `props` vs
`seedHints`, narrow vs wide, two keys vs one).

That still left three survivors, all at the CALL SITE rather than inside `hopSeek`: drop the
call, drop the plumbing, drop the plumbing one level up. A correct decision function nothing asks
is invisible to decision tests too. The witness for those is that **a seek cannot avoid touching
the index**: wrapping `graph.vertexPropertyIndex.equals` and counting calls during a real query
distinguishes a seek from a walk without timing anything. Two controls make the count mean
"chose to" rather than "touched it" — an unanchored count must register ZERO hits, and so must an
anchor on an unindexed key.

| mutant                                     | first sweep     | after               |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------- | ------------------- |
| revert: never seek                         | **survived**    | caught (index hits) |
| seek even when WIDER than the bucket       | **survived**    | caught (`hopSeek`)  |
| pick the WIDEST candidate                  | _anchor failed_ | caught (`hopSeek`)  |
| drop the label check on a seeked vertex    | caught          | caught              |
| drop the predicate re-validation           | _anchor failed_ | caught              |
| drop the inline constraint re-validation   | caught          | caught              |
| ignore the edge TYPE in the degree sum     | _anchor failed_ | caught              |
| `cstart` never reaches the clause scan     | **survived**    | caught (index hits) |
| `cstart` never reaches the INLINE scan     | —               | caught (index hits) |
| `buildOneHopCount` never receives `cstart` | —               | caught (index hits) |

Three anchors first failed to apply because `startOnlyHopCount` and `farOnlyHopCount` share
identical bodies, so the substring matched twice; a fourth failed later because `fmt` reflowed an
object literal the anchor had spelled on one line. The `applied` assertion is the only reason
none of those was scored as caught.

The fixture is built around one vertex: `x0` shares `name: 'user0'` with `u0`, carries a
`FOLLOWS` edge, and is NOT a `User`. An index seek on `name` returns it BY VALUE, so the label
check has to reject it — and a seek returning 2 vertices where the answer counts 1 is what makes
the label test evidence. Without that vertex every test in the file passes with the label check
deleted.

## 177. The fused hop projection took the one filter it cannot gate — 98x, and a margin that had to be measured

Item 176 left `farOnlyHopCount` recorded as the unseeded mirror of the walk it fixed. Pricing that
first, as the method asks, found something larger beside it. On 20,000 users, `name` indexed:

|                                    | index hits |      us/op |
| ---------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------: |
| far-anchored `count(*)` (clause)   | 0          |      459.6 |
| far-anchored `count(*)` (inline)   | 0          |      357.0 |
| **far-anchored returning a VALUE** | **0**      | **3966.1** |
| far-anchored `count(u.name)`       | 1          |       41.7 |
| two-clause spelling                | 1          |       40.7 |
| start-anchored, item 176's fix     | 1          |       34.7 |

The count mirror is real but it is an 11x; a far-anchored hop **projection** was 3966us with no
index hit at all. Spelled five ways:

|                                                                                 |    us/op |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------: |
| `(u)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x:User) WHERE x.name = $n RETURN u.name`                      |   3966.1 |
| `(u)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x:User {name: $n}) RETURN u.name`                             |   3531.5 |
| `(u:User)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x:User) WHERE x.name = $n RETURN u.name`                 |   4279.8 |
| **the same query with the ARROW FLIPPED** `(x:User {name: $n})<-[:FOLLOWS]-(u)` | **35.3** |
| the same query plus `LIMIT 1`                                                   |     43.3 |

**97x between a query and the same query with its arrow flipped**, and adding a `LIMIT` was enough
to make it fast — because the projection guard refuses a paged projection, so the query fell
through to the path that seeds.

### The fast path accepted precisely the filters it is worst at

A trace settled which walk each spelling takes: all three slow ones reach `filteredHopWalk`,
which iterates `candidateVertices(graph, startLabel)` — and `startLabel` is undefined for an
unlabelled start, so that is every vertex — binding the far end and evaluating the gate per EDGE.

`carriedWhere` accepts a clause `WHERE` **only if it reads the far variable** (line 128). So:

- a far-reading filter is carried, and it cannot reject a start vertex before expanding it, while
  the end it constrains — the seekable one — is not the end the walk drives;
- a START-reading filter declines at compile time and reaches the general path's seed, which is
  why `WHERE u.name = $n RETURN x.name` was 49.6us all along.

One guard therefore routed the gateable filter away and kept the ungateable one.

### A runtime decline, because the decision needs the graph

Whether an index seek exists is not knowable when the closure is built, so `RowsFn` may now
return `null` to mean _decline_ and the call site falls through to the general clause loop. The
general path is where the start-reading spelling already went, so this makes the two spellings
take the same route — which is the point, not a side effect.

| row                                                    |                           before |                            after |           |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------: | -------------------------------: | --------- |
| **far clause, project the start**                      |                  4025.7 / 3966.1 |                  **52.2 / 38.6** | **~98x**  |
| **far INLINE, project the start**                      |                  3656.5 / 3531.5 |                  **37.4 / 31.0** | **~105x** |
| **far clause, labelled start**                         |                  4270.0 / 4279.8 |                  **43.3 / 40.6** | **~99x**  |
| a seek matching 1,000 of 20,000                        |                           3999.1 |                       **1086.2** | 3.7x      |
| CONTROL start-reading filter (never reached this walk) |                             43.8 |                             42.0 | flat      |
| CONTROL the flipped spelling                           |                             33.1 |                             36.2 | flat      |
| CONTROL UNFILTERED hop, far projected                  | 1873 / 1903 / 1966 / 2118 / 3214 | 1863 / 1942 / 1997 / 2965 / 3021 | flat      |
| CONTROL UNFILTERED hop, start projected                | 3005 / 3081 / 3325 / 3331 / 3365 | 2862 / 2862 / 2961 / 3191 / 3567 | flat      |
| CONTROL unindexed far filter (keeps the walk)          |                            ~4272 |               4360 / 4364 / 4381 | flat      |
| CONTROL a seek matching 10,000 (keeps the walk)        |                           4741.1 |               4574 / 4709 / 4759 | flat      |
| CONTROL unanchored `count(*)`                          |                             30.3 |               29.4 / 30.1 / 31.5 | flat      |

The two UNFILTERED rows carry five observations a side because a single pair read **1949 against
2954, a clean 1.52x** on the hot path items 159/160 measured — and both distributions turn out to
be bimodal around ~1950 and ~3000, fully overlapping, mins 1873 against 1863. That is last tick's
lesson arriving a second time: one observation either side of a bimodal row invents a regression.

### The margin is load-bearing, and the first version got it wrong

The guard written first was `narrowest < candidateCount(startLabel)` — the rule `hopSeek` and
`buildNodeCount` use. It is wrong here, and measurably: those choose between two walks with the
same per-element cost, while this chooses between a walk that builds **no rows** and a path that
builds one per match. The fused walk is FLAT in the filter's selectivity (it visits every edge of
the start source either way); the general path costs about 1.2us per matched far vertex. Both
arms forced, 20,000 users and 40,000 edges:

| far matches |   declining | fused walk |                 |
| ----------- | ----------: | ---------: | --------------- |
| 2           |        43.4 |     3871.8 | decline, 89x    |
| 10          |        60.3 |     3897.0 | decline, 65x    |
| 100         |       187.4 |     3827.5 | decline, 20x    |
| 1000        |      1092.7 |     3970.4 | decline, 3.6x   |
| **10000**   | **13998.5** | **4527.5** | **FUSED, 3.1x** |

So the crossover sits near 3,250 of 20,000, and the plain guard sent the last row the wrong way:
measured at **13430us against the 4272 it replaced, a 3.1x regression** on an indexed-but-
unselective filter — found by including that case as a control rather than by the headline row.
`SEEK_MARGIN = 8` puts the threshold at 2,500 for this source: inside the region where declining
still wins by 3.6x, clear of the one where it loses.

### Teeth: 13 tests, 7 mutants, 7 caught

A decline changes no row, so the answers and the choice need separate assertions. Every
answer test compares the INDEXED graph against the UNINDEXED one — which is to say the declined
plan against the fused walk — as a row MULTISET (row order is unspecified and does differ) and on
COLUMN order (which is bytes). The choice is witnessed by counting `vertexPropertyIndex.equals`
calls, as in item 176, and here that witness is three-way: a selective far filter DECLINES
(hits > 0), an indexed-but-unselective one KEEPS the walk (0), and an unindexed one KEEPS it (0).
The margin is therefore testable, which is what caught the guard mutant.

| mutant                                            | result                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| remove the decline entirely                       | caught                                       |
| **drop the measured `SEEK_MARGIN`**               | **caught — only by the unselective control** |
| invert the decline comparison                     | caught                                       |
| take the WIDEST far candidate                     | caught                                       |
| `cfar` never reaches the walk                     | caught                                       |
| the call site treats a decline as an EMPTY result | caught                                       |
| the call site returns the decline as a row array  | caught                                       |

One mutant survived the first sweep and was **not** a test gap: widening `RowsFn` had given the
DISTINCT detector a `?? []` at its call site, and since that closure never declines, replacing it
is equivalent code. Rather than leave an untestable branch, the distinct path got its own
`AlwaysRowsFn` type and its call site lost the branch — a suite that cannot distinguish two
behaviours because only one is reachable is how a test file comes to look like it has teeth it
does not.

The fixture is 40 users rather than a dozen, deliberately: the decline needs a seek 8x narrower
than the start source, so a 13-vertex graph cannot reach it and every margin test would pass
vacuously. At 41 vertices a `name` seek (1-2) declines and a `t` seek (~14) does not, so one
fixture exercises both sides.

### Not fixed here

`farOnlyHopCount`, the count-shortcut mirror, is still unseeded — 421.1 / 347.9us for the two
far-anchored `count(*)` spellings against 41.7us for `count(u.name)`. It is the item 176 fix
applied to the far side and wants the compiled far node threaded into the count shortcut, which
is the same shape of change as this one; the projection was taken first because it is 98x and the
count is 11x.

`MATCH (u:User {name: $n})-[:FOLLOWS]->(x:User {name: $m}) RETURN count(*)` reads

it does not visit — so it routes to `tallyHopCount`, which scans the edge bucket and seeks

lookup. That is a ~40x shape and it is the remaining member of this family.

## 179. The both-ends tally seeds too — 35x and 59x, and the family is closed

The last unseeded route. With BOTH endpoints constrained neither per-vertex walk can take the
query — `startWalkFits` needs `inFar === undefined` and `farWalkFits` needs
`inNear === undefined`, because a walk summing bucket SIZES cannot apply a constraint on an end
it never visits — so it fell to `tallyHopCount`, which scanned every edge of the type and seeked
nothing. Measured first, 20,000 users and 40,000 edges, `name` indexed:

|                                                                    | index hits |      us/op |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | ---------: |
| `(u:User {name: $n})-[:FOLLOWS]->(x:User {name: $m})` `count(*)`   | 0          |     1187.3 |
| the clause-`WHERE` spelling of the same question                   | 0          | **2300.4** |
| inline start + clause far                                          | 0          |     1202.4 |
| the same question as `count(x.name)`, which the general path seeds | 1          |   **41.4** |

29x for the inline spelling, 56x for the clause one — and 1.94x between those two, because the
tally evaluates a compiled predicate per edge where an inline constraint goes through
`inlineHolds`.

### The fix, and why its guard is not the other two routes' guard

`tallyEdges` draws the edges from the seeded end instead of the whole bucket. Both ends are asked
and the narrower set wins; a candidate's `build()` returns the index's own stored set rather than
a copy, so asking twice is O(1).

`hopSeek`'s guard — narrower than that end's bucket — is **necessary but not sufficient here**,
and this is the one place the three routes legitimately differ. The two per-vertex walks read
bucket SIZES, so any seek that narrows the vertex set wins. This source must WALK each seeded
vertex's edges, paying an adjacency lookup per vertex to save the edges of the vertices it skips,
and at degree 2 that trade turns over well before the bucket is exhausted. Both arms forced:

| seeded-end matches |     seeded | full tally |                  |
| ------------------ | ---------: | ---------: | ---------------- |
| 2                  |       53.2 |     1328.8 | seed, 25x        |
| 10                 |       52.8 |     1171.2 | seed, 22x        |
| 100                |       94.3 |     1207.6 | seed, 13x        |
| 1000               |      428.8 |     1229.8 | seed, 2.9x       |
| **10000**          | **2030.0** | **1422.3** | **TALLY, 1.43x** |

So the crossover is near 7,000 of 20,000 and `hopSeek`'s guard alone sends the last row the wrong
way: measured at 1946-2076us against the 1383 it replaced. `TALLY_SEEK_MARGIN = 8` puts the
threshold at 2,500 here. Item 177 landed on the same divisor for a different cost model; the
number coinciding is not a shared rule, so it is measured and named separately.

**A generator layer was worth 1.2x of that margin.** The first version delegated per vertex to an
`edgesOfVertex` generator, so a wide seek paid two nested frames per vertex: `bothwide` read
2323us, which one layer brought to 1946-2076. That is the reading behind
`harness-must-resemble-caller` showing up again, and it narrowed the gap without closing it —
the 10,000 adjacency lookups are the rest, which is why the margin is still needed.

### Measured, three observations a side

| row                                  | before                                              | after                                               |          |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------- |
| **TARGET both ends inline**          | 1218.7 / 1250.1 / 1288.9                            | **34.2 / 35.6 / 38.8**                              | **~35x** |
| **TARGET both ends clause `WHERE`**  | 2336.8 / 2372.1 / 2387.6                            | **36.2 / 39.7 / 39.9**                              | **~59x** |
| **TARGET inline start + clause far** | 1235.6 / 1236.4 / 1342.3                            | **34.0 / 37.4 / 39.6**                              | **~33x** |
| CONTROL a WIDE seek at both ends     | 1376.3 / 1413.1 / 1424.6                            | 1406.3 / 1416.7 / 1451.5                            | flat     |
| CONTROL neither end indexed          | 1219.5 / 1223.9 / 1234.3 / 1246.6 / 1251.0 / 1251.9 | 1237.6 / 1241.9 / 1245.7 / 1269.0 / 1287.6 / 1350.0 | flat     |
| CONTROL unanchored `count(*)`        | 30.7 / 31.3 / 32.1                                  | 30.8 / 31.3 / 44.5                                  | flat     |

The unindexed control has six a side because three read 1219-1251 against 1242-1350 — barely
overlapping, and the kind of reading items 175-178 learned not to call either way on three
samples. At six it overlaps and `min/min` is 1.015.

### Teeth: 13 tests, 8 mutants, 8 caught

Three kinds of assertion, because the change has three kinds of claim. The ANSWER is compared
between the indexed and unindexed graphs (which is the seeded plan against the scanning one) for
every shape, including a SELF-LOOP — `loop` is incident to u3 on both sides, so a source that
unioned the two adjacencies would double it. The SOUNDNESS guard is tested with a graph whose
every edge carries two labels: an untyped hop must decline the seeded source (a per-vertex bucket
holds that edge under both labels), while one concrete type may still seed. And the CHOICE is
witnessed by which adjacency the tally reads — seeding the start reads `edgesFromByLabel`,
seeding the far end reads `edgesToByLabel` — so "the narrower end wins" is a result, not a timing
claim.

| mutant                                              | result                |
| --------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| revert: the tally always scans every edge           | caught                |
| drop the multi-type soundness guard                 | caught                |
| drop the `TALLY_SEEK_MARGIN`                        | caught                |
| prefer the WIDER end                                | caught                |
| seed the start from the REVERSE adjacency           | caught                |
| seed the far end from the REVERSE adjacency         | caught                |
| **each end's seek measured against the FAR bucket** | **survived** → caught |
| `edgesOfVertices` ignores the type restriction      | caught                |

The survivor is the sharpest fixture-blindness case of this run: both ends of the fixture were
`:User`, so `candidateCount(pa)` and `candidateCount(pb)` are **the same number** and comparing a
seek to the wrong end's bucket is EQUIVALENT CODE. It needed a pattern whose two ends have
different labels — a `:User` start (200) against an `:Other` far end (1), where a `g20` seek of 10
clears x8 against 200 and cannot clear it against 1.

The fixture is 200 users, also deliberately: two indexed keys have to BOTH clear the x8 margin
while differing in width (`name` matches 1-2, `g20` matches 10, `t` matches 100 and so does not
seed at all). A 10-vertex fixture cannot separate "the narrower end won" from "the wider end was
refused by the margin".

### The bench screen

No `bench:usage` row constrains both ends, so the bench is a regression screen only. Thirteen of
fourteen rows overlap; `interleaved: write + point read` reads 49.4-50.2k before against
50.9-54.4k after — non-overlapping in the FASTER direction, on a point read this code cannot
reach, so it is noise rather than a win to claim.

### The family, closed

| item    | route               | shape                       |                      |
| ------- | ------------------- | --------------------------- | -------------------- |
| 149     | `buildNodeCount`    | a constrained node count    | —                    |
| 176     | `startOnlyHopCount` | start-anchored hop count    | 27x on the bench row |
| 177     | `filteredHopWalk`   | far-filtered hop PROJECTION | 98x                  |
| 178     | `farOnlyHopCount`   | far-anchored hop count      | 13x                  |
| **179** | **`tallyHopCount`** | **both ends constrained**   | **35-59x**           |

Every route that walks a bucket now asks `hopSeek` first, and it is ONE function rather than five
copies — which is the answer to how this family kept recurring. Items 176 and 178 each shipped a
version that wired one branch and left its twin, and item 177 found a guard that accepted one
end's filter and refused the other's.
