## 207. A start-only filter on a hop projection — 2.2x, and a bug in item 204 found on the way

Item 205 priced this at 3.9x and specified the fix, warning that it needed a measured runtime
decline whose far-side twin had been wrong by 3.1x. **It needed no decline at all**, for the same
reason item 206 needed none — and the investigation turned up a silent defect in item 204.

### The decline was right, and became wrong when the walk learned to seed

`carriedWhere` refused any clause `WHERE` that did not read the FAR variable, so a start-only
`WHERE a.k = $v` declined `detectHopProjection` entirely. Item 177 measured why: the fused walk did
not SEED, so taking an anchored filter meant scanning a whole label while the general path went
straight to the index — 3966µs against 49.6. Refusing it was the fix available at the time.

`hop-projection.ts` still never called `hopSeek` — only `candidateVertexSource`. So the decline was
a workaround for a missing seed, and items 176 and 206 had already established the better answer
for the counts: **a walking fast path should not decline an indexed filter, it should seed from the
index and keep walking.** That is now the third instance, and the rule generalizes: the decline
exists to protect the index, and a path that seeds needs no protection.

### The ORDER inside the walk was most of the win

Two changes, and the second was the larger:

|                                       |  unindexed |   indexed |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------: | --------: |
| before (declined to the general path) |     51.8ms |     0.6ms |
| seeded, gate applied PER ROW          |     31.5ms |     0.6ms |
| seeded, gate applied PER START VERTEX | **17.0ms** | **0.6ms** |

Reading the adjacency before the gate was the obvious order and it costs every REJECTED vertex an
`index.get(id)?.get(type)`: on 20,000 users with a selective filter that is 19,999 adjacency
lookups to serve one surviving start, and it measured 52ns a vertex against 34ns for the bare node
scan the same filter drives. `startOnlyHopCount` has had this right since item 164 — _"the degree
is now summed only for vertices the predicate KEEPS"_ — so the fix was to copy an order that was
already in the file, including its fault handling.

The walk is a THIRD closure rather than a branch in the existing loop, because this function
records both halves of that trade: item 159 measured adding even a branch to the hot unfiltered
inner loop at 1.6x, and a shared module-scope walk at 1.29x because its call sites go polymorphic
across compiles. That is the opposite of what item 206 needed in `shortcuts.ts`, and the difference
is whether the walk is called from one compile or many.

### Raise parity, and the test design that had to be thrown away

The general path evaluates a clause `WHERE` once per COMPLETE match, so a start that yields no row
never has it evaluated. Gating per vertex breaks that, so on a fault the walk asks whether the
general path would have reached this vertex — and a non-empty bucket is **necessary but not
sufficient**, because every far end may still fail the far label or the far predicate. Hence
`anyFarMatches` rather than a degree check. Two mutants pin exactly that distinction and both are
caught.

My first version of those tests was unusable and the reason is worth recording: I wrote the fault
as `WHERE a.name = 'q' AND <faulting expr>`, expecting the false conjunct to shield it. **TS does
not short-circuit a data exception behind a false conjunct** (`and-chain-seeding-divergence`), so
the fault fires on every vertex, both paths raise, and the test isolates nothing. The working
design makes the fault PER VERTEX instead — `a.v / 1 > 0` where `v` is numeric on most vertices and
a string on the two that produce no rows.

### The item 204 bug

`rowLocal`, item 204's allowlist, rejected **all arithmetic**. An `arith` node is
`{ head, tail: [['/', <Expr>]] }` — an array of ARRAYS — and the walk descended only one array
level, so it called itself on `['/', <Expr>]`, whose `kind` is `undefined`, and rejected the node.

Two things about that are worth more than the fix:

- it was **silent and one-sided**: rejecting only declines a fast path, so every arithmetic
  expression quietly took the general path and no answer changed;
- **item 204's own test for it passed vacuously.** "a computed item, not just a bare property"
  compares the fast path against the general path, and both WERE the general path. A test that
  compares two plans proves nothing when it has silently selected the same plan twice — the same
  failure as `passing-suite-is-not-equivalence`, one level up.

It surfaced only because an arithmetic predicate refused to reach the new walk and I instrumented
the detector to find out why. Fixed by recursing into arrays at any depth and into non-`Expr`
objects, which is safe because every `Expr` carries a `kind`, so the allowlist still sees every
expression on the way down.

### What still declines, and why

A start-only predicate is taken only when `rowLocal` accepts it, and what that refuses here is the
subquery arms. Item 175 gave the seed gate a CHEAP-CONJUNCT-FIRST order precisely so
`WHERE u.k = 'nope' AND <faulting subquery>` never reaches the subquery; a walk that evaluates the
whole predicate at once loses it. Five of item 175's tests caught this as RAISES rather than wrong
rows, which is the only way it could have been caught.

### Measured

A bench row joins the corpus — **`traverse 1-hop project + start filter`**,
`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(x) WHERE a.age > 60 RETURN x.name AS n`:

|        | ts                          |
| ------ | --------------------------- |
| before | 248.2 / 262.9 / 264.3ms     |
| after  | **110.8 / 112.2 / 112.3ms** |
|        | **2.21x, ranges disjoint**  |

Checked on all three engines first: ts 108.7, ffi 24.7, wasm 27.4 — and ts/ffi falls from ~10.4x to
**4.40x**. The three-run screen's other two separations are both sub-5% on small rows and both
dissolve at six readings: `query: project 3 columns` 1.05x (after-range 8.0-9.5 contains the before
8.8-9.3) and `query: top groups by count` 1.02x (3.7-4.2 contains 3.8-4.0).

### Teeth: 18 tests, 15 mutants, 13 caught

Both survivors are perf-only: the index seed never taken, and the revert. Caught include all three
raise-parity mutants, the seeded label re-check, `startOnly` set for a predicate that also reads
the far end, and the subquery acceptance.

One fixture blindness, found by a mutant and fixed in the fixture rather than the anchor: **no
start had `T` edges to BOTH a valid and an invalid far label**, so the emitting loop's far-label
check was unobservable — a walk that dropped it answered correctly on every case in the file.
Giving `a1` a second `T` edge to a wrong-label vertex made the duplicate the signal.

Anchors went stale twice: once on indentation (my loop and the pre-existing one are textually
identical four spaces apart) and once because the formatter reflowed the `anyFarMatches` call after
a `max-params` fix bundled its arguments. Both printed `NOT APPLIED` rather than passing silently —
seventh tick running.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as its own command; lint wanted `max-params` ≤ 6 on
`anyFarMatches` and an unused fixture binding named. All three re-run after the formatter, and the

- A two-hop PROJECTION with a start filter is untouched at 54.9ms — the count got its walk in 206,
  the projection has no equivalent.
- The `rowLocal` fix means item 204's node projection now accepts arithmetic for the first time.
  Unmeasured: the screen moved `query: project 3 columns` 1.05x, which is inside the noise, and no

## 208. A subquery belongs in an ITEM, not in the predicate — 2.7x, and a grep that hid two AST arms

Item 204 gave a plain node scan its own path and applied ONE guard — `rowLocal` — to both the
predicate and the projected items. The predicate needs that strictness. The items did not, and the
asymmetry is worth about 2.7x.

### Why the two differ

- The **predicate** is evaluated by the per-vertex gate, and item 175 gave the seed gate a
  CHEAP-CONJUNCT-FIRST order precisely so `WHERE k = 'nope' AND <faulting subquery>` never reaches
  the subquery. A gate that evaluates the whole predicate at once loses that, which is exactly
  what item 207's five failing tests demonstrated. Subqueries stay refused there.
- An **ITEM** is evaluated once per row that SURVIVES the filter, on either path. A subquery there
  costs the same whichever plan runs, so refusing it buys nothing and costs the whole scan.

### And the cost was the scan, not the subquery

20,000 users, three `FOLLOWS` each:

|                                           | ns/vertex scanned |                  |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------: | ---------------- |
| plain item (item 204's path)              |              38.2 |                  |
| `COUNT { (u)-[:FOLLOWS]->{1,3}(x) }` item |              94.3 | the bench row    |
| `EXISTS { (u)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x) }` item     |              91.4 |                  |
| **a ONE-HOP `COUNT{}` item**              |          **90.7** | the decisive row |

The fourth line is why this was worth taking: a one-hop `COUNT{}` subquery walks three edges and
costs within 4% of the 1-to-3-hop version. **The subquery is ~4ns of the 94; the other ~52ns over
the fast path's 38 is the general-path scan.** Pricing the subquery itself would have found
nothing — the shape to compare was the same query with a CHEAPER subquery, holding the scan fixed.

### A grep that silently hid two AST arms

The first version of `SUBQUERY_KINDS` was `['exists', 'scalar']`. Both halves were wrong: `scalar`
is `{ kind: 'scalar', category }` and not a subquery at all, while the two that matter —
`countSubquery` and `valueSubquery` — were missing.

The cause was a grep. I had listed the AST's expression kinds with
`grep -oE "kind: '[a-z_]+'"`, which **silently skips every camelCase arm**, so `countSubquery`,
`valueSubquery`, `anyRecord`, `callInline`, `callNamed`, `graphPred`, `isLabeled`, `isNull`,
`isTruth`, `isTyped`, `letIn` and `shortestK` were never in the list I worked from. A
character-class that happens to exclude uppercase does not fail; it returns a shorter answer.

The MEASUREMENT caught it, not a test: after the first fix `EXISTS{}` went 91.4ns → 34.2 and
`COUNT{}` **did not move at all**, which is only possible if one was being accepted and the other
was not. An answer test could not have seen it — accepting fewer shapes only declines a fast path.

### What the item guard is

`itemLocal` keeps item 204's allowlist in full OUTSIDE subqueries and STOPS at a subquery rather
than descending, which is what makes it sound: the interior is a nested scope the general path
compiles and runs identically, and its variables are bound by its own patterns. An aggregate is
still refused, and the check applies only outside subqueries — `count(*)` inside a `COUNT { … }`
belongs to that subquery. That aggregate rule is load-bearing and not defensive: removing it makes
`RETURN max(a.n)` answer `[{m:1},{m:2},{m:3}]` instead of `[{m:3}]`, and `collect` likewise.

The free-variable check is skipped for a subquery-bearing item, because `freePredicateVars`
descends into one and reports the variables bound INSIDE it — the `x` of
`COUNT { (u)-[:FOLLOWS]->(x) }` — so it would refuse every such item. Nothing is lost: with exactly
two clauses, one pattern and no segments, the node's own name is the only name anything can be
bound to, so both paths evaluate the SAME compiled expression against a binding holding exactly
that one name. Mutation confirms re-applying the check changes no answer.

### Measured

|                               | before |      after |                   |
| ----------------------------- | -----: | ---------: | ----------------- |
| `COUNT{}` item                | 94.3ns | **35.0ns** | **2.69x**         |
| `EXISTS{}` item               | 91.4ns | **30.4ns** | **3.01x**         |
| one-hop `COUNT{}` item        | 90.7ns | **30.3ns** | **2.99x**         |
| CONTROL subquery in the WHERE | 89.6ns |     90.5ns | correctly unmoved |
| CONTROL plain item            | 38.2ns |     34.6ns | flat              |

`bench:usage`: **`analytic: fan-out spread 1-3 hops` ts(−) 565-597 → 1.3k ops/s**, stable at 1.3k
across three runs — **2.2x**. `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` is unchanged at ~525-543,
correctly: its subquery is in the WHERE, where item 175 still owns it.

A bench row joins the corpus — **`query: subquery item`**, which moves **240.9-250.1 →
205.1-209.7ms, 1.17x+, ranges disjoint**. Checked on all three engines first: ts 208.0, ffi 6.4,
wasm 7.4, no `n/a`.

**1.17x there against 2.2x in `bench:usage` is the finding restated, not a contradiction.** The
main bench's filter is `age > 60` over 200,000 Persons, so roughly 66,000 rows SURVIVE and each
pays its own subquery — the subquery dominates and the scan is a minority of the work. `fan-out
spread` filters on `name = $n`, so ONE row survives and the scan is essentially all of it. The win
is in the scan, so it scales with how much the filter rejects; a row whose filter keeps a third of
the graph is the least favourable case this path has, and it still gains 17%.

The three-run screen separates one other row — `query: project 3 columns` at 1.01x, driven by a
17.8ms outlier in the before side's max against a real spread of 8.1-9.1. Noise.

### Teeth: 12 tests, 10 mutants, 3 caught — and that ratio is the honest number

The three caught are every mutant that can change an ANSWER: the predicate using the item guard,
an aggregate accepted outside a subquery, and the walk not descending into children. **All seven
survivors only NARROW the path** — using the strict guard for items again, descending into a
subquery, re-applying the free-var check, losing `countSubquery` or `exists` from the set, or
adding a non-subquery to it. Declining more can never change an answer, so no answer test can
reach them, and that is a property of the change rather than a gap in the fixture.

Worth naming, because a 3-of-10 sweep looks bad and is not: **for a change that only widens which
shapes a fast path accepts, mutation measures the correctness of the WIDENING, and the engagement
of the path is measurable only by timing it.** That is the same limitation as "the index seed is
never taken", which has survived three sweeps now.

One mutant I initially misread as surviving — the aggregate one — was caught; I confirmed the
guard's reachability independently by removing it and seeing `max(a.n)` return three rows. Reading
a survivor list is not the same as reading the whole output.

The 12 tests include the case that would catch the most likely real bug: a subquery whose inner
variable SHADOWS the outer node's name (`COUNT { (x)-[:T]->(a) }` under `MATCH (a:A)`). The walk
reuses one binding map across the whole scan, so a subquery whose scope leaked into it would make
the next row's gate read the wrong vertex.

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as its own command, all three re-run after the
formatter, and the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree. 12 new tests (1353 in the gql
package), full TS suite exit 0 first run, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three
sweeps.

- `analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` (~530 ops/s unindexed) has its subquery in the WHERE. Taking
  it would mean teaching the per-vertex gate item 175's conjunct ordering rather than evaluating

- A two-hop PROJECTION with a start filter is still 54.9ms; the count got its walk in item 206.
- Item 207's `rowLocal` fix means arithmetic items reach item 204's path for the first time, still
  unmeasured — no bench row projects a computed value.

## 209. A subquery in the node scan's predicate — 2.1-3.1x, and why the hop cannot have it

Item 208 admitted a subquery into a projected ITEM and left the predicate strict, noting that
`analytic: cycle detection` — whose subquery is in the WHERE — was the last unindexed serving row
and would need the per-vertex gate taught item 175's conjunct ordering. It needed less than that.

### The diagnosis, by item 208's technique

Hold the SCAN fixed and vary the subquery's cost. 20,000 users, three `FOLLOWS` each:

|                                               | ns/vertex |
| --------------------------------------------- | --------: |
| no subquery at all (items 204/207's path)     |        53 |
| **a TRIVIAL subquery in the WHERE**           |    **86** |
| the 2-to-4-hop cycle subquery (the bench row) |        98 |

**33ns for merely HAVING a subquery, against 12ns for the subquery's own extra work.** So the
cost was the general-path scan, not the subquery — the same shape of answer as item 208's, reached
the same way. Pricing the subquery itself would have found a 12ns target.

### Why this is admissible here and refused for a hop

Item 207 refuses a subquery in `detectHopProjection`'s predicate, and that stands. The difference
is the SEGMENT COUNT: a node scan's pattern has ZERO segments, so **every candidate vertex yields
exactly one row** — "once per vertex" and the general path's "once per complete match" are the same
evaluation set, so moving the predicate to a per-vertex gate changes neither how many times it runs
nor which rows raise. A hop has neither property: one start can yield many rows or none, which is
the whole reason item 207 needed `anyFarMatches` on its fault path.

So the guard splits: `itemLocal` for the node scan's predicate and its items, `rowLocal` for the
hop's. The two now differ on purpose and the file says why.

### The ordering came free, and was checked rather than assumed

The gate is **`gatePredicate` — the general path's own prefilter**, exported rather than
re-derived, so item 175's cheap-conjunct-first order and its stop-at-first-non-TRUE semantics come
along by construction.

The question that could have sunk this is raise parity: deferring a subquery behind a cheap
conjunct means `WHERE k = $miss AND <faulting subquery>` does not fault, and if the general path
DID fault there, the fast path would diverge. It does not — measured before the code was written:

```
MATCH (u:U) WHERE u.name = $miss AND EXISTS { … x.name / 0 … } RETURN u.k
  unindexed => []        indexed => []
```

Cheap-first is therefore already the observable semantics for this shape, and the change inherits
it rather than introducing it. Both directions have tests: a false cheap conjunct defers the fault
(no raise, either path), and a cheap conjunct that SELECTS the faulting vertex raises on both.

### Measured

| shape                                      | before |      after |           |
| ------------------------------------------ | -----: | ---------: | --------- |
| the 2-4 hop cycle subquery (the bench row) | 39.0ms | **18.8ms** | **2.07x** |
| the subquery conjunct written FIRST        | 35.2ms | **18.0ms** | **1.96x** |
| the INLINE anchor spelling                 | 31.2ms | **10.2ms** | **3.06x** |
| a TRIVIAL subquery in the WHERE            | 34.4ms | **22.4ms** | 1.54x     |
| CONTROL no subquery at all                 | 21.2ms |     20.1ms | flat      |

Worth noting what the numbers now say: the 2-4 hop shape (47ns a vertex) costs the SAME as the
trivial one (56ns), where before they were 98 and 86. That is the ordering working — the subquery
runs once for the vertex the cheap conjunct selects, so its depth stops mattering.

`bench:usage`: **`analytic: cycle detection 2-4 hops` ts(−) 485-569 → 1.1-1.4k ops/s**, about
**2.4x**, which closes the last unindexed serving row in that suite; `fan-out spread` holds at
1.3k from item 208.

**No indexed regression**, which is the thing this family of changes has to prove: at 15 reps the
indexed column reads 0.6 / 0.5 / 1.9 / 1.5 / 1.6ms against the before's 0.7 / 0.8 / 2.1 / 1.7 /
1.6. An earlier 7-rep reading had shown 2.1 → 2.2 and that was low-rep noise.

The three-run screen flags three rows, all at or under 1.06x and all dissolved at six readings:
`decode csv` 1.00x (after-range 228.8-238.2 contains the before 223.0-230.8), `traverse 1-hop +
filter` 1.06x "faster" (46.2-51.6 contains 50.1-51.3) and `decode pg-json` 1.03x, which runs no
GQL. Nothing moved.

### Teeth: 14 tests, 8 mutants, 5 caught

The five are every mutant that can change an answer or a raise, including all three against
`gatePredicate` itself — keeping the source order, keeping a conjunct that is not cleanly TRUE, and
never reordering. Two survivors are path-narrowing (the strict guard again; the free-var check
re-applied), which cannot change an answer.

**The third survivor earned its keep by correcting a comment.** "Every predicate goes through
`gatePredicate`, so `props` are never lifted" survives the suite, and I had written that `props` is
what the seek reads — so I expected a 50x in the manner of item 204. Measured: **95.4k → 80.8k
ops/s on the indexed point lookup, 18%.** The seek reads the compiled `CNode` through
`indexCandidates`, independently of the `InlinePred`; `props` is a per-vertex shortcut inside
`inlineHolds`, which is exactly what an 18% looks like. The comment now says that, and says the
mutation measurement is what corrected it.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as its own command. Lint wanted a complexity cut —
the subquery branch took `detectNodeProjection` to 37 against a limit of 35 — so the clause `WHERE`
handling is extracted to `nodeWhereOf`, which is the natural seam: everything in it concerns the
one predicate and nothing touches the projection or the scan. All three gates re-run after the
formatter, and the mutation sweep re-run twice — the extraction moved every anchored line two
spaces shallower and all five `shortcuts.ts` anchors printed `NOT APPLIED` rather than passing
silently, eighth tick running. 14 new tests (1367 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0, all
seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps.

### Still open

- A two-hop PROJECTION with a start filter, still ~54.9ms: the count got its walk in item 206 and
  the projection has no equivalent.
- `bench:usage` now has no unindexed read below ~1.1k ops/s against native's 37-48k, so the
  remaining gap there is broad rather than concentrated — the next thing to do is re-rank it rather
  than assume the old order still holds.

## 210. The write rows' 84x is 1.47x of path and the rest is constant factor — and `props` is not lifted

Items 204-209 moved every unindexed READ in `bench:usage` from 60-82x behind native to 3-13x, so
the suite was re-ranked rather than worked down from the old order. The field has inverted: the
worst unindexed rows are now WRITES.

| workload                                | ts(−) | engine(−) |         |
| --------------------------------------- | ----: | --------: | ------- |
| `write: property update`                |   540 |     45.1k | **84x** |
| `write: 100 updates in one transaction` |   499 |     38.2k | 77x     |
| `interleaved: write + point read`       |   322 |     22.9k | 71x     |
| `interleaved: append + link`            |   540 |     37.3k | 69x     |
| `interleaved: write + traversal`        |   463 |     22.4k | 48x     |

Their `ts(+)` is 43-105k, which is the signature the reads had before item 204: an index hides it,
so the unindexed scan is the cost. `write: property update` is
`MATCH (u:User) WHERE u.name = $n SET u.score = $v` — a node scan with a row-local predicate and
one write, and `detectNodeProjection` requires a `RETURN`, so it takes the general scan.

### The write is free

A write fast path has to preserve undo, events, constraints and transaction buffering, so it is far
riskier than a read one and wanted pricing first. An impossible filter scans everything and writes
nothing, so the gap between it and the real query IS the write:

|                                                  | ns/vertex |
| ------------------------------------------------ | --------: |
| the same scan with `RETURN` (item 204's path)    | **49-57** |
| `SET`, one row matches (the bench row)           |     82-84 |
| **`SET`, NOTHING matches — scan only, no write** | **82-85** |

**The no-match case costs the same as the one-match case.** The write is free at this scale and the
entire difference is the scan: ~28ns a vertex of general-path overhead above the gated scan. So the
headroom is **about 1.47x, not 84x** — the rest is the constant-factor interpretive gap that
`ts-ingest-is-constant-factor` and item 203 both reached by other routes. `REMOVE` measures the
same (83ns); `DETACH DELETE` is genuinely heavier (158ns) because removal really does work.

A fast path for the write shapes is therefore **not worth its risk at 1.47x**, and that is the
finding rather than a deferral.

### The residual is a spelling gap, and it is already a known blocked one

Of that 28ns, most is explained precisely. Three spellings of one anchor:

|                                     |          ns/vertex |
| ----------------------------------- | -----------------: |
| clause `WHERE u.name = $n`          |                 82 |
| inline `(u:User WHERE u.name = $n)` | **83 — identical** |
| inline `(u:User {name: $n})`        |             **71** |

So `pushWhereIntoNode` works exactly as its comment claims — the clause form plans as the inline
`WHERE` form — and the residual **1.16x is `props` against a compiled EXPRESSION**: a `props` entry
is a direct property comparison in `satisfies`, while a node `where` is an evaluated expression.

That merge is NOT available for free, and `inline-props-null-is-is-null` already records why.
Confirmed again here:

```
MATCH (n:P {k: null})          → 2 rows   (stored-null AND absent-key)
MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = null   → 0 rows
MATCH (n:P {k: 1})             → 1 row    ─┐ the two agree for every
MATCH (n:P) WHERE n.k = 1      → 1 row    ─┘ NON-null value
```

So lifting an equality conjunct into `props` is sound for a non-null value and changes the answer
for `null` — and a `$param` cannot be ruled out at compile time. The merge needs either a decision
on `{k: null}`'s semantics or a `props` entry that carries expression-equality semantics instead of
inline ones. Recorded, not taken.

### `props` is not lifted, and this is the third version of that comment

Item 209's comment claimed `compilePredicate` lifts equality conjuncts into `props`. It does not:

```ts
export const compilePredicate = (properties, where): CPredicate => ({
  props: compileProps(properties),
  where: where ? compileExpr(where) : undefined,
});
```

It compiles the `properties` it is GIVEN and the `where` into an expression, and nothing moves
between them. Called with `undefined` properties — which is how item 209 calls it — it yields
`{ props: [], where: compileExpr(where) }`, so **`props` is empty on BOTH branches of that
discrimination**. The 18% that mutant measured is `gatePredicate`'s indirection applied to every
predicate, not lost `props`.

Item 209's first version of the comment said `props` was what the SEEK reads (corrected by that
mutant), its second said `compilePredicate` lifts into `props` (corrected here). Both were
plausible from reading the call site and neither survived a measurement. The comment now states
what the function does, and says which claim each measurement killed — worth the three attempts
because a wrong note about WHY a branch exists is what makes the next person delete it.

### Gates

No behaviour changed this item: one comment corrected, one probe retired. `typecheck` / `lint` /
`fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, full gql suite 1367 passing.

### Still open

- The `{k: null}` decision above, which blocks a measured 1.16x on every clause-`WHERE` node scan
  that is not a `RETURN` (so: every filtered write).
- A two-hop PROJECTION with a start filter, ~54.9ms.
- `bench:usage`'s remaining gap is now broad: no unindexed row is a concentrated outlier, the reads
  sit at 1.2-2.6k and the writes at 322-540, and the writes are priced above as constant factor.

## 211. A correlated `COUNT { (u)-[:T]->(x) }` is a DEGREE — 5.3x a row, 2.2x the bench row

Item 210 priced the write rows as constant factor, so the main bench was re-ranked. The biggest
ratio left is one item 208 created: **`query: subquery item`, ts 205ms against ffi 6.4 — 32x.** Its
filter keeps ~66,000 rows and each runs a `COUNT{}`, so ~3.1µs a subquery against native's ~97ns.

### Diagnosis: the matcher invocation, and the obvious fix was worth 2%

Varying the surviving-row count at a FIXED subquery size separates per-row cost from per-query
setup; varying the subquery's SIZE at a fixed row count separates setup from walk. 20,000 vertices
at degree 3:

|                                          | per outer row |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------: |
| `COUNT { (u)-[:T]->(x) }`                |    **1650ns** |
| the same degrees via a grouped hop count |     **262ns** |
| a 2-hop sub-pattern                      |        5196ns |

So the floor for this answer is 262ns and the subquery pays 6.3x it.

The obvious culprit was wrong, which is the part worth keeping. `compileCountSubquery` read
`[...matchClauseBindings(…)].length` — **an array built per outer row purely to read its length**,
20,000 arrays holding 60,000 bindings then discarded. `compileExists` beside it never had that (it
pulls one with `.next()` and stops). Fixing it measured **1650 → 1614ns, 2%.** The allocation was
not the cost; **`matchClauseBindings` itself was** — a general matcher invoked per row to produce
three bindings. The fix is kept because it removes an allocation for free, but on its own it would
have been a wasted item.

### The real fix

`COUNT { (u)-[:T]->(x) }` with `u` already bound is the DEGREE of `u`, which `side()` in
`shortcuts.ts` already computes — the same helper item 206's two-hop walk uses for its far leg. So
the shortcut is a shape check plus one existing call, with the general count as the fallback.

Every compile-time condition is there because the alternative is a different question: one pattern,
one segment, no path variable; an anonymous DIRECTED rel (a rel variable is bindable, and `both`
counts both directions); plain start and far nodes; no sub-`WHERE`.

**Two conditions can only be checked at RUN time**, because the subquery's own text does not say
which names the outer scope has bound — and each is a WRONG answer if missed:

- **the start must BE bound.** `COUNT { (z)-[:T]->(x) }` with `z` free counts every `z`'s edges —
  7 in the test fixture, identically for every outer row. Reading the unbound name as an anchor
  answers 0.
- **the far variable must NOT be bound.** `COUNT { (u)-[:T]->(w) }` with `w` from the outer pattern
  counts the edges from this `u` to THAT `w` — the pair, not the degree. And `has`, not truthiness:
  an `OPTIONAL MATCH` can bind a name to null, and the subquery correlates on that null.

Either failing falls back to the general count, so the fast path never answers a question it was
not handed.

### Measured

|                                          | before |     after |            |
| ---------------------------------------- | -----: | --------: | ---------- |
| `COUNT{}` per outer row                  | 1650ns | **309ns** | **5.3x**   |
| — against the grouped-hop-count floor    |  262ns |     262ns | within 18% |
| a 2-hop sub-pattern (correctly declines) | 5196ns |    4943ns | unchanged  |

The three-run screen separates **exactly one row and it is the target**: `query: subquery item`
**204.8-214.8 → 91.5-93.2ms, 2.20x+, ranges disjoint**, ts/ffi from 32x to ~13.5x. Nothing else
moved. `bench:usage`'s `fan-out spread` is unchanged at 1.3k, correctly — its subquery is
`->{1,3}`, a quantified segment the shortcut declines.

2.2x on the bench row against 5.3x a row is the usual shape: that row's filter keeps a third of
200,000 vertices, so the remaining 66,000 degree lookups are real work, where the probe's per-row
figure isolates the subquery.

### Teeth: 20 tests, 15 mutants, 12 caught

Three survivors, all accounted for: two perf-only (the degree path never taken; the materialization
restored) and one genuinely EQUIVALENT — "the far variable may equal the start variable" is
redundant with the runtime bound-check, because the start is bound by definition, so a far variable
equal to it is bound too. That is now written at the compile-time check rather than left for someone
to delete as dead.

Two real fixture gaps, both found by mutants and both fixed in the fixture:

- **a start LABEL that does not match.** My test used `COUNT { (u:U)-[:T]->(x) }` under
  `MATCH (u:U)`, where the inner label always passes — so a shortcut ignoring it agreed by luck.
  `COUNT { (u:X)-… }` under `MATCH (u:U)` answers 0 for every row and the degree would not.
- **a REL VARIABLE bound outside.** `MATCH (p)-[r:T]->(q) RETURN COUNT { (p)-[r:T]->(z) }` answers
  1 — that one edge — where `p`'s degree is 2. So the rel-variable guard has the same reason as the
  far-variable one, and nothing had tested it.

Also worth recording: the undirected case needed the right ROW to be observable. `a` has four
out-edges and a self-loop, and counts 5 either way; only `b`, with one out-edge and one in-edge,
shows that `side` would answer 1 where the matcher answers 2. A fixture with only `a` in it would
have let the `both` decline look unnecessary.

### `bun run typecheck` earned its place again

`matchClauseBindings` is typed `Iterable<Binding>`, not `Iterator`. It IS a generator at run time,
so `matches.next()` works and **all 1387 tests passed** — only `typecheck` objected. Fixed with
`[Symbol.iterator]()`. That is the second time this session the suite was green on code `tsc`
rejects, which is why `local-gates-vs-ci` lists typecheck as its own gate.

### Noted, not chased

ISO's abbreviated edge pattern `-->` does not parse in this engine at all (`MATCH (u)-->(x)` is a
syntax error; the untyped form must be written `-[]->`). Found while writing the untyped-rel test.
Not this item's business, but it is a surface gap rather than a performance one.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, all re-run after the formatter,
and the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree. 20 new tests (1387 in the gql package),
full TS suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps.

## 212. The degree shortcut generalised to two hops — 5.5x a row, 2.36x the bench row, and an ORDER BY bug found en route

Item 211 answered `COUNT { (u)-[:T]->(x) }` as a degree and left the two-hop form at 4943ns an outer
row, the deepest remaining shape. The inner computation already existed: item 206's
`buildFilteredTwoHopCount` walks the first leg, checks the middle label and adds `side()` for the
second.

### What changed

`side`'s two-segment counterpart, `twoHopSide`, is lifted out of that walk into `shortcuts.ts` so
the executor trunk can use it without needing the adjacency primitives — `executor.ts` imports
`labelsMatch` and not `matchesLabel`, and reaching for more of them to inline a loop would have put
adjacency logic in the wrong file.

The detector is now arity-generic: `hopOf` validates ONE segment and the caller composes one or
two. That matters beyond tidiness — every guard is now stated once, so the second leg cannot drift
from the first, which is exactly how `relTypeNames`-style conditions diverge between near-identical
branches.

|                             |        per outer row |
| --------------------------- | -------------------: |
| 1-hop `COUNT{}`             |                459ns |
| **2-hop `COUNT{}`, before** |           **4943ns** |
| **2-hop `COUNT{}`, after**  | **891ns** — **5.5x** |
| 3-hop (correctly declines)  |              14136ns |

A bench row joins the corpus — **`query: 2-hop subquery item`**, which the three-run screen moves
**559.4-584.3 → 225.9-237.5ms, 2.36x+, ranges disjoint**, ts/ffi 11.76x. It separates exactly one
row and it is that one; nothing else moved. All three engines answer it (ts 269.7, ffi 22.9, wasm
25.6, no `n/a`).

Worth noting what the floor comparison now says: the 2-hop subquery at 891ns is **faster than the
grouped-hop-count spelling of the same question** (6950ns), because the subquery counts while the
grouped form materializes every two-hop row. Item 211's floor argument does not carry over to two
hops, and assuming it did would have set the target 8x too low.

### Teeth: 30 tests, 24 mutants, 23 caught

The single survivor is the perf-only revert. Caught include both runtime guards, the repeated-
variable check, every field of the two-hop plan, and `twoHopSide`'s own middle-label and edge-end
reads.

**One fixture blindness, and it is the "two-of-the-thing" shape again.** My two-hop fixture used
type `T` on BOTH legs, so the mutant that swaps `t1` and `t2` is a no-op and survived. Two different
types make the swap observable: `(a)-[:P]->(m)-[:Q]->(e)` finds one path and `-[:Q]->…-[:P]->` finds
none. That is the fourth time a mutant has found a fixture that exercises a path without
distinguishing its arms, and all four had the same cause — one instance of a thing where the code
has two.

Three anchors also went stale when the formatter reflowed `hopOf`'s four-clause condition onto
separate lines; each printed `NOT APPLIED` rather than passing silently. Ninth tick running.

### An ORDER BY bug, found while writing a test

My first version of the bound-middle test read
`RETURN COUNT { (a)-[:T]->(m)-[:T]->(c) } AS c ORDER BY c` and came back **unsorted**. The values
were right; the order was not. Isolated:

```
… RETURN COUNT { MATCH (m)-[:T]->(c) } AS c ORDER BY c    →  [2, 1]   NOT sorted
… RETURN COUNT { MATCH (m)-[:T]->(z) } AS c ORDER BY c    →  [1, 2]   sorted
```

So **an `ORDER BY` alias that collides with a variable bound inside a subquery in the same
projection item silently sorts by nothing.** It is not a general scope leak — `RETURN COUNT { (a)-[:T]->(z) } AS k, z`
raises `variable z is not defined`, as do the `ORDER BY z` and `WHERE`-side spellings — so the inner
name is not reaching the outer binding; something in sort-key resolution is finding it anyway and
yielding a constant.

Narrow (it needs the collision) but a silent wrong ORDER, and `ORDER BY` is specified where row
order otherwise is not. **Left for its own item rather than folded in here**: mixing a name-resolution
fix into a perf commit is precisely what makes a later regression impossible to attribute. The test
now uses distinct names and says why.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, all re-run after the formatter,
and the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree at 23/24. 30 tests in the file (1398 in the
gql package), full TS suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps.
`mutate-212.py` supersedes `mutate-211.py`, whose anchors referenced the single-segment shape.

- **The `ORDER BY` alias collision above.**
- A QUANTIFIED sub-pattern (`->{1,3}`) has no shortcut, which is why `bench:usage`'s `fan-out spread`

  quantified patterns carry, so it is not a degree.
- Three or more segments: 14136ns a row, and the plan would need to be recursive rather than a
  fixed pair.
- ISO's abbreviated `-->` still does not parse (item 211).

## 213. An `ORDER BY` that did not order — a live cross-engine divergence, and three comments of mine that were wrong

Item 212 found this while writing a test and deliberately left it for its own item. It is a
correctness fix, not a performance one.

### The bug

```
MATCH (a:A)-[:T]->(m:M) RETURN COUNT { MATCH (m)-[:T]->(c) } AS c ORDER BY c
  ts      [2, 1]   ← NOT sorted
  native  [1, 2]
```

Rename the subquery's internal variable from `c` to `z` and TS sorts correctly. So: **an `ORDER BY`
alias that collides with a variable bound inside a subquery in the same projection item silently
sorted by nothing.** Values right, order wrong — and `ORDER BY` is specified where row order
otherwise is not ([[order-is-unspecified]] is about the absence of `ORDER BY`, not its failure).

**It was a live cross-engine divergence**, which makes it a byte-identity violation rather than a
TS-only wart. Verified against the FFI engine on the same graph, before and after.

### Root cause: `freePredicateVars` does not descend into a subquery

`aliasDefinition` substitutes a sort alias with the expression it names — item 145 widened that to
ANY expression reading only input variables, which fixed a different divergence. It is guarded:
_"substituting is sound exactly when no free name of the expression is an OUTPUT name — a shadowed
name would resolve to the output column in the sort scope and mean something else."_

That guard is exactly right and it could not see this case, because **`freePredicateVars` returns
the EMPTY set for `exists` / `countSubquery` / `valueSubquery`.** It does not descend into one at
all. So:

1. the guard found no collision and substituted, making the sort key the subquery itself;
2. `orderNeedsOutput` then overlays the projected output on the binding, which bound `c` to the
   COUNT VALUE;
3. the sub-pattern's `(c)` was therefore matched against a number, found nothing, and counted **0
   for every row**;
4. every key compared equal, so the input order survived.

The fix is one guard: decline substitution for any item containing a subquery. It falls through to
the non-substituted path, which sorts by the output column and agrees with native. The cost is item
145's top-k-over-input-bindings for subquery items only.

**Why no fuzzer caught it:** the alias must equal a name the subquery binds, and the generators do
not produce colliding names. A hand-written test found it, and only because the colliding name was
the natural one to write (`COUNT { … (c) } AS c`).

### Three comments of mine said the opposite, and are corrected

Items 204, 207 and 208 each assert that `freePredicateVars` descends into a subquery and reports the
variables inside it. **It does not.** The code in those items is still correct — each declines for a
different, real reason — but the stated reason was wrong in all three:

- item 207's `carriedWhere`: a free-variable check cannot see inside a subquery, so the ALLOWLIST
  (`rowLocal`) is the only thing refusing one there, not the variable test.
- item 204/208's item check: for a BARE subquery the skip is a no-op. It matters only for a MIXED
  item such as `COUNT { … } + n.k`, where the arithmetic's names are reported and the subquery's are
  not.

All three now say what the function does. Worth the correction because a wrong note about WHY a
guard exists is what gets it deleted — and here the same misreading is what let the bug through in
the first place.

### Teeth: 11 tests, 9 mutants, 6 caught

Caught: removing the decline (restores the divergence), declining everything (reverts item 145),
dropping the shadowing guard, matching the alias by column name only, and both directions of
`orderNeedsOutput`.

Three survivors, all EQUIVALENT rather than untested, and the file now says so:

- **substituting an AGGREGATE alias changes no answer**, because the sort runs AFTER aggregation, so
  `count(*)` as a sort key folds over the same group and gives the same number as the output column.
  Checked against groups of sizes 1, 2 and 3 — with equal-sized groups the two readings agree by
  luck, which is why the first version of that test let the mutant survive.
- the `var` and `star` guards are equivalent for a structural reason: with a non-`var` key
  `sortExpr.name` is undefined, and with `RETURN *` there are no items, so the lookup finds nothing
  either way.

The tests pin the direction both ways: insertion order here IS descending, so ASC is what proves
sorting happens and DESC is what proves the key is read rather than ignored. There is also a
`LIMIT 1` case, because a wrong sort key under a window returns the wrong ROW, not merely the wrong
order — the shape in which this bug would have been silently load-bearing.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command. One slip worth noting: while
adding the explanatory comment I dropped the `if` statement under it, and **`tsc` caught it** (three
`'item' is possibly undefined` errors) where the formatter and lint were both happy — the third time
this session typecheck has caught something the other gates and the suite would have let through.
11 new tests (1408 in the gql package), full TS suite exit 0 on the second run (the known
`run-many` flake), all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps.

The three-run screen flags three rows, every one at or under 1.03x: `decode ndjson (5 edges/node)`
1.01x "slower" — a 19ms margin on a 2800ms row that runs no GQL, dissolved by three more readings
(six now span 2686.6-2907.0, containing the before range) — plus `decode pg-json` 1.01x and
`query: subquery item` 1.03x. Nothing moved.

### Still open

- A QUANTIFIED sub-pattern (`->{1,3}`) still has no `COUNT{}` shortcut, so `bench:usage`'s
  `fan-out spread` holds at 1.3k.
- Three or more segments in a `COUNT{}` (14136ns a row) would need a recursive plan.
- ISO's abbreviated `-->` does not parse (item 211).
- The `{k: null}` inline-versus-`= null` decision (item 210), where the ISO artifacts point at our
