## 214. The differential fuzzer could not see a row-order divergence, and had no subquery coverage at all

Item 213 fixed an `ORDER BY` that did not order — a live TS-vs-native divergence — and I recorded
"no fuzzer caught it because the generators do not produce colliding names". That was half the
reason. The other half is worse, and it is this item's finding.

### Two gaps, and the second is the one that mattered

**One: zero subquery coverage.** `EXISTS {`, `COUNT {` and `VALUE {` appear **zero** times across
all seven fuzzers' generators. Items 208, 209, 211, 212 and 213 all worked on subquery paths, and
none of them was fuzzed.

**Two: `canonResult` SORTS THE OUTER ROWS ARRAY.** So `resultsEqual` — what the differential fuzzer
compares with — **cannot see a row-order divergence at all.** An `ORDER BY` that silently sorted by
nothing was byte-identical to a correct one after canonicalization. Item 213 was undetectable here
**by construction**, and no amount of new shapes would have changed that.

The sorting is right for an unordered result: ISO `US001` leaves the sequence of an unordered
binding table to the implementation, and `order-is-unspecified` is this repo's standing position. It
is wrong for a query whose `ORDER BY` imposes a total order, which is exactly what the file's own
convention guarantees — _"Every ORDER BY ends with the distinct `n.n`"_.

### What changed

`resultsEqualInOrder` canonicalizes each row's keys but preserves the row SEQUENCE, and
`totallyOrdered(q)` decides when to use it: the query projects `n.n AS t` and its final sort key is
`t`. `n` ranges over distinct vertices and `n.n` is distinct per vertex, so the order is total and
the sequence is comparable. Everything else keeps the unordered comparison, because a TIE leaves the
sequence unspecified and comparing it would report the engines' free choice as a bug.

Subquery generation went in two places:

- a **predicate** arm in `genPred`, carved out of the OR fallback's tail so no band below 0.9 moves;
- a **projection** shape in `genQuery`'s fallback, half its share, where the alias may COLLIDE with a
  variable the subquery binds — the shape item 213 needed, generated deliberately and often (155
  per seed), because without the collision the bug is unreachable.

`genPred` takes `allowSub`, defaulting FALSE, so with it unset the function is byte-for-byte what it
was and every existing seed keeps its meaning. Only a clause `WHERE` and a `FILTER` opt in.

### Teeth, verified rather than assumed

This is the step that makes the rest worth anything, and the first attempt FAILED it: with the new
shapes in place but the comparison still sorting rows, item 213's reverted fix passed three seeds.
That is the generator reaching the path and the harness throwing the distinction away — the same
shape of blindness as a fixture that exercises an arm without distinguishing it, one level up.

After the ordered comparison:

|                         | seeds 11, 12       |
| ----------------------- | ------------------ |
| item 213's fix REVERTED | **fails**          |
| item 213's fix restored | passes (and 13-17) |

All seven fuzzers green across three full sweeps on random seeds.

### Two NATIVE feature gaps, found on the generator's first seeds

Both are recorded rather than excused, and the registry explicitly cannot take either: it has no
`value` axis, and `accept` refuses a value difference whatever an entry says — one engine answering
where the other raises on a determinate question is a bug in one of them, not an axis.

**A named aggregate inside a `VALUE { … }` body.**

```
MATCH (n:T) RETURN VALUE { MATCH (n)-[:E]->(x) RETURN max(x.n) } AS v
  ts      [{v:2},{v:null}]
  native  E_UNKNOWN_FUNCTION: unknown function `max`
```

Native resolves `max` at the TOP level, and `count(*)` inside a `VALUE` body, but a named aggregate
inside one falls through to the scalar-function table in `gql.rs` — so that body is not lowered as an
aggregating projection. The generator emits only the bodies both engines support (`count(*)` and a
bare property) until the feature exists; generating the rest would make the gate red for a missing
feature rather than for a regression.

**A subquery inside an INLINE node predicate.**

```
MATCH p = ANY SHORTEST (a:T)-[:E]->*(n:T WHERE (n.n >= 4 AND EXISTS { MATCH (n)-[:E|F]->(b) }))
  ts      9 rows
  native  E_INVALID_VALUE
```

Hence `allowSub` being opt-in per context rather than global.

### Gates

No engine code changed — only the harness and the generator — so there is nothing a bench screen
could move, and none was run. `typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command;
full TS suite exit 0; all seven fuzzers green across three sweeps, plus seven individual
differential seeds.

### Still open

- The two native feature gaps above.
- **Row order is still canonicalized away for every shape that is not totally ordered**, which is
  most of them. The convention makes the generated ones decidable; a shape whose order is total for
  a subtler reason is not, and tightening that means tagging shapes at generation rather than
  sniffing their text.
- The other six fuzzers still generate no subqueries. This item covered the differential one, which
  is the TS-vs-native oracle and so the one that matters most for byte-identity.

## 215. One question, two arrows, 4.6x apart — 3.3x, and the row I went after was already optimal

Item 214 left two native feature gaps, both needing IR work (an aggregating CORRELATED subquery for
the `VALUE` body; subqueries in inline node predicates). The loop asks for the TS side, so the field
was re-ranked there instead — and the row at the top of it turned out not to be the target.

### The row I went after is already on its best plan

`query: distinct over a hop` — `MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(f) RETURN DISTINCT f.age ORDER BY x` —
is ts 89ms against ffi 7.3, 12.2x, the biggest ratio left outside what items 197/200 closed. At
1,000,000 edges that is 66ns an edge, and four probes say nothing is declining:

|                                         | ns/vertex |
| --------------------------------------- | --------: |
| the bench row                           |       332 |
| without the `ORDER BY`                  |       311 |
| without the start label                 |       321 |
| a node dedup with no hop, for the floor |    **55** |

So the far-driven walk (items 195/198) IS firing — 200,000 vertices, not 1,000,000 edges — and the
332 against the node dedup's 55 is one adjacency lookup per vertex, which item 197 priced at ~183ns
and item 200 closed as unimprovable without regressing get-by-id. **Not a missing path.**

### What the same probe found instead

Separating the two axes — arrow direction, and which end the `DISTINCT` reads — gives a clean 2×2:

| arrow       | dedup end | ns/vertex |
| ----------- | --------- | --------: |
| forward     | far       |       344 |
| forward     | start     |       377 |
| reverse     | far       |       261 |
| **reverse** | **start** |  **1520** |

Three of four sit at 261-377. One is 4.4x worse, and it is the same QUESTION as the first:
`MATCH (f)<-[:KNOWS]-(a:Person) RETURN DISTINCT f.age` against
`MATCH (a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(f) RETURN DISTINCT f.age`. Both answer 90 rows. **One question, two
arrows, 4.6x apart** — the bug class this engine is named after, and the probe found it only because
it varied both axes rather than the one I was chasing.

### Why the reverse spelling was slow, and two fixes

The deduped vertex is the pattern's START, which `farDrivenFits` refuses by design — an in-edge says
a far vertex is reached from SOME source, not that the source matched a label. So it takes the
start-driven walk, and that walk resolved the far ENDPOINT for every edge in the graph (a
string-keyed `Map.get`, ~190ns, item 194) for one purpose: testing the other end's label.

1. **Stop at the first qualifying edge when keyed on the start.** `take(v)` is idempotent — the dedup
   keeps one entry per value and the count variant increments only for a value it has not seen — so
   every later edge of the same vertex re-offers the same element. 304 → 123ns an edge.
2. **A VACUOUS far label needs no resolve at all.** `needsFar` was computed at compile time from
   "the other end has a label"; whether a label actually constrains anything is a RUNTIME property,
   so it moved into a per-call `planFor`, the same idiom items 195/198 use for the walk choice.
   123 → **92ns**.

The spelling gap is now 92 against 66, **1.33x, down from 4.6x**. The residual is one adjacency
lookup the far-driven walk gets to skip, which is the floor item 200 established.

### Measured

A bench row joins the corpus — **`query: distinct over a reversed hop`** — which the three-run screen
moves **357.3-362.5 → 104.3-109.1ms, 3.27x+, ranges disjoint**. All three engines answer it (ts
100.4, ffi 9.6, wasm 12.4). Nine probe shapes held flat, including both forward spellings, the
far-keyed reverse, `count(DISTINCT)` and the node dedup.

The screen's other three separations are all ≤1.06x and all FASTER — `decode ndjson (nodes)` 1.00x,
`encode pg-text` 1.02x, `encode csv` 1.06x — on codec paths that run no GQL at all. Noise, and named
rather than quietly banked.

### Teeth: 12 tests, 9 mutants, 6 caught

All three survivors are the explicitly expected perf-only ones (the break removed; `needsFar`
ignoring `vacuousLabel`; `needsFar` always true — each only ADDS work). Both dangerous mutants are
caught: the break firing BEFORE the far-label test, and `vacuousLabel` read as its negation so a
resolve the label needs is skipped.

The fixture's load-bearing case is a vertex whose FIRST in-edge comes from a non-matching label and
whose SECOND comes from a matching one. Breaking before the label test drops that row entirely —
a wrong answer, not a slow one — and a fixture where every qualifying vertex's first edge already
matched would have let it through. Its mirrors are there too: a vertex reached ONLY through a
non-matching label must be excluded, and one with no in-edge at all.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, all re-run after the formatter,
and the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree at 6/9. 12 new tests (1420 in the gql
package), full TS suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green across three sweeps — including
item 214's new subquery shapes and its order-sensitive comparison, which is the first change to land
under them.

### Still open

- The two native feature gaps from item 214.
- `query: distinct over a hop` itself: 12.2x, and **already optimal** — floored by the adjacency
  lookup item 200 closed. Recorded so the next sweep does not re-derive it.
- A 1.33x residual between the two arrow spellings, which is that same lookup.

## 216. A generic evaluator read its element back out of a Map it had just been handed — 1.2-1.6x across the DISTINCT family

Item 215's ranking note left `query: distinct + order by` as the table's biggest TS ratio at 36.53x
and the tick began by retracting it: the row directly above it is the SAME QUERY plus `LIMIT 10`
and printed 2.2x faster, which no plan explains. In-process, alternating, on the bench's own
fixture, the unlimited form is **0.93x** of the limited one — marginally faster, as it should be.
Both bands run 6.2 to 16.0ms, so 15.3 was an ordinary draw. **The tell is free: two rows differing
only by a RESTRICTION where the more restricted one is faster is sampling, not a plan.**

That left the family as ONE number rather than a ladder — `count distinct` 5.3ms, `top distinct
values` 7.0, `distinct + order by` ~6.2, all seven spellings within 1.15x (items 187/188 keep them
equalized) — and a real target underneath it.

### The diagnosis

`detectDistinctProjection`'s walk is already tight: a `valueSet` rather than string keys (items
192/193), a row built only for a new value, both walks at module scope. What remained per vertex
was three operations, and one of them was an accident of plumbing:

```
binding.set(keyedVar, el);          // hand the element over
const value = evalFn(env);          // (env) => propOf(env.binding.get(variable), key)
seen.add(value);
```

`evalFn` is the GENERIC compiled expression, so it reads the element back out of the binding the
walk had just put it into. For `RETURN DISTINCT n.age` that is a `Map.set` plus a `Map.get` per
vertex to move a value the walk was already holding.

**The fix is a once-per-query decision, not a new path.** `directPropKey(source, keyedVar)` returns
the key when the walked expression is exactly `<keyedVar>.<key>`, and `needsBinding` is true only
when the gate or the generic evaluator actually wants the binding. Sound because `sourceFor` and
`evaluatorFor` are exactly parallel — `source` IS the AST `evalFn` was compiled from, in all three
of their cases (bare projection, `LET`-bound, `count` argument) — so `propOf(el, key)` is the same
call with the same undefined-to-null coalescing.

### Grepped, and one site deliberately left alone

`binding.set(` has 22 call sites. The same shape is in the count-mode sibling
(`detectDistinctCount`), so both changed. The near-miss is `shortcuts.ts:3006`, item 204's node
projection, which looks identical and is NOT a target: its own comment says it, and it is right —
the evaluations there are paid per SURVIVOR, after the gate, so the Map round-trip is per output
row rather than per scanned vertex. A 90-row answer pays it ninety times.

### The first measurement was wrong and was thrown away

The component ablation ladder (walk alone, + `binding.set`, + `evalFn`) came out non-additive:
`direct` at 63.6ns exceeded `eval` at 44.3 while doing strictly less. Three defects, all mine —
the `sink++` the ablations fed was dead code the JIT may drop, the branches did unequal final work,
and `LENKE_ABLATE=""` is not an unset variable, so the "baseline" row was itself an ablation.

Scrapped for the only comparison that decides anything: both variants producing the CORRECT answer,
alternated round by round in one process. The point generalises — **an ablation whose branches
differ in what they ultimately do is not a decomposition, and a sink the program never reads is
not work.**

### Measured

In-process A/B of the two built bundles, answers verified identical on all 12 cases first:

| shape                       |       |
| --------------------------- | ----: |
| `count distinct`            | 1.41x |
| `top distinct values`       | 1.30x |
| `distinct over a hop`       | 1.35x |
| `distinct + order by`       | 1.26x |
| `distinct`, no order        | 1.25x |
| `distinct via LET`          | 1.25x |
| **gated** (`WHERE` carried) | 1.03x |
| **generic** (`n.age / 2`)   | 0.97x |

The last two rows are the evidence the guard discriminates rather than the win being everywhere:
both still need the binding, and both are correctly untouched.

The three-run screen moves four rows with disjoint ranges — `query: distinct over a hop` **1.59x+**
(93.2-93.5 → 53.5-58.7), `count distinct` 1.24x+, `group, no aggregate` 1.23x+, `distinct + order
by` 1.16x+ — plus `encode graphson` 1.06x+, whose before band is 143-190 and which runs no GQL.

`group, no aggregate` was not predicted and is the honest surprise: `LET a = n.age RETURN a GROUP
BY a` routes through the same dedup walk, so it came along at 1.42x in-process.

**Two rows the screen called SLOWER, both refuted.** `traverse 1-hop + start filter` (1.03x+) and
`query: 2-hop subquery item` (1.02x+) use no part of the DISTINCT walk, but they share the module,
which is the `ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` signature and would be its fifth occurrence. Checked
rather than argued: in-process over 9 alternating reps they are **0.99x** and **0.97x** with
heavily overlapping bands (216.7-274.2 against 222.6-315.1). Not establishable — the repo's own
floor is ~10% for anything without an isolated harness. A ~3% module-level toll cannot be excluded
at this resolution, and is recorded as such rather than as a zero.

### Teeth: 17 tests, 9 mutants, 6 caught

The three survivors are accounted for and only one needed work:

- **`directPropKey` ignoring WHICH variable the prop reads is EQUIVALENT CODE.** `distinctShape`
  computes `reads = freePredicateVars(source)` and requires its single member to be the keyed end,
  so a `prop` source's variable IS `keyedVar` by construction. The conjunct cannot be reached, so
  no fixture can catch it. Kept as cheap documentation of the invariant, not as a live guard.
- two are the pre-216 behaviour (`needsBinding` always true; `directPropKey` always declining) and
  only ADD work.

The fixture gap a mutant did find: dropping the `kind === 'prop'` check survived, because
**`PROPERTY_EXISTS(n, k)` carries both a `.variable` and a `.key` while being a BOOLEAN, not a
property read.** A guard comparing only the variable specializes it and returns the property's
value. That is now two tests, and the mutant is caught.

One label of mine was wrong: I marked "use the generic evaluator even when a direct key exists" as
perf-only and it failed 111 tests. Correct — once `needsBinding` is false the binding is empty, so
forcing `evalFn` reads nothing. It is a real wrong-answer mutant, not an added cost; only the PAIR
of it and `needsBinding: true` is the old behaviour.

Also mine: two test expectations asserted nulls sort FIRST. They sort LAST under the engine
default. The engine was right.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, re-run after the formatter;
17 new tests (1437 in the gql package); full suite exit 0; all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.
Mutation ran under `timeout 600` plus a 16G cgroup with `MemorySwapMax=0`, both kill paths proven
first (137 on an allocator bomb, 124 on a bare spin).

### Still open

The family is still ~11x behind native, and the remaining gap is structural: at ~25ns a vertex
after this change, against native's ~2ns over 200,000 vertices, native is not scanning per-vertex
at all — it reads the property column's dictionary. Closing that in TS is a dictionary-or-index
FEATURE, the same shape of answer as item 200's, and should not be re-opened as a fast path.

## 217. A generator frame per vertex, and a label test that could not fail — 1.78x, and the spelling gap closes

Item 216 made the forward spelling of the deduped hop 1.59x faster and left the REVERSED spelling
untouched, which re-opened a gap items 215 and 216 had each partly closed: 53.3ms against 103.3ms
for the same question on the same fixture. That is this engine's named bug class, so it was the
target rather than a curiosity.

### Separating the two axes again

The 2x2 from item 215 still earns its keep. Varying arrow direction against which end the `DISTINCT`
reads, the gap splits in two:

|                                            | ns/vertex |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------: |
| forward, far-keyed (the fast reference)    |       313 |
| reverse, far-keyed                         |       431 |
| **reverse, start-keyed** (the benched row) |   **514** |

The fixture is degree-5 symmetric in BOTH directions, so neither step is a property of the data.

### Two causes, and I got the first guess wrong

**Wrong guess first, recorded because the measurement is what corrected it.** Reading the two walks,
the visible difference was that `walkFarSide` asks `bucket.size` while `walkStartSide` opens a `for
… of bucket` — a `Set` iterator allocated per vertex to look at one element. With `onStart` and a
false `needsFar`, `far` stays `v`, so neither the label test nor `take` reads the edge and item 215's
`break` leaves after the first one: the loop genuinely had nothing left to do. Replacing it with a
`size` test bought **3%**. Not the cause.

**The real one is a generator frame per vertex.** `candidateVertices` is a `function*` whose body is
`yield* graph.verticesById.values()`, so a whole-graph scan pays a generator frame and a `.next()`
per vertex to hand back the elements of an iterator it already had. `candidateVertexSource` returns
that iterable directly, and the far-driven walk has always used it — `walkStartSide` had not. Same
elements, same order, same liveness; both are single-use views over the same underlying iterator.

That alone took the far-UNLABELLED reverse spelling from 95.9 to 61.1ms, exactly level with the
forward one. The benched spelling, whose far end is `(a:Person)`, did not move — which isolated the
third cost.

**A far-label test that cannot fail.** The gate kept `matchesLabel(v, farLabel)`, and that was
**189ns a vertex** (494 against 305 for the unlabelled spelling), the random-order element lookup
this engine pays everywhere. It is not merely cheap to skip, it is unnecessary: under `onStart`,
`needsFar === (farLabel !== undefined && !vacuousLabel(graph, farLabel))`, so a FALSE `needsFar`
says the far label is either ABSENT or VACUOUS — and a vacuous label is one every vertex in the
graph carries. My own comment had talked me out of this a few minutes earlier, on the grounds that
`needsFar` is also false when there is no far label at all; both cases reach the same conclusion.

### Measured

`MATCH (f)<-[:KNOWS]-(a:Person) RETURN DISTINCT f.age`, 200,000 vertices at degree 5:

|                                       |          |
| ------------------------------------- | -------: |
| before                                |  102.8ms |
| + the bucket-size gate                |     99.8 |
| + `candidateVertexSource`             |     98.8 |
| + dropping the vacuous far-label test | **57.9** |

**1.78x**, and the spelling gap goes from 1.64x of the forward spelling to **0.95x** — marginally
faster than it. In-process A/B of the two built bundles, answers identical on all 8 cases:
`count distinct` 1.74x, `distinct + order by` 1.68x, `group, no aggregate` 1.60x,
`distinct over a reversed hop` 1.57x, with `distinct over a hop`, `traverse 1-hop + filter` and
`count(*)` flat.

The three-run screen, four disjoint rows and nothing slower:

| row                            | before             | after            |        |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------ | ---------------- | -----: |
| `distinct over a reversed hop` | 98.2, 100.7, 105.3 | 62.0, 67.4, 71.9 | 1.37x+ |
| `distinct + order by`          | 5.1, 5.4, 8.3      | 3.6, 4.0, 4.0    | 1.28x+ |
| `group, no aggregate`          | 3.9, 4.1, 4.3      | 3.3, 3.3, 3.3    | 1.18x+ |
| `count distinct`               | 3.9, 4.1, 4.3      | 3.1, 3.4, 3.5    | 1.11x+ |

### Grepped — and one of the five sites was dropped on the evidence

`candidateVertices` had five callers. Four are plain `for … of` scans and were swapped
(`hop-projection.ts` x3 plus the walk, `shortcuts.ts:3341`). The fifth,
`matching.ts:197`, is `yield* candidateVertices(…)` on the GENERAL path, where the swap would
remove one nested generator layer of two.

**It was swapped, measured, and reverted.** It contributed none of the four winning rows, and the
screen taken WITH it flagged `query: 2-hop subquery item` as 1.02x+ slower on disjoint ranges — a
row that uses none of this. With it dropped, that row is 0.99x in-process over 11 alternating reps
and OVERLAPPING on the three-run screen. Honest caveat: item 216's screen leaned 1.02x slower on
the same row while touching nothing in `matching.ts`, so I cannot pin the lean on the swap; what I
can say is that the general-path change bought nothing measurable and carried the broadest risk
surface in the diff, which is reason enough to leave it out.

### Teeth: 15 tests, 9 mutants, 5 caught

Four survivors, and the two that look dangerous are provably **equivalent code**:

- **dropping `onStart &&` from the gate.** `needsFar = !onStart || (…)`, so it is ALWAYS true when
  `onStart` is false — the gate cannot fire for a far-keyed dedup and the conjunct is unreachable.
- **`bucket.size > 0` always passing.** A present bucket is never empty, because de-indexing drops
  the entry when its set empties. Rather than leave that as an assertion, there is now a test that
  adds an edge, REMOVES it, and requires the vertex to stop being reached — it pins the invariant
  the cheap gate leans on, and would fail if de-indexing ever stopped removing the entry.

The other two restore the iterator and the per-vertex label test: the pre-217 behaviour, correct and
slower. The order tests matter more than usual here, because the dedup is FIRST-SEEN and that order
is observable without an `ORDER BY` — item 142 gave back 7.4x for getting it wrong — so the swap is
pinned element-for-element against the general path, including the unlabelled whole-graph branch,
which is the one place the two sources differ.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command. Lint caught two imports the
swap orphaned, and `fmt:check` then failed on the import block the deletions left — `fmt` exiting 0
is not `fmt:check` passing. All re-run after the formatter, and the mutation sweep re-run against
the formatted tree at 5/9. 15 new tests (1452 in the gql package), full suite exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green.

### Still open

- **reverse, far-keyed is still 1.33x** of the forward spelling (`MATCH (f)<-[:KNOWS]-(a:Person)
RETURN DISTINCT a.age`). It takes the far-driven walk over the mirrored index, so it is a
  different path from the one fixed here. Recorded rather than guessed at.
- The DISTINCT family remains ~7-9x behind native, which is the dictionary question item 216 closed
  as structural.

## 218. A degree product that resolved an endpoint per edge — 1.95x, 2.21x, 1.48x, and the win landed where I was not looking

`count 2-hop + start filter` was the biggest query row left that item 200 had not already closed as
floored: 209ms against native's 14.6. The diagnosis started from a formula rather than a profile.

### The unit says what the engine is paying per

On the bench fixture every vertex has out-degree 5 and in-degree 5, so a 2-hop count is
`Σ_b indeg(b) · outdeg(b)` — a per-VERTEX tally that needs no path visits at all. Checking the
formula against the engine's own answers first: unfiltered 200,000 × 25 = 5,000,000, filtered
64,438 × 5 × 5 = 1,610,950. Both exactly what it returns, which settles that the semantics are
plain homomorphic walk and a degree tally is sound rather than merely plausible.

Dividing each row's time by the number of counted PATHS then said what it actually pays per:

|                      |    ns per counted path |
| -------------------- | ---------------------: |
| 1-hop, no filter     | **0.0** (a true tally) |
| 1-hop + start filter |                    119 |
| 2-hop + start filter |                    154 |
| 2-hop, no filter     |                    128 |
| 3-hop + start filter |                    537 |

Everything except the pure 1-hop tally is a flat ~120-155ns A PATH, which is the signature of
visiting each path. And a two-hop count shortcut already existed, whose comment reads _"Unfiltered
stays on the degree product: it iterates the MIDDLE once and multiplies two degrees"_ — so either
it was not firing, or the degree product was not one.

### It was not one

```ts
export const side = (graph, bId, out, types, far) => {
  const byType = (out ? graph.edgesFromByLabel : graph.edgesToByLabel).get(bId);

  return countEdges(edgesOfTypes(byType, types), (edge) =>
    matchesLabel(out ? edge.to : edge.from, far),
  );
};
```

`side` is the per-middle "degree", and it ALWAYS ran a per-edge loop — through a generator
(`edgesOfTypes` is a `function*`), resolving `edge.to` (a string-keyed `Map.get`, ~190ns, item 194)
to test a label. With no far label at all, `matchesLabel(x, undefined)` is true for every edge it
had just resolved. Ten resolutions per middle vertex over 200,000 of them is ~380ms of the 639.

Three changes, each the same idea — _do not resolve what nothing reads_:

1. **`far === undefined` ⇒ the answer is a bucket SIZE.** `bucketSize` mirrors `edgesOfTypes`'s
   cases: one named type, or one bucket when all types are wanted, is a `size` read.
2. **A VACUOUS far label collapses to no label**, decided per EXECUTION by `effectiveLabel`, since
   vacuity is a property of the graph. This is the third time that reasoning has paid — item 215
   made the endpoint resolve conditional on it, item 217 removed a label test a false `needsFar`
   had already made constant.
3. **The start-filtered walk reads `e.toId` / `e.fromId`** instead of resolving the middle VERTEX.
   The middle is wanted for one thing, its label; its ID is what the second leg counts from, and
   the edge already holds it. Item 140 made the ingest path use these ids for exactly this reason.

|                        |           |
| ---------------------- | --------: |
| before                 |   248.3ms |
| + the size path        |     137.9 |
| + the vacuity collapse |         — |
| + the endpoint ids     | **120.3** |

2.06x on the target, and **6.12x** on the unfiltered 2-hop count (639.4 → 104.4ms), which the
vacuity collapse turned into an actual degree product.

### Grepped, and that is where most of the win came from

`side` has five callers, and the two I was not aiming at moved most:

| row                          | before              | after               |            |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------- | ------------------- | ---------: |
| `count 2-hop + start filter` | 212.1, 216.7, 221.2 | 106.0, 108.0, 108.7 | **1.95x+** |
| `query: subquery item`       | 85.7, 88.0, 88.3    | 35.7, 37.8, 38.8    | **2.21x+** |
| `query: 2-hop subquery item` | 222.6, 232.4, 261.7 | 136.8, 140.4, 150.1 | **1.48x+** |

The two subquery rows reach `side` through the correlated `COUNT { }` degree shortcut
(`executor.ts:1041`, items 211/212) — a path this item never touched and never measured until the
screen. Three disjoint rows on a full three-a-side screen, every other row overlapping, nothing
slower.

### Teeth: 25 tests, 11 mutants, 9 caught

Both survivors are the expected perf-only pair (`side` never taking the size path; `effectiveLabel`
never collapsing) — the pre-218 behaviour, correct and slower. **Every wrong-answer mutant is
caught**, including reading the wrong endpoint id, using the id path when the middle IS labelled,
collapsing a non-vacuous label, and inverting the vacuity test.

The dangerous case is `bucketSize`, because **one edge can carry SEVERAL labels** and so sit in
several type buckets — which is why `edgesOfTypes` keeps a `seen` set. Summing bucket sizes would
double-count it, so `bucketSize` reads a size only where exactly one bucket is in play and
otherwise counts through the deduping generator, still without resolving an endpoint.

**A mutant found the fixture blind anyway.** Reading only the FIRST bucket of a type disjunction
survived, because my multi-label fixture's single edge sat in BOTH buckets — so bucket `A` alone
happened to equal the deduped total. The distinguishing input needs the buckets to hold DIFFERENT
edges (`m` with one `:A` in-edge and one `:B` in-edge from different sources, giving 2 × 2 = 4
paths where a first-bucket read gives 1). That is the "two of the thing" shape
`mutants-find-fixture-blindness` describes, and it is now tested on both the product and the
filtered walk.

One test asserts the collapse is re-decided per execution: a label that is vacuous, then a vertex
without it is added, and the label must start filtering. A compile-time decision passes every other
test in the file and fails that one.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, re-run after the formatter, and
the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree at 9/11. 25 new tests (1477 in the gql
package), full suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

Two of my test spellings were wrong, not the engine: ISO's abbreviated `-->` does not parse here
(use `-[]->`), and `All` is a RESERVED word — the same trap `ts-spelling-probe` records for `Small`.

### Still open

- **`2-hop + MID filter` is 1385ns a path** (2231ms), by far the worst shape measured. A predicate
  on the MIDDLE is refused by the two-segment ladder on purpose — _"a predicate reading the middle
  or the end would have to be applied per expanded edge"_ — so it falls to the row pipeline. The
  degree product can carry it: iterate middles, gate once, then multiply. Not attempted here.
- **3-hop is 466ns a path** and has no tally at all; the ladder stops at two segments.
- The inline-start spelling is now 1.14x of the clause spelling (137.0 against 120.3) where before
  it was the faster of the two. Both well inside the spelling probe's tolerance, recorded so the
  next sweep knows it moved.

## 219. The easy case was being refused for the hard case's reason — 47.9x, and two spelling gaps close

Item 218 left `2-hop + MID filter` as the worst shape in the corpus: 2331.7ms, 1447ns a counted
path. The two-segment ladder admitted only a START-reading predicate, and said why:

> On a TWO-segment pattern only a START-reading predicate is admissible, because the walk gates a
> start vertex and then expands it — a predicate reading the middle or the end would have to be
> applied per expanded edge, which is the row pipeline this exists to avoid.

That is true of the start-driven walk. It is **false of the degree product**, which iterates
MIDDLES — so a middle-reading predicate is the CHEAPEST in the family, gated exactly once per
middle, where a start-reading one costs the product its start factor and forces the walk. The easy
case was refused for the hard case's reason, and the comment was accurate about the wrong shape.

### Four spellings, two gaps, one route

Before touching anything, every spelling of the same question — because fixing one and leaving
another slow is this engine's named bug class, and the measurement found it already open:

| spelling               |   before | after |           |
| ---------------------- | -------: | ----: | --------: |
| `WHERE b.age > 60`     | 2331.7ms |  52.5 | **44.4x** |
| `(b WHERE b.age > 60)` |   1183.1 |  52.9 |     22.4x |
| `WHERE b.age = 61`     |   1922.8 |  12.3 |  **156x** |
| `(b {age: 61})`        |    482.3 |   7.8 |     61.8x |

The first pair was **1.97x apart** and the second **3.99x apart**, answering identically
(1,610,950 and 55,550). Both gaps were live before this item. They now share one route: the clause
`WHERE` arrives through the ladder's gate, the three inline spellings through `inlineOf`, and both
land in the same `midPreds` list composed by the same `reduceRight` the node tally uses — so they
go through `inlineHolds` → `satisfies`, the general path's own implementation, rather than
re-deriving inline-pattern semantics.

`> 60` is now **1.01x** across its two spellings. The equality pair is 1.58x (7.8 against 12.3),
which is a property-equality predicate being cheaper to evaluate than a general comparison — inside
the probe's 2x tolerance, on a 4.5ms absolute difference, and recorded rather than claimed closed.

### The guard I relaxed, and why it is safe

`buildTwoHopCount` refused `!plainNode(s1.node)`, so an inline middle declined the shortcut
entirely. Carrying the constraint means relaxing that guard, which is the dangerous kind of edit:
a path that reaches the relaxed guard without carrying the constraint returns a WRONG COUNT.

Two things make it safe rather than merely tested. `midPreds` is a **required** parameter, not an
optional one, so "forgot to pass it" is a type error and not a silent miscount; and the function
has exactly one caller, which computes `midPreds` from `s1.node` itself. `s2.node` — the END —
keeps its guard, because the product reaches it only as a degree and a constraint there has no
once-per-element place to go.

### Measured

A bench row joins the corpus, **`count 2-hop + mid filter`**, which the three-run screen moves
**2280.3, 2416.0, 2422.6 → 45.7, 46.9, 47.6ms — 47.9x+, ranges disjoint.** Every other row
overlaps, with one exception: `traverse 1-hop project` came out 1.10x+ FASTER on disjoint ranges,
which this diff cannot do to a projecting traversal — the new row changed which neighbour warms it,
the effect `bench-sampling-traps` records. Faster either way, and named rather than banked.

Controls held: the START-filtered row is 112.9 → 113.2ms, the unfiltered product 104.5 → 82.6, a
middle LABEL alone 144.2 → 153.0.

### Teeth: 18 tests, 11 mutants, 10 caught

The single survivor is the expected perf-only one (a constant predicate declining instead of
keeping the start route). **Every wrong-answer mutant is caught**, including the three that attack
the relaxed guard directly: dropping the END guard as well, not carrying the inline constraint, and
not carrying the clause predicate.

What the tests had to pin beyond "the fast path agrees":

- the END predicate and a BOTH-ends predicate are still refused, and the tests assert their
  ANSWERS, because a route that half-applied one would be a wrong count rather than a slow query;
- a CORRELATED inline middle (`(b {age: a.age})`) must still decline — `inlineOf` refuses it, and
  carrying it instead is a mutant the suite catches;
- an ANONYMOUS middle (`({age: 61})`) has no `bindVar`, so `inlineHolds` must not need one;
- the gate runs BEFORE either degree is read, pinned by a middle that passes the gate and has
  out-degree 0, and by one with no in-edges;
- a constant `WHERE` keeps the start route it had before this item, which is a perf property and so
  only provable by the mutant surviving — stated as such rather than dressed up as a test.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command, re-run after the formatter, and
the mutation sweep re-run against the formatted tree at 10/11. 18 new tests (1495 in the gql
package), full suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

- **The END-filtered 2-hop is 2413.9ms**, untouched and now the worst shape in the corpus.
  `Σ_b indeg(b) · |out-edges of b whose target passes p|` is a correct formula and `side` already
  does a per-edge endpoint resolve for a LABEL, so the shape exists — but its second factor is a
  per-EDGE predicate evaluation, a different cost class from a once-per-middle gate, and it needs
  its own measurement rather than this item's reasoning.
- A start predicate COMBINED with an inline middle still declines both builders, as before.
- Three-or-more segments still have no tally (466ns a path).

## 220. The same question written backwards was already 20x faster — 19.5x, and no new walk

Item 219 left the END-filtered two-hop as the corpus's worst shape (2413.9ms) with a plan attached:
`Σ_b indeg(b) · |out-edges of b whose target passes p|`, whose second factor is a per-EDGE
predicate evaluation. That plan was not needed, and measuring first is why.

### The probe answered the question instead of pricing the plan

Counting `a-[r1]->b-[r2]->c` and counting `c<-[r2]-b<-[r1]-a` counts the same (edge, edge) pairs.
So the end-filtered question is the START-filtered question written backwards — and that one has
had a walk since item 206. Measured before writing anything, same question, same answer:

|                                     | broad (`> 60`) | selective (`= 61`) |
| ----------------------------------- | -------------: | -----------------: |
| `(a)-[:T]->(b)-[:T]->(c) WHERE c.…` |       2363.5ms |           2011.8ms |
| `(c)<-[:T]-(b)<-[:T]-(a) WHERE c.…` |      **118.1** |            **9.5** |
|                                     |      **20.0x** |         **211.8x** |

A **20x and a 212x spelling gap** between two readings of one query, both returning 1,610,950 and
55,550 respectively. The engine already had the fast answer; the planner just could not see that
the forward spelling was the same question.

So there is no new walk and no new formula in this item. `reversedTwoHop` flips the two legs'
directions and swaps which node is the start, and the existing `buildFilteredTwoHopCount` answers
it. A direction reads as "start -[e]-> node", so flipping is what turns `b -> c` into `c <- b`.

### Measured

| spelling               |   before | after |           |
| ---------------------- | -------: | ----: | --------: |
| `WHERE c.age > 60`     | 2363.5ms | 117.7 | **20.1x** |
| `(c WHERE c.age > 60)` |   1949.5 | 142.0 |     13.7x |
| `WHERE c.age = 61`     |   2011.8 |  12.7 |  **158x** |
| `(c {age: 61})`        |   1362.6 |  12.3 |  **111x** |

All four spellings go through one route, and the forward spelling now matches the hand-reversed one
(117.7 against 138.0) where it was 20x behind. A bench row joins the corpus,
**`count 2-hop + end filter`**, which the three-run screen moves **2255.6, 2274.3, 2284.6 → 106.4,
107.1, 115.5ms — 19.5x+, ranges disjoint.** Every other row overlaps, the `start filter` and
`mid filter` siblings included.

`cend` is plumbed through so the reversed walk can SEEK an index on the end property rather than
scanning its label bucket. `cfar` is `segments[0].node`, which is the MIDDLE when there are two
segments — not the end. Item 178 is both the precedent and the warning: wiring only one end left
"the far-anchored spelling of one question scanning the far label bucket while its start-anchored
twin seeked".

### Teeth: 32 tests, 13 mutants, 11 caught — and two of them took real work

**The direction flip is where the bugs live**, and a fixture of equal in- and out-degrees cannot
see them: a mis-flipped leg returns a number, and on a symmetric graph it returns the RIGHT number.
So the middle has in-degree 2 and out-degree 3, and all four direction combinations are exercised,
with a test asserting the four give DIFFERENT answers so that agreeing with the general path means
something.

Two survivors needed the fixture widened, and the second was a real bug:

- **"the reversed pattern starts from the MIDDLE"** survived twice. With all nodes NAMED, a variable
  collision makes the builder decline, so the mutant is harmless. With plain anonymous nodes the
  walk is _genuinely equivalent_, because only the start node's LABEL differs. The distinguishing
  input is a middle that is anonymous (no collision) AND labelled differently from the end
  (`(a)-[:T]->(:M)-[:T]->(c:C)`), where starting from `:M` gates the middles by the END's predicate
  and returns 0 instead of 7.
- **"an end-plus-other constraint falls through instead of declining"** was NOT defensive, which I
  had assumed. An INLINE start constraint plus a CLAUSE end predicate is a combination the `AND`
  spelling cannot produce (`WHERE a.x AND c.y` reads two variables and declines earlier). It falls
  through to the start-driven builder, whose `plainNode` checks both pass — because the end
  constraint is a clause, not inline — so it applies the start constraint and **silently drops the
  end predicate**. Removing that `return null` passed every other test in the file. The decline is
  load-bearing and now says so in the code.

The two remaining survivors ARE defensive, and the mutation is what establishes it rather than my
asserting it: with a start or middle constraint present, the reversed pattern places it where
`buildFilteredTwoHopCount`'s own `plainNode` guards reject it, so the route declines rather than
miscounting. The extra conditions are belt-and-braces over a guard that already holds.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command. Lint required two fixes: a
nested ternary in the direction flip (now a `Record` lookup) and `patternCountOf` hitting
complexity 40 against a cap of 35 — the two-segment routing is extracted as `twoSegmentCount`,
which is where the interesting part lives anyway, since all three shapes count the same thing and
differ only in which end they drive from. **The extraction moved every mutation anchor**, so the
sweep was re-run against the extracted code (11/13) rather than trusted from before it; the first
re-run reported ten `NOT APPLIED` and no teeth at all, which is exactly what a stale anchor looks
like. 32 new tests (1527 in the gql package), full suite exit 0, all seven fuzzers green.

### Still open

- An end constraint COMBINED with a start or middle one declines, as before.
- Three-or-more segments still have no tally (466ns a path), and now stand out: all three
  two-segment positions are answered and the ladder simply stops at two.
- The inline end spelling is 142.0 against the clause's 117.7 (1.21x) — both on the fast route,
  inside the spelling probe's tolerance, recorded because it moved.

## 221. The interior of a three-hop count is an EDGE, not a vertex — 26.9x off the slowest shape in the corpus

Item 220 finished the two-segment family — all three positions answered — and left the ladder
stopping at two segments. That was not a small gap: **the unfiltered three-hop count was 13.2
SECONDS**, 529ns a counted path, against the two-segment tally's 21.

### The formula was checkable before any code existed

The two-segment product iterates the middle VERTEX and multiplies the degrees either side of it.
One position along, the interior is an EDGE:

    paths a→b→c→d  =  Σ over middle edges (b → c) of indeg(b) · outdeg(c)

On the bench fixture that is 1,000,000 edges × 5 × 5 = **25,000,000**, which is exactly what the row
pipeline returned in 13.2 seconds. Checking the closed form against the engine's own answer first
is what makes the tally sound rather than plausible — the same step item 218 used.

Driven from the `b` VERTEX rather than a global edge list, because no such list exists: the
adjacency index is per vertex. `indeg(b)` then hoists out of the inner loop, so it is one lookup
per vertex plus one per middle edge rather than two per edge, and a zero there prunes the whole
inner loop.

### Measured

|                            |    before |     after |       |
| -------------------------- | --------: | --------: | ----: |
| 3-hop unfiltered           | 13226.2ms | **431.3** | 30.7x |
| 3-hop, vacuous start label |   10315.5 |     389.4 | 26.5x |
| ns a counted path          |       529 |    **17** |       |

17ns a path is the two-segment tally's own rate (21), which is the sign the shape is now paying per
INTERIOR EDGE and not per path. A bench row joins the corpus, **`count 3-hop`**, which the
three-run screen moves **10644.8, 10762.9, 10918.6 → 384.6, 392.9, 394.9ms — 26.9x+, ranges
disjoint.**

One neighbour, `count 2-hop + end filter`, came out 1.06x+ faster on disjoint ranges. That is the
documented warming effect of a row dropping from 10.7s to 0.39s next to it (`bench-sampling-traps`),
not something this diff does to an end-filtered two-hop. Faster either way, and named.

### A regression that was not one

Two rows that DECLINE the new path moved the wrong way on the first probe: the start-filtered
three-hop 3622 → 4326ms (1.19x) and its selective sibling 136.2 → 194.4 (1.43x). That is the
`ts-closure-size-is-load-bearing` signature and would have been its fifth occurrence, so it was
settled in-process over nine alternating reps rather than argued about:

    before [136.5, 136.7, 139.4, 139.7, 139.8, 142.1, 185.5, 190.8, 243.3]
    after  [137.7, 138.0, 138.2, 138.6, 139.9, 140.0, 154.8, 201.2, 253.0]

**0.99x.** Both sides carry the same long tail; the two-rep probe had simply drawn it on one side.
Every control flat (0.94-1.01x), and the target confirmed at 26.98x in the same process. The lesson
is the familiar one with a new edge: a shape whose own distribution spans 136 to 243ms cannot be
screened at two reps, and the apparent 1.43x was entirely in that spread.

### Teeth: 44 tests, 18 mutants, 16 caught

**The three direction flags are the risk surface** (`toAOut`, `fromDOut`, `midOut`), and a fixture
with equal in- and out-degrees cannot see a mis-read one, because the wrong factor is the same
number. So the interior is lopsided — `indeg(b) = 2` against `outdeg(c) = 3` — all eight direction
combinations are exercised, and a test asserts the eight do not all agree so that matching the
general path means something.

Two survivors were real fixture gaps, and both are the same shape of blindness — _a fixture where
two things that should differ happen to coincide_:

- **"the two end legs read each other's types"** survived because every leg used type `:T`, making
  `t1` and `t3` interchangeable. The distinguishing fixture gives the three legs distinct types
  with UNEQUAL counts, plus decoy edges of the wrong type at each end so a mutant finds something
  rather than zero.
- **"the `b` label is not checked"** survived because `candidateVertexSource` already seeds from the
  label bucket for a SIMPLE label, making the per-vertex re-check redundant. It is load-bearing
  only for a label EXPRESSION, which falls back to the whole graph — so the test uses `:Q|R`,
  `:!Q`, `:Q&R`, and asserts that a label and its negation PARTITION the count with both halves
  non-zero.

The two remaining survivors are the ladder's inline checks on the three segment nodes, which
mutation says are redundant with `buildThreeHopCount`'s own `plainNode` guards. **They stay, and
the reason is recorded in the code**: item 219 relaxed exactly such a guard one position over (the
two-hop product now accepts a constrained middle), so the inner guard is not a fixed property to
lean on. The START check is the load-bearing one and is caught — `inStart` is computed only for one
and two segments, so reading it here would have let `MATCH (a {k: 1})-[:T]->…` through un-applied.
I found that one by reading my own guard rather than from a mutant, which is the cheaper order.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command. Typecheck caught two `unknown`
reads where a test did arithmetic on a projected value, lint wanted a blank line, and **the
formatter reflowed one mutation anchor**, which the sweep reported as `NOT APPLIED` rather than
passing silently — re-run at 16/18 against the formatted tree. 44 new tests (1571 in the gql
package), full suite exit 0, all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

Three of my test spellings were reserved words, not engine bugs: `All`, and then `IN` / `OUT` as
edge types. That is the third time this session, so the rule is now explicit — **invent obviously
non-word names for test labels and types** (`Univ`, `LEGA`, `LEGM`, `LEGZ`), because the reserved
list is long and the failure reads as a parse error in a test that looks fine.

- Four or more segments still fall to the row pipeline. The interior generalises — for N segments

## 222. Gate the positions the walk already visits — 62.0x, and four more spelling gaps close

Item 221 gave three-segment counts a degree product and left all four filtered positions on the
row pipeline. Two of them are nearly free, and which two follows from the walk's shape rather than
from measurement: it ITERATES `b` (so a constraint there is gated once per VERTEX, before either
degree is read) and meets `c` as each middle edge's far end (gated once per MIDDLE EDGE). The `a`
and `d` ends are reached only as DEGREES and have no once-per-element place to go. That is item
219's reasoning one segment along.

### Four live spelling gaps, found by measuring first

|              |   clause |   inline |       gap |
| ------------ | -------: | -------: | --------: |
| `b.age > 60` | 9360.5ms | 3945.9ms | **2.37x** |
| `b.age = 61` |   7432.7 |    560.7 | **13.3x** |
| `c.age > 60` |   9460.7 |   4557.9 | **2.08x** |
| `c.age = 61` |   7705.2 |   1502.5 | **5.13x** |

All eight spellings answered identically (8,054,750 and 277,750) while costing up to 13.3x apart.
Three items running, measuring every spelling before building has found a gap already in the open —
it is the cheapest step in the method and the one most likely to change what gets built.

### After

|              |    clause | inline |   gap |
| ------------ | --------: | -----: | ----: |
| `b.age > 60` | **167.4** |  167.4 | 1.00x |
| `b.age = 61` |  **17.1** |   18.0 | 1.05x |
| `c.age > 60` | **550.1** |  562.5 | 1.02x |
| `c.age = 61` | **482.7** |  454.3 | 1.06x |

**55.9x, 435x, 17.2x and 16.0x** on the clause spellings, and every gap inside 6%. The clause form
arrives through the ladder's gate and the three inline forms through `inlineOf`; both land in the
same per-position list, composed by the same `reduceRight` the node tally uses, so they run
`inlineHolds` → `satisfies` — the general path's own implementation — rather than re-deriving
inline-pattern semantics.

`b` ends up far cheaper than `c` (167 against 550) because gating `b` prunes before the inner edge
loop while gating `c` runs per middle edge. Those are different questions, so that is a cost
difference and not a gap.

A bench row joins the corpus, **`count 3-hop + interior filter`**, which the three-run screen moves
**8750.9, 8916.1, 9102.8 → 134.2, 137.6, 141.1ms — 62.0x+, ranges disjoint.** Every other row
overlaps.

### Teeth: 26 tests, 18 mutants + 1 double, 16 caught

The subtle correctness point is that **`c` is gated per middle EDGE, and must still contribute once
for each**. A `c` reached from two different middles counts twice — `Σ over middle edges` — so a
gate that deduped it would silently undercount. The fixture has exactly that vertex and the test
asserts 6 rather than the 4 deduping would give.

Also pinned: the `b` gate runs BEFORE the degrees (a middle that passes the gate but has no `a`
side contributes nothing); a clause predicate on an ANONYMOUS interior node is refused rather than
misapplied, since it has no variable to bind, while the inline spelling works there because
`inlineOf` needs none; and `bindVar` is load-bearing — dropping it evaluates the predicate against
an empty binding, which a mutant confirms.

**The two survivors are mutually redundant, and a DOUBLE mutant proves the pair protects
something.** The ladder's `inlineOf(s3.node)` check and `buildThreeHopCount`'s own
`plainNode(s3.node)` both refuse an END constraint, so removing either alone changes nothing —
whichever goes, the other still declines. Single mutation cannot distinguish "redundant guard" from
"guard nothing needs", so the sweep now also removes BOTH at once, which **is caught**. That is the
difference between asserting a guard is defensive and showing it.

## 223. A 48.7x that must not be taken — the end-filtered multi-hop reversal, retracted

Item 222 left the three-hop count's two END positions on the row pipeline: `a` 4417.9ms, `d`
9327.3ms, the largest absolute times in the engine. **No code changed this item.** What follows is
why, with the numbers, because a 48.7x sitting in a probe is exactly the thing a later sweep would
re-derive and chase.

### The number is real

Reversing an end-filtered pattern by hand, same question and same answer:

|                                          |  forward | hand-reversed |           |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------: | ------------: | --------: |
| 3-hop `count(*)`, `d.age = 61`           | 7247.5ms |     **148.8** | **48.7x** |
| 3-hop `count(*)`, `a.age = 61` (control) |    140.3 |             — |           |
| 2-hop `count(b.age)`, `c.age = 61`       |   1923.6 |      **52.3** | **36.8x** |
| 3-hop `count(*)`, `d.age > 60`           |   9878.4 |        3743.9 |     2.64x |

The reversed time landing on the start-filtered control (148.8 against 140.3) is the tell: reversing
makes an end-filtered question cost what the equivalent start-filtered one costs. And it is the
GENERAL path, not a shortcut — `count(b.age)` is an aggregate over a projected value, so no count
tally applies to either spelling.

### Why TS may not take it

`orient` already handles multi-segment patterns and reads the end node, so this is not a missing
case; it is a DECLINED one. Its final test is `endEst.count < startEst.count`, and with both ends
unlabelled both estimates are the whole graph, so it ties and stays put.

**Native declines the same reversal deliberately, and has already measured the downside.** From
`orient_declines_an_unlabelled_far_node` in `crates/lenke-engine/src/opt/tests.rs`:

> An UNLABELLED far node does not reverse, even though the predicate is seekable. … Measured, it
> trades on selectivity and can lose badly: `b.age > 98` (1% pass) went 1652us -> 669us, but
> `b.age > -1` (100% pass) went 788us -> 3805us. Fire only on a provable win; the speculative case
> needs a cardinality estimate.

Native fires only when `seed_fraction_of` proves selectivity from an INDEX, or when a label lifts
onto the seed (`orient_is_worth_it`). So my 48.7x is the 1%-pass end of exactly the trade native
priced — and a 100%-pass predicate on the same shape would pay ~4.8x for the same rewrite.

That settles it twice over. The engine cannot tell the two apart without a cardinality estimate for
an unindexed predicate, and **byte-identity forbids TS reversing where native does not** — this
would be a two-engine planner change, not a TS one, and the loop's own rule is to fire only on a
provable win.

### The hypothesis I formed, and its refutation

I expected a narrower, TS-local gap. `estimateSeedFrom` reads a node's OWN constraints through
`indexCandidates`, so an INLINE end constraint should produce a small estimate and reverse, while a
CLAUSE `WHERE` — never lifted onto the end node for a multi-segment pattern — should stay invisible.
Native reads the clause predicate straight off the Filter (`reverse_slots(pred, far)`), so it would
orient on either spelling, and the clause form would be a TS-only loss.

**It does not reproduce.** With a hash index on `age`:

|                             | unindexed |  indexed |
| --------------------------- | --------: | -------: |
| `c` CLAUSE `= 61`           |  1963.5ms | **36.6** |
| `c` INLINE `= 61`           |    1375.1 |     32.8 |
| `a` CLAUSE `= 61` (control) |      59.2 |     36.7 |
| `a` INLINE `= 61` (control) |      51.9 |     32.4 |

All four land at 32-37ms, a **53.6x** improvement on the clause spelling, and the clause-vs-inline
gap is 1.12x. The clause predicate IS visible to the seek-and-orient machinery when an index exists
— `collectHints` lifts seekable conjuncts as seed hints, which is the path I had forgotten. There is
no TS-side spelling gap here, indexed or not.

### What this is actually worth knowing

**The remedy for the nine-second query is an index, and it already works.** 1963.5 → 36.6ms on the
clause spelling with one `createIndex({on: 'vertex', kind: 'hash', keys: ['age']})`. That is a
discoverability finding rather than an engine one, and it belongs in the perf guidance: a multi-hop
pattern filtered at its FAR end pays the whole expansion unless the filtered property is indexed,
at which point both engines seed and orient from that end.

The unindexed case stays slow ON PURPOSE in both engines, and the next sweep should read this entry
before re-deriving the 48.7x.

### Gates

No engine code changed, so there is nothing a bench screen could move and none was run — the same
position item 214 took. `typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command; full
suite exit 0 (1597 tests); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

One thing I did NOT do and will not claim: I did not independently time NATIVE on the unindexed
shape. The decline is established from native's own test and its recorded measurement, which is
documentation of a deliberate decision rather than a fresh observation.

### Still open

- Four or more segments still have no tally.
- The three-hop END positions remain on the row pipeline, and that is now a recorded WON'T-FIX for
  the unindexed case rather than an open target.
- A cardinality estimate for an unindexed predicate would unlock it in both engines. `cost.rs`
  exists on the native side; nothing equivalent prices a predicate's selectivity in TS.

## 224. The inline `WHERE` paid for a binding it did not need — and a harness bug that faked a result

Seven planner items this session, and not one of them had been added to the spelling probe, which
the repo's own rule requires. Running it first was the right move twice over: it reported **0 groups
disagreeing on the ANSWER** (no divergence introduced) and it pointed at a systematic gap none of
those items created.

### The probe found one cause behind three groups

| group               | inline prop | clause | **inline `WHERE`** |
| ------------------- | ----------: | -----: | -----------------: |
| node count          |      3.82ms |   5.80 |           **8.51** |
| hop, FAR filtered   |        5.61 |   6.94 |           **7.52** |
| hop, START filtered |        5.09 |   6.58 |           **7.02** |

`(n:P WHERE n.k = 2)` is the slowest spelling in all three, at 2.2x the inline-property form of the
same predicate. Read from the code rather than guessed: an inline PROPERTY compiles to
`structuralEq(propOf(element, key), …)`, a direct read, while an inline `WHERE` compiles to the
generic expression evaluator, which reads its element back out of the BINDING — a `Map.set` by the
caller plus a `Map.get` per property read, to hand over an element `satisfies` already holds. That is
**item 216's finding in a second place**: 8.51 − 3.82 over 200,000 vertices is ~23ns a vertex, the
same figure item 216 measured for the same round trip.

`directEqProps` recognises an inline `WHERE` that is exactly one `<own>.<key> = <non-null literal>`
and compiles it as a property-style check, reusing the existing comparison semantics rather than
reimplementing them.

### Three restrictions, each forced rather than cautious

- **`=` only.** For `=`, a nullish property gives UNKNOWN through `compare` and `false` through
  `structuralEq` — the same outcome. For `<>` they DIVERGE: `compare` still yields UNKNOWN (the row
  is rejected) where a negated structural check yields `true`. Verified: `(n WHERE n.k <> 2)` is 1
  on the fixture, and would be 3 if widened.
- **A non-null literal.** `{k: null}` matches a stored null AND an absent key while `n.k = null`
  matches neither, so a null value makes the two forms different questions.
- **One comparison, never an AND-chain.** `AND` does not short-circuit here, by design and for
  byte-identity. Verified: `n.k = 999 AND CAST(n.s AS INTEGER) > 0` RAISES even though the first
  conjunct matches nothing — hoisting it would let `satisfies` reject the element first and swallow
  the raise.

**Kept out of `props` deliberately.** `indexCandidates` reads `pred.props` to decide seeding, so
merging there would change which vertices seed FIRST — an observable row-order change whose
byte-identity against native cannot be checked here, because the fuzzers canonicalise unordered row
order. A separate `eqProps` list gets the evaluation win and changes no seeding.

### Measured

No bench row writes an inline `WHERE` — the corpus uses inline properties and clause `WHERE`s — so
**the screen cannot show this change and the in-process A/B is the measurement of record.** Answers
identical on all ten cases, nine alternating reps a side:

|                                              | before | after |           |
| -------------------------------------------- | -----: | ----: | --------: |
| node count, inline `WHERE`                   | 7.31ms |  4.80 | **1.52x** |
| mirrored `2 = n.k`                           |   8.42 |  5.02 | **1.68x** |
| hop FAR, inline `WHERE`                      |  18.26 | 14.33 |     1.27x |
| hop START, inline `WHERE`                    |  17.86 | 14.17 |     1.26x |
| inline property (reference)                  |   4.59 |  4.60 |      flat |
| `<>` / param / AND-chain / clause (controls) |        |       |  all flat |

The inline `WHERE` now sits at 4.80 against the inline-property reference's 4.60 — 1.04x. The probe
previously flagged one or two groups depending on the run (`node count`, `hop START`, and the item-204
projection all appeared); it now flags exactly one on three consecutive runs: **`a filtered node
projection: inline vs clause WHERE (item 204)` at 2.2x**, which has no inline-`WHERE` member and is
the clause-vs-inline-property gap blocked on the inline-null question. The screen moved two rows
with disjoint ranges, both ~1-2% (`traverse 1-hop + filter` 1.01x slower, `count 2-hop + start
filter` 1.02x faster) on rows this diff cannot reach — below the ~10% this repo can resolve without
an isolated harness, and recorded rather than claimed.

### A harness bug that produced a false result, and then 14 failures

Adding a cross-file double mutant, I replaced the sweep's tail — and removed the
`TARGET.write_text(pristine)` that restored the file before it. So the double read the LAST mutant's
file as its "original" and restored to that afterwards, **leaving mutant 11 applied in the tree**.
Two consequences, both of which I initially mis-read:

1. The double mutant reported `caught (14 failing)` and I believed it. It was detecting mutant 11
   still in the tree. With a correct restore the double **SURVIVES**.
2. The next full run came back 14 failing with a red fuzzer, which looked like the change breaking
   byte-identity and was a mutant left in the source.

CLAUDE.md states the rule this broke — _restore before applying the next mutant, never only after
the loop_ — and the lesson generalises: **a "caught" verdict is only evidence if the tree was clean
when the mutant was applied.** A sweep that reports teeth while leaving a mutant behind reports them
for the wrong reason.

Once fixed, the double genuinely survived, which exposed a real coverage gap: `(y WHERE x.k = 2)` —
an inline `WHERE` reading the OTHER variable — is valid GQL and was in none of my tests. With it
written down (`x.k` is 2, `y.k` is 9, so a mis-targeted check answers 0 instead of 1) the double is
caught for the right reason.

### Teeth: 21 tests, 11 mutants + 1 double, 6 caught

Every wrong-answer mutant is caught: any operator accepted, a null literal accepted, the check never
evaluated, the wrong key, comparing the prop side to itself, the verdict inverted. The five
survivors are accounted for, and one of them corrected me:

**I justified excluding params with the null-param semantics. That is not why the code excludes
them.** Accepting params survives the whole suite, and a trace shows `directEqProps` is never
called for `(n WHERE n.k = $p)` at all: `inlineOf` refuses an inline `WHERE` containing a param
first, because `freePredicateVars` reports `$p` as a free name that is not the node's variable. The
semantic difference is real; it is not the mechanism. Comment corrected — the same class of error as
items 208, 210 and 213, found this time by a surviving mutant rather than by re-reading.

### Gates

`typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each exit 0 as their own command (lint required an if/else in
place of a nested ternary). 21 new tests (1618 in the gql package), full suite exit 0, all seven
byte-identity fuzzers green, mutation re-run against the formatted tree.

### Still open

- The item-204 projection group's 2.2x, which is clause-vs-inline-property and blocked on the
  inline-null question recorded in the audit.
- The probe still has no groups for the shapes items 219-222 added (the 2-hop and 3-hop position
  filters). Those four families were each verified by a dedicated probe at the time, but the
  standing instrument does not guard them.

## 225. Four fixes that nothing was guarding — the multi-segment families join the spelling probe

Item 224's last open note: the probe had no groups for the shapes items 219-222 added. Each of
those four families was verified by a throwaway probe at the time and then left unguarded by the
standing instrument. **No engine code changes here.** This is the regression guard the four fixes
should have shipped with.

### Why these four and not speculative coverage

Every one of them was a LIVE gap before the item that closed it, which is the argument for guarding
them rather than trusting them:

| item | the question               | before                                                                           |
| ---- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 219  | 2-hop, middle filtered     | clause 2331.7ms / inline `WHERE` 1183.1 / inline prop 482.3 — **2.4x and 13.3x** |
| 220  | 2-hop, end filtered        | forward 2363.5 against the hand-reversed spelling's 118.1 — **20.0x**            |
| 221  | 3-hop, vacuous start label | the label cost an endpoint resolve per edge                                      |
| 222  | 3-hop, interior filtered   | clause 9360.5 / inline `WHERE` 3945.9 / inline prop 560.7 — **2.4x and 13.3x**   |

### What the groups read now

| group                       | members                     | spread |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------- | -----: |
| 2-hop MIDDLE filtered       | 8.45 / 9.59 / 10.13ms       |  1.20x |
| 2-hop END + reversed arrows | 9.50 / 9.54 / 11.31 / 12.35 |  1.30x |
| 3-hop SECOND position       | 12.31 / 13.39 / 13.52       |  1.10x |
| 3-hop THIRD position        | 223.74 / 226.05 / 237.01    |  1.06x |
| 3-hop vacuous start label   | 218.04 / 219.50             |  1.01x |

**0 groups disagree on the ANSWER**, which is the check that also proves the spellings I wrote are
genuinely equivalent rather than merely similar — the probe would have reported a disagreement
first, and for new groups that is the more valuable of its two signals.

The reversed-arrow member is the fastest of the END group (9.50 against the forward clause
spelling's 9.54), so item 220's planner reversal is still firing. It is the member that matters
most in that group: item 220's whole finding was a 20x gap between a question and the same question
written backwards, and a reversal that stops firing is invisible to every other spelling.

The two three-hop groups differ from each other by ~18x (12-13ms against 224-237). That is expected
and not a gap: the second position is gated once per VERTEX and the third once per MIDDLE EDGE, so
they are different questions. Keeping them as two groups rather than one is what lets the probe
compare only what should be equal.

### What is deliberately excluded

**The 3-hop END-filtered question.** Item 223 established that it stays on the row pipeline on
purpose in both engines — reversing it is a selectivity gamble native priced and declined — so it
runs ~9s on this fixture. A group whose slowest member takes seconds would make a probe nobody can
afford to run, and the probe's value is that it is cheap enough to run on every planner change. The
exclusion is recorded here so a later reader does not mistake it for an oversight.

### Cost

The probe gains roughly 16 seconds at `SPELL_N=200000`, nearly all of it the two three-hop groups.
That is a real cost on an instrument meant to be run often, and it buys regression cover for four
fixes whose combined measured win was 20-435x. Worth stating rather than hiding: if the probe ever
becomes too slow to run routinely it stops being used, which is the failure mode that let these
four families go unguarded in the first place.

### Gates

No engine code changed, so there is nothing a bench screen could move and none was run — the
position items 214 and 223 took. Mutation does not apply either: there is no engine branch to
mutate, and mutating the probe would only test the probe. `typecheck` / `lint` / `fmt:check` each
exit 0 as their own command; full suite exit 0 (1618 tests); all seven byte-identity fuzzers green.

Across three probe invocations: **0 answer disagreements every time, and none of the five new groups
flagged in any of them.** The over-2x count read 1, 0, 0 — the item-204 projection group sits right
on the 2x boundary and flags intermittently, which is the behaviour this file already records for a
group near the threshold (the absolute spreads are inflated by running twenty-odd queries in one
process). Stated as 1/0/0 rather than as "clean", because rounding that to clean is how a
